title: 3 Three Approaches to Causal Inference
text: The Elaborate Theories approach has alternatively been referred to as “pattern matching” (Reichardt, 2019; Trochim, 1985, 1989). Expressed by Shadish et al. (2002; quoted in Reichardt, 2019): “The more complex pattern that is successfully predicted, the less likely it is that alternative explanations could generate the same pattern, and so the more likely it is that the treatment had a real effect”.↩︎
crumbs: 3  3 Three Approaches to Causal Inference

title: 4 Attributes of CLS’s Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference
text:
4.1 Breadth and Depth
Our thesis in this document is that the richness of the data in CLS’s cohort studies can support researchers in making causal inferences. In this section, we highlight several features of these data that are especially useful – specifically, the breadth and depth of the data, the ability to perform data linkage, the longitudinal nature of the studies, the extended timespan they collectively comprise, their large sample sizes, and their capacity for harmonisation with other cohort studies.
Collectively, CLS’s cohort studies include several tens of thousands of variables available by standard “Safeguard data” End User Licence on the UK Data Service. These variables are largely derived from survey questionnaires – the ability to link with other data increases this number dramatically. Combined, these data represent a profound insight into participants, their lives and the milieus in which they are situated. Data collections span birth (or, in the case of Next Steps, adolescence) to the current day. Within a survey sweep, data are collected on a range of participant characteristics – for instance, batteries of questions on mental and physical health, psychosocial development, socioeconomic circumstances and the home environment. This includes frequently analysed factors, such as employment status, but also relatively niche information, such as participants’ use of suncream, which was asked at the Age 42/44 year Biomedical Sweep of the NCDS. (In Section 5, we will argue that seemingly unimportant information like this can be used to support causal inference – for instance, as falsification tests.) The range of data available also makes assumptions of no unobserved confounding (in standard regression) or missingness at random (in multiple imputation) more plausible (Mostafa et al., 2021). Extensive data are also available on cohort members’ parents, partners, children and siblings. This can enable several causally informed research designs, such as sibling comparison and parental comparison designs and within-family-based Mendelian Randomisation.
crumbs: 4  4 Attributes of CLS's Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference

title: 4 Attributes of CLS’s Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference
text:
4.2 Extensive Data Linkages
Data linkage only increases the size and variety of information available, mechanistically increasing the possibilities for causal inference (e.g., increasing sample representativeness; Rajah et al., 2023). Nevertheless, some data linkages represent opportunities that are specific to the type of data being linked. Some of this data linkage may be qualitative and contextual; for instance, linkages that are possible from knowing significant dates (e.g., interview dates or dates of birth). Fitzsimons & Vera-Hernández (2022) use information on whether MCS participants were born at the weekend as an instrument for maternal breastfeeding (due to lower staffing on maternity wards, new mothers are less likely to be offered breastfeeding support on weekends). Other examples of this contextual linkage include the effects of news and current events on mental health and other outcomes using interview date as a determinant of exposure to the information (Muñoz et al., 2020).
CLS’s cohorts are increasingly linked to administrative and geographical data and each cohort has also now been genotyped, allowing for genetic data to be linked with survey responses. Administrative data and geographic linkages provide many opportunities for utilising quasi-experiments – events or episodes in which exposures are allocated as-if randomly. For instance, studies exploiting arbitrary thresholds that are used to decide eligibility for programmes or interventions (e.g., thresholds for determining low birth weight, grading schemes in education that determine a pass or a fail, or geographic boundaries that determine the government policies one is subject to). Genetic data enable a specific form of instrumental variable analysis – Mendelian Randomisation – that exploits random assortment of parental genes during meiosis.
crumbs: 4  4 Attributes of CLS's Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference

title: 4 Attributes of CLS’s Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference
text:
4.3 Longitudinal Assessment
The longitudinal nature of the studies means that the same or similar measures are asked across time. For instance, in the MCS, there are questions on several dimensions of mental health asked across childhood to late adolescence and now into early adulthood. Longitudinal data have four properties that aid causal inference. First, prospective data collection and repetition can enable more accurate measurement of study variables. Second, longitudinal assessment allows researchers to specify the correct temporal ordering (causes should precede consequences) with variables measured at different sweeps. Third, repeated measurement allows researchers to control for prior exposures and outcomes. Controlling for prior exposure allows for the ‘treatment’ to be more specifically defined (e.g., unemployment at age 33y among those who have not yet been unemployed), and controlling for prior exposure and/or outcomes can absorb some of the confounding bias that may otherwise exist as well as account for reverse causality processes (VanderWeele et al., 2020). Fourth, one can use within-person variation, rather than rely solely on between-person differences. Using within-person variation enables researchers to, e.g., account for time-invariant confounding factors by design, rather than through statistical control (Section 5.5).
crumbs: 4  4 Attributes of CLS's Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference

title: 4 Attributes of CLS’s Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference
text:
4.4 Extended Timespan
Mainstage data collections in CLS’s cohorts collectively span the 68 years from 1958 to the present day. This period can be increased when combined with other cohort studies, such as the National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD; the 1946 British Birth Cohort Study; Kuh et al., 2011). Several profound societal-level changes have occurred over this period, including the obesity epidemic, the expansion of further and higher education, and the greater participation of women in the labour market (Anders & Dorsett, 2017; Erikson & Goldthorpe, 2010; Gondek, Bann, Patalay, et al., 2021; Johnson et al., 2015). As will be expanded upon in Section 5, these societal-level changes offer several opportunities for causal inference. Briefly: confounding structures for some exposure-outcome relationships may have changed across time or causal effects may be confined to some periods or may vary across time in predictable ways (e.g., stronger in some periods rather than others). Elucidating each of these possibilities is one way in which theories can be made elaborate and causal arguments can be developed.
crumbs: 4  4 Attributes of CLS's Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference

title: 4 Attributes of CLS’s Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference
text:
4.5 Large Sample Sizes
The large sample size of CLS’s cohorts is important in its own right for precise statistical estimation – some causal inference methods, such as instrumental variables, are power hungry – but it also means that important subgroups can be identified. For instance, where an exposure is confined to a local geographic area (e.g., the London smog), a large overall sample size can mean sufficient numbers appear in the exposed group. There may also be circumstances where a research design is more plausible within a subgroup; for instance, Rosenbaum (2020) argues that a frequently used instrumental variable, time to nearest hospital, can be made more plausible by focusing on individuals outside large cities who have less choice over the hospital they use. Further, some subgroups possess particular properties that make them useful for analyses. This includes groups that are frequently used in family-based designs. Each of CLS’s cohorts contains a number of twins and data are sometimes collected from other (older or younger) siblings, too; for instance, MCS contains two sweeps of information from an older sibling. NCDS also contains a number of adopted children – again, useful in particular family-based study designs. Some of these subgroups may be small, but as the next section notes, CLS’s cohorts may be harmonised and analysed alongside other cohort data, so the subgroups within CLS’s cohorts can contribute to a larger analytic sample.
crumbs: 4  4 Attributes of CLS's Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference

title: 4 Attributes of CLS’s Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference
text:
4.6 Ability to Harmonise Data
Harmonising data with other cohorts can expand the time span of studies or the geographic area covered. This again enables studies that test elaborate theories: confounding structures may differ across space as well as time, and causal effects may be present, weaker or stronger in some areas than others. For instance, Brion et al. (2011) use a UK and Brazilian cohort to assess the effect of breastfeeding on development – the (confounding) association between SEP and breastfeeding is strong in the UK, but not in Brazil. Various efforts have been made to collate and harmonise data across different cohorts.
CLOSER (2023) has released several projects harmonising data from CLS’s cohorts on, among other things, socioeconomic status (see also Centre for Longitudinal Studies, 2026). Also useful are the Atlas of Longitudinal Datasets (2024) and the Catalogue of Mental Health Measures (2026), whose names are self-explanatory, and Harmony (2023), an online tool that uses natural language processing to identify survey items that are similar semantically across different studies (including non-CLS studies).
crumbs: 4  4 Attributes of CLS's Cohort Studies That Support Causal Inference

title: 5 The Methods of Causal Inference
text:
In this section, we list individual methods that can, when assumptions are met, either directly help estimate causal effects with CLS’s cohort data, or strengthen any causal inferences made. Generally, we focus on methods that account for confounding, though methods to account for measurement error or selection bias are also discussed. This section is something of a gallimaufry: some of these methods relate to statistical estimators (e.g., multivariable regression; Section 5.1), others to identification strategies (e.g., instrumental variables; Section 5.9), and others to falsification tests (e.g., negative controls; Section 5.15). As with the ‘Three Approaches to Causal Inference’ described in Section 3, the individual methods are not mutually exclusive, and a single study may use a mix of them (e.g., multiple imputation to address missing data, with statistical control to meet the assumptions behind instrumental variables analysis).
For each method, we provide three pieces of information: Method, Applications, and Opportunities. Method provides a brief overview of the method, its strengths and limitations, with references for further reading. The focus is on intuition, rather than the statistical and algorithmic nuts and bolts. Applications gives examples of papers using the method with CLS data. We focus on particularly well-executed studies or examples that demonstrate issues that can arise. For other examples, please search the CLS Bibliography website. Opportunities discusses general research ideas that could utilise the method in question with CLS data. Readers interested in learning more about these methods are invited to read textbooks by Huntington-Klein (2022, 2026), Cunningham (2021), Fox et al. (2021), Rosenbaum (2019, 2020), Hernán and Robins (2023), and van Buuren (2018). Some of the examples and explanatory material in this section are derived from these textbooks.

title: 5.1 Control via Regression Adjustment
text:
5.1.1 Method
The most common method for accounting for confounding bias is by taking a model-based approach and controlling for confounders or other nuisance factors via regression adjustment – for example, by adding covariates to an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression model. The data-generating process is modelled mathematically, with elements of the model (e.g., regression coefficients) learned from the data itself (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983). Statistical adjustment models the effect of relevant differences between treatment and comparison groups to block backdoor or other nuisance paths between exposure and outcomes, isolating variation in the exposure and outcome unrelated to these (observed) confounders.
This description is not just poetically true but reflects the underlying mechanics. The Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem demonstrates that the coefficient obtained by multivariable regression of an outcome upon an exposure plus covariates is equivalent to (1) obtaining residuals from regressions of (a) the exposure on covariates and (b) the outcome on covariates and then (2) regressing the residuals from (b) upon (a). In other words, statistical control winnows, and then utilises, residual variation. Readers can confirm this in R or Stata using the below code.
# Stata Code
sysuse auto, clear
regress price mpg length foreign // full model
regress mpg length foreign
predict mpg_resid, residuals
regress price length foreign
predict price_resid, residuals
regress price_resid mpg_resid
# R Code
data(iris)
lm(Sepal.Length ~ Sepal.Width + Petal.Length + Species, iris) # full model
width_mod <- lm(Sepal.Width ~ Petal.Length + Species, iris)
length_mod <- lm(Sepal.Length ~ Petal.Length + Species, iris)
lm(residuals(length_mod) ~ residuals(width_mod))
Statistical control is an example of a ‘non-equivalent groups design’: the analyst starts with groups expected to differ systematically but attempts to model the effect of these differences on the outcome in order to remove them. Nick Huntington-Klein (2022, p. 469) evocatively likens methods like this to creating a statue by taking a large block of marble and chipping away until the desired form is revealed underneath. Where successful – i.e., using a suitably accurate model, possibly reflecting an appropriate DAG – a valid causal estimate can be obtained. However, validity cannot be ascertained directly. Unlike a sculptor, the data analyst cannot say whether the finished product looks quite right. They do not know if they are left with Michelangelo’s David or Emanuel Santos’ bust of Cristiano Ronaldo.
Not including a sufficient adjustment set in the statistical model leaves open backdoor or other biasing paths between exposure and outcome variables and will generate a biased estimate of the causal effect. The size of the bias will equal the (aggregate) strength of the biasing paths. For confounding paths, it will reflect the strength of the associations between the confounders and the exposure and between the confounders and the outcome. Adding too many covariates – the Causal Salad ‘approach’ (McElreath, 2020) – can also bias estimates where covariates serve as colliders or mediators of the effect of the exposure upon the outcome (the latter where an estimate of the total causal effect is sought). The statistical adjustment approach will also obtain a biased estimate if confounders are not modelled appropriately or measured accurately. Simple models with variables incorporated as linear terms without interactions or other non-linearities (e.g., absence of required polynomial terms) may not reveal suitable residual variation.
Theory may not be sufficiently strong to clarify the correct functional form a priori, which limits standard regression algorithms like OLS, where the functional form requires explicit parameterisation. On the other hand, machine-learning and deep-learning algorithms, such as the random forest and neural networks, are capable of modelling non-linearities without their express inclusion in a model. The Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem has motivated the development of other methods, notably the double machine learning method (Chernozhukov et al., 2018), where machine-learning algorithms are used to obtain residuals for exposures and outcomes, increasing the plausibility that data-generating processes have been modelled correctly. Still, ever more complicated algorithms cannot use data that aren’t there; bias via backdoor paths (and incorrectly closed front-door paths or conditioned colliders) is still a fundamental issue regardless of the method used for statistical control.
Though non-parametric in nature, DAGs can help identify control variables that are sufficient to identify causal effects: the software DAGitty (2025) can be used to programmatically identify minimal sufficient adjustment sets or biasing pathways, while Cinelli et al. (2024) provide a “crash course” with example DAGs showing where adjustment would reduce, increase or leave bias unchanged.1 There are also situations where controlling for a variable could go either way; Figure 5.1 shows two DAGs where control closes one path but opens another due to the variable operating as a collider (‘damned if you do, damned if you don’t’; Cinelli, Forney, et al., 2024; Tomova, Silverwood, Tennant, et al., 2026; Woolf et al., 2023). Whether bias would be reduced is an empirical question and depends on the relative strength of the paths in question; judgements about this benefit from domain expertise. Regardless, adjustment sets will only be valid in so far as the assumptions encoded in the DAG (e.g., the set of variables, causal arrows, and their direction) are valid, too. Though some assumptions in a DAG may be testable empirically (i.e., implied [conditional] independencies), ultimately not all can be – e.g., there is no statistical way to identify the correct direction of an arrow between two adjacent variables, measured at the same moment in time.
VanderWeele (2019) offers principles for selecting confounders when knowledge of underlying causal structures is incomplete or uncertain. Specifically, he recommends, with two caveats, conditioning upon any pre-exposure covariate that is a cause of the exposure or the outcome or both. This ‘disjunctive cause criterion’ avoids issues that can arise if simply controlling for any pre-treatment variable (i.e., M-bias) or insisting confounders must be common causes of both exposure and outcome (which can miss variables that are valid controls); see Figure 5.2 below.
VanderWeele’s first caveat to this rule is that analysts should not control for any instrumental variable (Section 5.9) – that is, a variable which is only related to the outcome via its effect on the exposure – as this can generate ‘Z-bias’ where the bias from an unconditioned common cause of exposure and outcome is amplified by adjustment for an instrument (Ding et al., 2017). This is because controlling for the instrument removes a source of variation in the exposure that was unbiased, meaning a greater proportion of the variation that is left will represent bias or measurement error.2 VanderWeele’s second caveat is that analysts should also consider conditioning on ‘proxy confounders’ – variables that explain sufficient variation in true confounders, such that they can be used instead of them, for example when the confounders themselves are not available or are poorly measured. These proxy confounders can be thought of as imperfect measurements of the true confounders. However, a drawback of including these is that there may also exist an unobserved common cause of the proxy confounder and the outcome, which could then create M-bias if the proxy confounder is conditioned upon. This would be the case if C were considered a proxy confounder for U2 in Figure 5.2a above.
VanderWeele (2019) also discusses issues that can arise when covariates and exposures are measured simultaneously as it is possible that covariates are in fact mediators rather than confounders – for instance, conditioning upon cognitive ability when trying to estimate the causal effect of educational attainment as this is a consequence of education, as well as a cause (Ritchie & Tucker-Drob, 2018; Strenze, 2007). A key benefit of CLS’s cohorts is that multiple sweeps of data are available which include repeated measurement, so it is usually possible to find measurements for confounders from prior to the measurement of the exposure (as well as to find measurements of the exposure prior to the outcome), thereby respecting temporality. Additionally, it may also be possible to control for lagged measurements of exposures and/or outcomes (VanderWeele et al., 2020), which can again reduce bias, particularly where time-invariant confounders exist or there are confounders that have effects on exposure and outcome at multiple time points. Note, controlling for earlier exposures more specifically links the study estimate (exposure to treatment at a specific time point) to a specific intervention and to the randomised controlled trial design; we discuss this further in Section 5.11. However, one issue is that the time between adjacent sweeps can be quite long (e.g., a nine-year gap between the Age 33 year and 42 year NCDS sweeps), so control may be imperfect when this strategy is used.
Less abstractly, VanderWeele et al. (2020) provide a list of variables they suggest should be considered for inclusion as covariates in regression models, given these represent confounders of many different associations in the health and social sciences.3 Ideally these should be measured prior to exposure and outcome, or otherwise with consideration to the possibilities these mediate rather than confound associations (see Table 5.1). Most or all of these variables are available in each of CLS’s cohorts.

title: 5.1 Control via Regression Adjustment
text:
5.1.2 Applications
There are thousands of papers using CLS data that have used the statistical adjustment approach. A particularly rigorous example of statistical control is Purba et al. (2025), who use data from MCS to assess the effect of time spent on social media on cigarette and e-cigarette use. The authors based their (pre-registered) analysis upon a DAG developed from subject knowledge, existing evidence, and input from a policy advisory group, from which they identified a minimally sufficient adjustment set for their analysis. A further virtue, though not related to reducing bias via regression adjustment, is that the authors also elected to use a more reliable time-diary-based measure of social media use rather than other available measures, reducing measurement error.
crumbs: 5  5.1 Control via Regression Adjustment

title: 5.1 Control via Regression Adjustment
text:
5.1.3 Opportunities
The regression adjustment approach is straightforward to implement and particularly suited to CLS’s cohort data given the amount and variety of data available on participants, including their individual characteristics and the characteristics of their backgrounds, families and localities in which they live. Control can be made for many common and important confounders, such as sex, ethnicity, psychological traits, and lifetime socioeconomic position. While not all confounders may be available, nor all confounders known, the ability to incorporate additional plausible confounders may still improve upon existing work; bias may not be fully ameliorated but at least reduced. The statistical adjustment approach may also be beneficial when treated as a data point within a broader literature – where remaining bias is unrelated to biases hampering other studies, particularly those using different study designs, consistency of results across studies (“triangulation”) makes a causal interpretation more plausible (Lawlor et al., 2016). Additionally, as will be discussed further in Section 5.20 on Quantitative Bias Analysis, information on important confounders can be used to calibrate expectations about whether remaining confounders are sufficient to explain observed associations.
crumbs: 5  5.1 Control via Regression Adjustment

title: 5.1 Control via Regression Adjustment
text:
Control for some variables does not reduce bias, but by reducing residual variation, increases statistical power and the precision of estimates.↩︎
This is also known as ‘bias amplification’. Bias amplification can occur even if the confounder is a weak cause of the outcome because, again, once conditioned upon, the residual variation in the exposure may be more confounded than before. Similar logic also applies to sibship studies and other fixed effects designs as discussed in Sections 5.5 and 5.14.↩︎
In Section 8.2 (Appendix), we also offer some general theoretical perspectives on confounding processes.↩︎

title: 5.2 Matching
text:
5.2.1 Method
Section 2.2.3 showed that confounding arises where treated and untreated individuals differ on background characteristics that also influence the outcome variable, with the consequence that a naïve comparison of outcomes would mix the effect of treatment with the effect of these pre-existing differences. Matching – a non-equivalent group design – addresses confounding by identifying sets of treated and untreated individuals who are similar on observed confounders. If these capture all the relevant differences between the groups, the only systematic difference within matched sets is treatment itself, and any difference in outcomes can be attributed to it. Like regression adjustment (Section 5.1), this relies on confounders being observed and measured well – matching on observed confounders does not ensure no systematic differences on unobserved confounders, too.
There are multiple matching algorithms, which differ in how ‘similar’ is defined. Many attempt to identify, for each treated individual, untreated individuals who are as similar as possible on confounders (or vice versa), with outcomes then compared within matched sets. Exact Matching identifies individuals who have the same values for a set of characteristics. However, as the number of possible combinations of these characteristics explodes exponentially as more are added (the curse of dimensionality), exact matching can only be feasibly done for a small number of characteristics with few unique values or, alternatively, with sample sizes that are very large (e.g., as in whole population administrative data). Coarsened Exact Matching makes matching more feasible by coarsening the variables used to match upon – e.g., matching within age groups, rather than by integer age. But again, the curse of dimensionality applies – with just four variables, each taking four values, there are 256 (44) possible strata in the data. Matching can instead be approximate and utilise statistical measures of ‘distance’ that aggregate difference on many dimensions simultaneously. For instance, individuals may be matched upon Mahalanobis distance, a multivariate analogue of Cohen’s d. Though matching may not be exact, differences between treatment and control are made smaller than they otherwise would be.
Another alternative metric is the propensity score (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983). In propensity score matching (PSM), individuals in treatment and comparison groups are matched upon their probability of having been treated, with this probability typically estimated (e.g., using a regression model) based on a set of predictors of treatment. Importantly, this probability is a single scalar value (ranging 0-1) making matching more straightforward. However, as there may be numerous profiles of covariates that yield the same probability of being treated, pairs of individuals matched upon propensity scores do not necessarily share similar values on underlying covariates – balance is instead a property of the overall matched sample rather than of each matched pair. Yet, given covariates can differ within matched pairs, where poor matches are pruned past the point groups are approximately balanced, matching upon propensity scores can increase the risk of imbalance (King & Nielsen, 2019), though the extent to which this matters in practice has been questioned (Ripollone et al., 2018). Matching on the propensity score can also reduce statistical efficiency compared to more direct matching methods. (Note, the issue of imbalance applies to using the propensity score to identify matches, rather than for inverse probability weighting, which is discussed in Section 5.3.)
Matching does not have to be 1:1 – several matches can be obtained for each ‘treated’ individual and vice versa. Matches can also be made with replacement, so that one individual may be matched to multiple others. The advantage of matching with replacement is that it can reduce bias as the best match is used in each case. However, it also decreases statistical power as the effective sample size is reduced – in other words, there is a bias-variance trade-off (Huntington-Klein, 2022). Conversely, using several matches per individual increases statistical power but also increases bias as more data than just the very best match are used.1 Bias can be reduced by using a caliper – i.e., setting a maximum dissimilarity between matches – and by using kernel weighting, where matches are weighted more highly the better they are. An alternative is entropy balancing (Hainmueller, 2012), which instead of identifying similar individuals identifies weights to create matched treatment and control groups that are overall balanced for specified moments of the distributions of the matching variables (e.g., same means, variance and skewness for covariates).
As with statistical adjustment, the validity of causal estimates obtained via matching depends on whether, within matched groups, there is no remaining confounding. Unlike statistical adjustment, matching can be thought of as a data preprocessing step rather than an estimation procedure, per se (Ho et al., 2007) – matching is a way to identify an appropriate analytical sample before substantive analyses are undertaken. Matching can therefore be combined with regression – e.g., by estimating a regression model within a group of matched individuals. This two-step approach has the advantage that it can be “doubly robust” (Stuart, 2010) – robust to the failures of one method, if the other is valid. For instance, a valid causal estimate may be obtained with a mis-specified regression model, if matching was sufficient for achieving non-confoundedness, or vice versa. Note, where treated individuals are matched to, matching yields the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT). This may not be equal to the ATE if there is effect heterogeneity.2
Matching has several advantages versus regression adjustment. First, matching itself does not require the outcome to be modelled as the method focuses on approximating the data-generating process for treatment specifically. This is useful where it is difficult to model the outcome (e.g., where the outcome is rare) or where there are multiple outcome variables – i.e., when performing an outcome-wide epidemiological analysis (VanderWeele, 2017; VanderWeele et al., 2020). One drawback, however, is Z-bias (Section 5.1) if unobserved confounders remain.
A second advantage of matching is that it can ensure comparisons between treatment and control groups are made within regions of ‘common support’ (overlap in covariate distributions), whereas regression approaches, which interpolate between data points, do not. Some combinations of characteristics may not appear in both treated and control groups (i.e., positivity may be violated) – this is at least explicit in matching but hidden when performing regression. While interpolation may be reasonable in a given case, its validity cannot be ascertained with the data at hand. Interpolation is also more plausible if matching has been used as a data preprocessing step. Relatedly, the assumptions of propensity score matching are partly testable as balance can be assessed within strata of the propensity score, though of course this does not tell the analyst anything about confounders that are unobserved.
Matching does have several disadvantages, however. First, if matches cannot be obtained for all observations, some units may need to be discarded, potentially yielding a valid causal estimate, but within a sample with no clear interpretation or potentially no wider applicability. Second, matching creates challenges where exposures are continuous rather than binary, though extensions, such as kernel matching, have been developed.

title: 5.2 Matching
text:
5.2.2 Applications
Persson (2014) uses data from BCS70 to assess whether the strong association between higher education and political behaviour (e.g., voting in general elections) reported in prior studies is causal. Unlike data used in previous studies, the BCS70 allowed the author to match upon important confounders measured prospectively from childhood, such as parental behaviour and cognitive ability at ages 5 and 10 years. The author used genetic matching – an algorithm that identifies weights for a generalised Mahalanobis distance matrix minimising imbalance between treatment and control groups (Diamond & Sekhon, 2013) – observing that the procedure performs better than coarsened exact matching and propensity score matching in the BCS70 sample (due to larger retained samples and better balance, respectively). He finds little evidence of association after matching is performed. In support of the matching, the author reports multiple tests of balance, including a comparison of the imbalance remaining against that expected under random assignment and placebo tests using pre-treatment variables that higher education could not have caused. A caveat is that only 569 cohort members were treated and confidence intervals are not reported – the analysis indicates no detectable effect rather than the absence of one.
In two papers, Jerrim & Sims (2019, 2020) use data from the MCS to assess the causal effect of grammar (i.e., selective) school attendance upon an array of non-cognitive factors, such as wellbeing and educational aspirations. As with Persson (2014), the authors exploit the rich life course information on confounding variables (e.g., prior measures of cognitive ability and wellbeing), though do not observe entry test results, the main basis upon which entry is determined. In both papers, the authors match upon propensity scores, but use two separate groups from which to draw untreated observations. In Jerrim & Sims (2019), the authors use geographic variation across Local Education Authority (LEA) areas, comparing those attending grammar schools with matched cohort members living in LEAs with no selective schools at all. In Jerrim & Sims (2020), the authors compare individuals who attended grammar school with those who applied but ultimately did not attend.3 They find little evidence of association with non-cognitive outcomes overall, except some evidence of an effect on educational aspirations (Jerrim & Sims, 2019). One limitation of their papers is a lack of discussion of what unobserved confounders may be present, especially for the analysis using grammar school applicants for the control group. A second is precision: the 2019 estimates draw on 4,785 cohort members, whereas the 2020 analysis matches roughly 650 in England and 500 in Northern Ireland. Several estimates are large enough to be substantively meaningful but have wide confidence intervals.

title: 5.2 Matching
text:
5.2.3 Opportunities
As with statistical adjustment (Section 5.1), there are ample opportunities in CLS’s cohorts to apply matching methods. An additional advantageous property of CLS’s cohorts is their large sample size – matching can lead to a large loss of observations if few or no comparison observations can be found for a treated observation. Though not a design that matches on treatment, CLS’s cohorts can also provide general population controls in case-control designs – for instance, the MCS provided a control group as part of the National Evaluation of Sure Start (Joshi & Fitzsimons, 2016) and the NCDS is part of the Wellcome Case Control Consortium, which was used in many of the first molecular genetic studies of health and disease (Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium, 2007).

title: 5.2 Matching
text:
That said, many-to-one or one-to-many matching can also guard against overfitting.↩︎
Where untreated individuals are matched to, the procedure will yield the Average Treatment Effect on the Untreated (ATU), which again may differ from the ATE. Combining the two (weighted) can produce the ATE. Which estimand – ATE, ATT, ATU – is relevant and most useful, depends on the research application. For a policy to be expanded across the population, the ATU may be of most interest. For a policy to be rolled back, it may be the ATT.↩︎
The authors note that individuals usually apply for grammar school after they have received entry test results, so applicants, regardless of whether they ultimately attend or not, are likely to have passed the entry test.↩︎

title: 5.3 Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting
text:
5.3.1 Method
Section 5.2 discussed issues with using propensity scores to match treatment and control groups. Regardless of this problem, when used as a covariate or to weight observations, propensity scores can recover causal effects: the propensity score theorem (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983) shows that if treatment is independent of potential outcomes conditional on covariates, U, then treatment will also be independent of potential outcomes conditional on the propensity score (the probability of treatment conditional on the same covariates). Intuitively, where a binary exposure is influenced non-deterministically, confounders can be thought to influence the probability of an exposure occurring, rather than the exposure itself. Conditioning upon the propensity score thus closes a backdoor path. See Figure 5.3 for a DAG.
The typical way of using a propensity score is as a weight in Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting (IPTW). In IPTW, treated observations are weighted by the inverse of their probability of treatment and untreated units are weighted by the inverse of their probability of non-treatment (i.e., 1 – treatment). The upshot is that, when implemented successfully, data are reweighted to create a pseudo-population in which treatment assignment is independent of the measured confounders, thereby mimicking a feature of randomisation. The schematic in Figure 5.4 displays the procedure where there is a single confounder, education, that is associated with both the probability of treatment and potential outcomes.
In Figure 5.4, a naïve comparison of treated and untreated groups would yield a downwards biased estimate due to the disproportionate number of treated individuals who are degree-educated and who have lower potential outcomes than those with less education – i.e., the naïve comparison is 1.13 = (6*28 + 9*24)/52 – (4*12 + 7*36)/48, instead of the correct causal effect, which is 2 (compare the potential outcomes Y[T = 1] and Y[T = 0] in each group). Using IPTW recovers the true causal effect as, when weighted, both treated and untreated groups contribute the initial sample size of the groups they were drawn from (i.e., n = 40 for those with a degree, n = 60 for those without): 2 = (6*28*1/0.7 + 9*24*1/0.4)/100 - (4*12*1/0.3 + 7*36*1/0.6)/100. This example generalises to scenarios where the propensity score is based on more than one covariate.
Inverse probability weighting (IPW) can also be used to account for bias from non-response, where responding units are weighted to reflect their respective frequency in the target population (i.e., their probability of response or selection). We discuss IPW for missing data further in Section 5.4. Note, as with other ‘non-equivalent groups design’ methods, IPTW will provide unbiased estimates only in so far as control variables are sufficient to close backdoor confounding paths. Another issue that can arise with IPTW is where there are extreme weights, most typically where some treated units have very low probabilities of treatment and/or control units have very high probabilities of treatment. In this case, trimming is often used, either by winsorising (capping) particularly large weights or by dropping observations with extreme weights or propensity scores. As with matching, discarding observations or winsorising weights can, in some cases, shift the population for whom the effect is being estimated, by focusing on those within the region of common support. Typically, this is an unintended side effect of trimming, in which case the resulting estimate may no longer answer the original research question and may be challenging to interpret. That said, the effect in the overlap region can sometimes answer policy-relevant questions and therefore may still be of interest (e.g., if one does not expect treatment effect heterogeneity).

title: 5.3 Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting
text:
5.3.2 Applications
Madia et al. (2022) use data from Next Steps to estimate the causal effect of school exclusion on labour market outcomes. They use several analytical approaches to address different sources of confounding, including school fixed effects (Section 5.5), matching (Section 5.2) and IPTW, with IPTW used to address statistical power issues with matching given the small number of treated individuals (i.e., persons permanently excluded from schools; N = 86). IPTW estimates show sizeable effects upon several outcomes, including higher risks of being not in employment, education, or training (NEET) or unemployed, specifically. Estimates are similar in size to those obtained using propensity score matching, but are more statistically precise as no observations are discarded.
The authors condition on multiple factors, exploiting Next Steps’ rich data collection on individual characteristics and the family environment, and apply non-response weights alongside the IPTW weights to account for attrition. However, they are unable to control for prior educational attainment or detailed measures of cognitive and non-cognitive skills, which plausibly confound associations. The authors pay attention to the consistency assumption, comparing individuals who have been excluded with those who have never been suspended or excluded (though, an alternate, policy-relevant option could have been to compare excluded individuals with those only suspended). Finally, the authors use quantitative bias analysis (QBA) methods (Mantel-Haenszel and Rosenbaum bounds) to assess sensitivity to unobserved confounding. Two omissions are that no diagnostics for the weights are reported and the plausibility of the estimates given the QBA results is not discussed.

title: 5.3 Inverse Probability of Treatment Weighting
text:
5.3.3 Opportunities
Similar to matching and statistical adjustment, there are ample opportunities in CLS’s cohorts to apply IPTW methods given the number of plausible confounders that can be included in IPTW models. Additionally, the longitudinal nature of the cohorts enables the creation of plausible non-response weights, as discussed in the next section.

title: 5.4 Missing Data Methods
text:
5.4.1 Method
In Section 2.2.4, we discussed how large-scale intensive and longitudinal data collections, characteristic of CLS’s cohorts, can contain a sizeable amount of missing data through unit, sweep, and item non-response. Where non-response is not random, missingness can lead to selection bias, impacting internal (and even external) validity (Type 1 and Type 2 selection bias; Lu et al., 2024). For instance, if individuals with poorer mental health are more likely to drop out from a cohort, associations between factors that cause mental ill-health and measurements of mental health may be attenuated in available (complete case) data.
There are two main methods for addressing missingness: inverse probability weighting (IPW) and multiple imputation (MI). IPW in this setting involves two steps. First, the probability of response is calculated or estimated, typically with a regression model using data available on participant characteristics for both respondents and non-respondents (in longitudinal data, this would be data collected prior to an individual attriting). Second, the inverse of this probability is taken and used to weight (non-missing) observations in substantive analyses. By taking the inverse, individuals with lower probability of response are given greater weight – in effect, they are used to represent more individuals whose data are missing. For instance, an individual with only a 10% predicted probability of response will be weighted ten times as highly as someone certain to respond as the former is used to reflect both themselves and nine other individuals with the same (10%) probability of response predicted to have not in fact responded.
MI is typically performed using chained equations: in this procedure, missing data are imputed using a series of regression models where the statistical relationships between observed values are used to predict values that are missing. For instance, in longitudinal data where some participants drop out, BMI collected during childhood could be used to predict adulthood BMI by applying the association detected in individuals for whom BMI was observed on both occasions. These imputed values are then used to predict and impute missing data in other variables. As predictions are unlikely to be perfect, multiple imputed datasets are created to reflect imputation uncertainty. Substantive analyses are then performed in each imputed dataset and results pooled accounting for the variation both within and between imputations – typically, pooling is done by applying ‘Rubin’s Rules’ (Rubin, 1987), though bootstrapping is also possible (Bartlett & Hughes, 2020; Schomaker & Heumann, 2018). Note, MI (and IPW for non-response) are not methods for estimating causal effects in themselves; rather, they address a source of bias in onwards analysis.
In MI, imputation and substantive models should be ‘congenial’ (van Buuren, 2018); that is, the imputation model should be no more restrictive than the substantive model, accommodating every variable and functional form the substantive model contains – i.e., outcome, exposure, covariates, and interactions or nonlinear terms. Otherwise, excluded terms are implicitly set to zero in the imputation models and are not directly reflected in imputed values, attenuating associations in downstream analyses.1
MI and IPW rely on assumptions about the mechanism by which data became missing. These mechanisms can be classified into Missing Completely at Random (MCAR), Missing at Random (MAR) and Missing Not at Random (MNAR). To illustrate each, we take the example of using partially observed data to obtain an unbiased estimate of average (mean) income:
Note, in MNAR Example I, missingness was due to an unobserved variable, rather than income itself, whereas in Example II, it is income itself that is the cause of missingness. However, both are still MNAR processes, though if we had data on whether a participant derived income from illicit sources, the former example would be MAR.
MCAR, MAR and MNAR processes all reduce statistical power because each leads to a loss of information. However, they have different consequences for bias (Figure 5.5). MCAR processes do not generate bias. MAR processes bias complete-case analyses, unless the variables related to missingness are conditioned upon in the substantive model or MI or IPW is used with imputation or response models including those variables appropriately. MNAR processes also generate bias, and neither MI nor IPW can address this. However, this is partly a question of degree: in longitudinal data, the plausibility of the MAR assumption can be increased using lagged measurements and other rich information from over the life course (e.g., data on early-life cognitive ability, socioeconomic background, prior measures of income, etc.; Mostafa et al., 2021; Silverwood, Narayanan, et al., 2024); the extent of violation of the MAR assumption can at least be reduced, if not fully ameliorated. Admin linkages – which can continue even if the participant stops responding to the main survey – can also help here (Rajah et al., 2023). In Section 5.20, we describe a variant of MI – Pattern Mixture Modelling – that can account for MNAR processes.
An advantage of MI over IPW for handling missingness is that, by retaining partially observed cases rather than discarding them, MI uses more of the available data and can therefore yield more precise estimates. Nonetheless, higher missingness entails lower statistical power and potentially greater sensitivity to modelling choices in either method. In IPW, low probabilities of response can generate large weights for some observations, which inflates the variance of estimates and increases dependence on the response model being correctly specified. In MI, greater missingness increases both the contribution of imputed values to estimates in substantive models and variation between imputed datasets as imputation models are less precisely estimated. Predictive accuracy can be increased by including ‘auxiliary’ variables into imputation or response models – additional variables that are predictive of missing values, but which do not appear in substantive models.
MI and IPW are not mutually exclusive and can be used alongside each other. For instance, it can be useful to use IPW to account for sweep non-response, and within a responding sample, use MI to address item missingness (see, for example, L. Wright, Davies, et al., 2024). It is also possible to use MI to impute missing values in variables to be used to create IPW weights. There are methods for combining IPW and MI in ways that are ‘doubly robust’; see Seaman & Vansteelandt (2018) for more details. IPW can also be performed combining weights for selection (i.e., response) and for treatment (IPTW, Section 5.3).
Note, the potential outcomes framework conceptualises causal inference as an inherent missing data problem (Parra et al., 2021); counterfactuals are not observed and are therefore unknown. Some newer methods approach estimating causal effects as a missing data issue (e.g., Matrix Completion; Athey et al., 2021); given these methods are more advanced and niche we do not discuss these further here.

title: 5.4 Missing Data Methods
text:
MCAR: Missingness is unrelated to observed or unobserved values.

Example: Income data for a random subset of participants are lost due to hard disk failure.

MAR: Missingness is unrelated to unobserved values, conditional on observed data.

Example: Participants in jobs that involve frequent travel are more likely to miss a survey interview, and these jobs may pay more on average. However, among those in such jobs, who is away – and so whose data are missing – is unrelated to income.

MNAR: Missingness is related to unobserved values, even conditional on observed data.

Example I: Participants whose income derives from illicit sources (and who may have higher income, on average) decline to answer questions on income, so whether income is reported is related to income itself, even among participants who otherwise look alike on everything observed (e.g., education level).
Example II: Due to social desirability concerns, people with low income refuse to answer questions on income.








Figure 5.5: Simulations displaying MCAR, MAR and MNAR processes in a variable, income. Left panels show all data points (blue points), regardless of whether they are observed or not. Right panels show observed data points (pink dots) surviving the missing data process (missing data are shown in light grey). Red lines show average (mean) income in relevant data. We use the observed data to attempt to obtain an unbiased estimate of income that would be obtained if all data points were available. In row (a), data are MCAR – missingness unrelated to the value of income – and mean income in the observed data (pink dots, right panel) is an unbiased estimate of mean income. In row (b), data are MAR – missingness due to type of work, with different types of work paying different wages. The unconditional estimate of income is biased, but conditioning on type of work removes bias. In MI, predicting income from observed type of work would yield an unbiased estimate of a person’s income and the resulting imputed data would yield an unbiased unconditional estimate of average income. In row (c), data are MNAR – people with high incomes less likely to report income. Even conditioning upon a predictor associated with high income (e.g., education level), estimates of average income with observed data are biased, though less so than when not conditioning upon this variable.

title: 5.4 Missing Data Methods
text:
5.4.2 Applications
Wright et al. (2024) use a combination of IPW and MI to estimate the association between a polygenic score (a summary measure of genetic predisposition to a trait) and observed BMI over the life course in four different cohorts (including the NCDS, BCS70 and MCS). As genetic data were only collected in later sweeps of each cohort (44y, 46y, and 14y for the NCDS, BCS70 and MCS, respectively), there was a high amount of missing data, including for BMI at later ages. The authors therefore used IPW to weight observations in the genotyped sample. MI was then used to impute remaining item missingness; earlier observations of BMI were used to impute later values of BMI and several auxiliary variables predictive of missingness (Mostafa et al., 2021) were also included in imputation models. Code used in the study is available here: https://osf.io/nxusz.

title: 5.4 Missing Data Methods
text:
5.4.3 Opportunities
There are many opportunities to apply IPW and MI in CLS data. The longitudinal nature of data collection means there is generally a lot of information available with which to create non-response weights or to incorporate into imputation models. This includes earlier measurements of variables that may predict non-response (e.g., measures of mental health earlier in life [including in adulthood]). Several papers show that this information can increase the plausibility of the MAR assumption, as evidenced by ability to recover initial characteristics in imputed data (Katsoulis et al., 2024; Mostafa et al., 2021). These papers also give useful information on which factors predict non-response that can be incorporated into analysts’ own models. CLS have additionally produced an accessible and extensive user guide on Handling Missing Data, which readers may find helpful (Silverwood, Narayanan, et al., 2024).

title: 5.5 (Longitudinal) Fixed Effects
text:
5.5.1 Method
Each of CLS’s cohorts benefits from the tracking of the same individuals over the life course. Section 4.3 described four advantages of longitudinal data for estimating causal effects: more accurate measurement, ability to establish temporal ordering, availability of baseline and lagged measures of exposures and outcomes, and the ability to use within- rather than between-person variation. This section focuses on methods that exploit within-unit variation.
Some confounders vary over time; others are time-invariant. Income, sex and country of birth may confound an association of interest, but income varies throughout life, while sex and birth country are fixed attributes of an individual. Utilising within-person variation fixes time-invariant confounders, accounting for their contribution to outcomes by design (Huntington-Klein, 2022); see Figure 5.6 for a DAG. This is the idea behind the longitudinal fixed effects method. The approach can be understood as a form of matching (Section 5.2), in which each observation is matched not to an observation from a similar individual but to other observations from the same individual, so that time-invariant characteristics are balanced exactly, whether or not they have been measured.
The equations below show the typical fixed effects set-up when used with longitudinal data. i and t index individuals and time periods, respectively. The outcome, \(Y_{it}\), is related to an exposure of interest (\(D_{it}\)), time-variant confounders (\(X_{it}\)), and time-invariant confounders that can be aggregated into a single person-specific fixed effect, \(u_{i}\). Person-specific means for each variable are indicated with the ‘bar’ accent (e.g., \(\overline{Y_{i}} = \ \sum_{t = 1}^{T}Y_{it}\)).
\[Y_{it} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} \cdot D_{it} + \beta_{K} \cdot X_{it} + u_{i} + \varepsilon_{it}\qquad \left[\varepsilon_{it}\ \sim\ N\left( 0,{\ \sigma}^{2} \right)\right]\]
\[\overline{Y_{i}} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} \cdot {\overline{D}}_{i} + \beta_{K} \cdot \overline{X_{i}} + \overline{\mu_{i}}\qquad \left[{\overline{\overline{u}}}_{i} = u_{i};{\overline{\overline{\varepsilon}}}_{i} = 0\right]\]
\[Y_{it} - \overline{Y_{i}} = \beta_{1} \cdot (D_{it} - \ {\overline{D}}_{i}) + \beta_{K} \cdot (X_{it} - \ \overline{X_{i}})\  + \varepsilon_{it}\qquad \left[\beta_{0} - \beta_{0} = 0;\overline{\mu_{i}} - u_{i} = 0\right]\]
In the usual implementation (performed automatically by statistical software), time-invariant confounding is accounted for by calculating person-specific means for each variable and subtracting these from observed values (the ‘within’ transformation). As time-invariant confounders are (by definition) fixed, the average is the same as the individual data points. Subtracting person-specific means therefore has the effect of implicitly removing the influence of these time-invariant factors (i.e., as \(u_{i} - \overline{\mu_{i}} = 0\)).1
The advantage of the fixed effects method is that time-invariant confounders are accounted for without needing to measure them or even know what they are. It is not without limitations, however. Importantly, fixed effects do not account for time-varying confounding or reverse causality, which may be important sources of bias in a specific application. Fixed effects also do not account for the time-varying effects of time-invariant factors – fixed characteristics like sex and birth country may not differ across life, but their importance can vary considerably over development. For instance, sex could have larger effects on outcomes post-puberty.2 This is less of an issue where the time span used is small, but CLS’s cohorts extend decades, typically with several years between survey sweeps. The large gap can also mean few observations per individual, so person-specific averages can be overfitted.
Because it uses only within-person variation, the fixed effect method also cannot be used to assess the (time-invariant) effects of time-invariant variables, which may be of substantive interest. Additionally, only individuals whose exposure does in fact vary contribute to the estimated outcome-exposure association. Where treatment effects are heterogeneous, this can raise interpretational issues. Specifically, fixed effects estimates the change in an outcome accompanying a change in exposure between measurement occasions, averaged over individuals whose exposure changes during follow-up, and weighted towards those whose exposure varies most. For instance, fixed effects has been frequently used to examine the effect of unemployment on health (see, e.g., Schmitz, 2011) but this implicitly utilises data from people whose employment status changes (frequently), rather than those with unbroken (un)employment episodes. Moreover, where classical measurement error is an issue, focusing on within-variation makes the problem worse as a larger proportion of within-variation compared with between-variation will reflect noise rather than signal.
There are several other methods that address some of these limitations, which readers can delve into further by following the references. Random effects models capture person-specific time-invariant effects as random variables, but assume the random effects are independent of covariates, which may be unrealistic in practice (and is in fact a reason to use the fixed effects model in the first place). However, specific parameterisations of the random effects model (e.g., the within-between [REWB] model; Bell et al., 2019; Bell & Jones, 2015) can get round this limitation. Methods also exist to account for reverse causality and for serial correlation in the outcome variable (note, the absence of an arrow between Yt=1 and Yt=2 in Figure 5.6) – specifically, dynamic panel data methods (Wooldridge, 2010) and the random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015) and its extensions (Mulder & Hamaker, 2021; Zyphur et al., 2019, 2020).
Longitudinal data are a type of hierarchical data – observations are nested within individuals. The fixed effects method can be applied to other types of hierarchical data, too. For instance, Next Steps recruited multiple students from participating schools – using variation within schools allows one to account for school-level confounders (see, e.g., Madia et al., 2022). Another important type of hierarchical data used frequently in the causal inference literature is sibships (Sjölander et al., 2022). Using sibling fixed effects controls for family-level confounders by design (discussed further in Section 5.14). Note, fixing effects at one level also fixes characteristics at higher levels the units are nested within – e.g., looking within schools also controls for local educational authority; looking within neighbourhoods also controls for town, region, and so on (Abdellaoui et al., 2022).
To best make use of fixed effects, researchers should consider at which level confounding is expected to occur. To give an (admittedly niche) example, Cinelli & Hazlett (2020), in their analysis of the causal effect on political beliefs of being a victim of violence during the Darfur war, note that once an army had reached a village, violence was likely largely indiscriminate and thus using data from multiple individuals within a village could achieve unconfoundedness. Similarly, Evans (1986) studies the effect of seatbelts on car crash fatalities using data from crashes where one occupant was belted and the other unbelted. This design controls for many pertinent shared factors (e.g., the speed the car was travelling at the time of crash, the road conditions, etc.), producing estimates that are likely less biased than comparing belted and unbelted individuals overall (Rosenbaum, 2019). The fixed effect design is an expression of what Zubizarreta et al. (2018, p. 16) term ‘isolation’: “Within a large but biased data system, isolation means constructing or finding a smaller set of comparisons that are likely to be much less biased”. Nevertheless, this is situation specific, and it is also possible that within-unit variation is more confounded, not less, than the between-person variation, producing problems akin to Z-bias (discussed in Section 5.1).

title: 5.5 (Longitudinal) Fixed Effects
text: Figure 5.6: DAG representing the fixed effect method with longitudinal data. X and Y are measured at two time points and their contemporaneous association is confounded by a time-variant factor, Ct=x, and a time-invariant factor, U. Using within-variation effectively controls for person, which implicitly conditions on all time-invariant factors having constant effects.

title: 5.5 (Longitudinal) Fixed Effects
text:
5.5.2 Applications
Scott (2022) uses BCS70 data to estimate the causal effect of university education upon political attitudes measured on multiple occasions between ages 16y and 42y. Using two-way fixed effects (Section 5.6) and REWB estimators he shows substantial within-person change in attitudes after graduation (compared to prior to enrolment). A key strength of the study is an explicit statement on the estimand and its causal aim.
Fitzsimons & Pongiglione (2019) use MCS to assess the effect of maternal employment on child BMI, showing children have higher BMI in periods in which their mothers are employed. Interestingly, no such within-person change is observed for paternal employment, though as the authors note, in the MCS sample, fathers’ employment is more stable – thus a different sample contributes to the estimated causal effect. Speyer et al. (2022) use RI-CLPM models to assess the effect of parenting behaviours on children’s socioemotional development (as assessed by the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire) across early to mid-childhood (3y, 5y, and 7y), allowing for reverse causality. They show that harsh parenting practices (e.g., hitting) are followed by worse SDQ scores, and vice versa. The authors also perform Quantitative Bias Analysis to assess sensitivity to unobserved confounding.

title: 5.5 (Longitudinal) Fixed Effects
text:
5.5.3 Opportunities
Given the extent of repeat measurement in CLS’s cohorts, there are potentially many opportunities to use fixed effects methodology with the data. As discussed, a key issue, however, is the gap in age between data collections: time-invariant confounders may not have time-invariant effects over these periods. This can also be the case even when data collection is more frequent if this occurs over periods of substantial developmental change (e.g., MCS has five data collections to age 11y, but this spans early to mid-childhood and even initiation of puberty). Further, where one is using (e.g.) RI-CLPM and similar models to assess lagged effects, the gap in age may be implausible for the causal effect under study. For instance, one study that used MCS data to assess the effect of social media upon mental health relied upon 3-year gaps between data collections (Kelly et al., 2022). This would not capture effects that were more temporary.

title: 5.5 (Longitudinal) Fixed Effects
text:
This is known as the within-estimator. It is also possible to account for \(u_{i}\) by adding person-specific fixed effects (i.e., person dummies) to the regression model.↩︎
Within person differencing does, however, account for the average effect of these time-invariant confounders.↩︎

title: 5.6 Difference in Differences
text:
5.6.1 Method
In Section 3.3, we introduced some of the evidence that John Snow marshalled to demonstrate that cholera was transmitted via faecal-infected water rather than miasmas. This was not the only evidence he brought to bear. A further piece of evidence was his “Grand Experiment”, comparing cholera cases in households supplied by either of two London water companies, the Southwark-Vauxhall Company and the Lambeth Waterworks Company. Both companies drew water from the River Thames, but in 1852, Lambeth moved its intake pipes upstream of the main location where sewage was discharged (Cunningham, 2021). Cholera cases in households supplied by the two companies in two years, before and after Lambeth relocated its pipes, are shown in Columns 2-3 of Table 5.2.
Multiple comparisons are possible with these data to try to determine the causal effect of Lambeth Waterworks Company’s decision to move the pipe up the River Thames (and serendipitously reduce customers’ exposure to cholera-infected water; Huntington-Klein, 2022). One can treat Southwark-Vauxhall as a control group and use the data cross-sectionally, comparing rates in 1854 between the two companies (19 - 147 = -128). Alternatively, one can treat the data as an event study and make a simple before-and-after (pre-post) comparison, looking at incidence in Lambeth before and after it moved the pipes (19 - 85 = -66). However, these rely on a number of assumptions, which the decomposition in Columns 5-7 of Table 5.2 clarifies. In those columns, the observed incidence is decomposed into a water company fixed effect (\(u_{WC}\)) which contributes regardless of time period, a water-company time effect (trend; \(t_{WC}\)) which contributes to the change between 1849 and 1854, regardless of whether the water company’s pipes were moved, and a treatment effect (\(d_{WC}\)) which affects outcomes if ‘treated’ – i.e., the water pipes have been moved. \(d_{L}\) – the treatment effect of moving the pipe for Lambeth-supplied households – is the quantity (causal effect) of interest.
Cross-sectionally, the observed difference between Lambeth and Southwark-Vauxhall in 1854 is a function of the treatment effect, but also the time effects and fixed effects (\(d_{L} + u_{L} + t_{L} - u_{SV} - t_{SV}\); Column 6, Row 3). Intertemporally, the observed difference is a function of the treatment effect and the time effect – i.e., it is confounded by time differences that would have occurred anyway (\(d_{L} + t_{L}\); Column 7, Row 2). A DAG representing Snow’s Grand Experiment is displayed in Figure 5.7.
Table 5.2 shows that a further comparison is possible: the difference in differences over time between treated (Lambeth) and untreated (Southwark-Vauxhall) units (-66 - 12 = -78). The decomposition shows that this is a function of the treatment effect and the difference in the time trends in Lambeth and Southwark-Vauxhall (\(d_{L} + t_{L} - t_{SV}\)). This is the (2x2) Difference-in-Differences (DiD) estimator. 1 It is unbiased where the time-trends in treated and untreated units are the same (i.e., \(t_{L} - t_{SV} = 0\)); that is, the counterfactual time-trend is the same regardless of treatment assignment. Here, that means Lambeth’s cholera incidence in 1854 would have been 12 units higher than its 1849 level – 97 per 100,000 – had it not moved the pipe upriver. This is known as the ‘parallel trends assumption’.2
The quantity DiD recovers is the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) – the effect among units that actually received treatment over the periods observed – rather than the average treatment effect (ATE) for the population as a whole (Section 2.2.1). The purpose of the DiD estimate is to use within-variation in treated and control groups to condition on unit and time, simultaneously (i.e., blocking Pipe Location ← Time → Cholera and Pipe Location ← Water Company → Cholera in Figure 5.7). The basic 2x2 DiD empirical set-up is:
\[Y_{it} = \beta_{0} + {\beta_{1} \cdot Treat}_{i} + {\beta_{2} \cdot Post}_{t} + {\beta_{3} \cdot Treat}_{i} \cdot {Post}_{t} + \varepsilon_{it}\]
Where \({Treat}_{i}\) is an indicator for whether the observation is treated at any point and \({Post}_{t}\) is an indicator for whether the observation falls in the period after the treated unit was treated. The coefficient \(\beta_{3}\), which is the unique difference post-treatment in the treated group, represents the causal effect of treatment (subject to the parallel trends assumption). In practice, a regression model may also include control variables that make the parallel trends assumption more plausible or could be paired with matching to identify plausible comparator observations.3
As the parallel trends assumption relates to counterfactual outcomes (how the outcome would have changed over time in the treated group, absent treatment), it cannot be verified (Cunningham, 2021). However, in settings where more pre-treatment data are available, it is possible to perform two types of placebo test to at least explore the plausibility of the assumption. First, one can assess empirically whether trends were parallel in this pre-treatment period (e.g., one might assess whether changes across 1844-1849 were the same in Lambeth and Southwark-Vauxhall). Second, one can use placebo treatment dates to assess whether non-zero ‘treatment’ effects are observed (e.g., one could use data from 1839 and 1844 and pretend that the pipe was moved in 1844).
Though violations of either of these tests do not necessarily disprove the parallel trends assumption is correct (given the assumption relates to trends in the post-treatment period, specifically), they may provide some cause for concern. However, one should also consider the degree to which the assumption would need to be violated to overturn results (i.e., taking a quantitative bias analysis approach; Rambachan & Roth, 2023). Further, including extra untreated comparator groups similarly violating the parallel trends assumptions can sometimes still identify causal effects. For instance, to estimate the effect of government provision of emergency birth control on teen pregnancy rates using local authority (LA) level data, Girma & Paton (2011) use pregnancy rates among older women as extra controls (difference-in-difference-in-differences) on the assumption that these share similar within-LA time trends to younger women.4 See Cunningham (2021) for a decomposition of the ‘triple-difference’ design.
Parallel trends can be violated for several reasons, in addition to treated and untreated groups evolving separately. One reason is changes in composition in the groups over time (e.g., if Southwark-supplied households moved to Lambeth-supplied houses). A specific issue in cohort data is where there is non-random attrition. Another issue is anticipatory effects, a type of reverse causality, where the promise of treatment in future affects pre-treatment outcomes (e.g., fear of future job loss could affect present wellbeing). Finally, the assumption of parallel trends is dependent on the scale of the outcome; it may, for instance, hold on the natural (linear) scale but not on the log (percentage) scale, or vice versa.
In cohort data, more than two time periods may be available. In this case, the set of time and unit fixed effects can be added to the regression model – including both time and unit fixed effects in a model is referred to as the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimator, and is an extension of the standard fixed effects estimator seen in Section 5.5. Having data from more than two time periods can also enable one to assess treatment effect dynamics – i.e., how the differences between treated and untreated groups develop over time. For example, by adding further interaction terms between group and time dummies or modelling time trends in each group parametrically (e.g., with linear terms). This is useful where causal effects depend on length of exposure (e.g., long-term unemployment vs. short-term unemployment). Note, when using repeated data from the same observational units (i.e., cohort members), care must be taken to ensure standard errors reflect potential interdependencies (e.g., by using clustered standard errors).
In many settings, including in cohort data, the ‘event’ may occur at different times for different people (e.g., due to a policy being rolled out to different areas over time or people experiencing an event [e.g., unemployment] at different ages). This creates issues where treatment effects vary over time. To see this, imagine we have three groups: never treated, early treated, and late treated. With these data, there are four 2x2 DiD comparisons, which would be captured by a standard DiD estimator: early treated vs. never treated; late treated vs. never treated; early treated vs. late treated in the early post-treatment period; late treated vs. early treated in the late post-treatment period. Table 5.3 decomposes the DiD estimator for the late treated vs. early treated comparison, which causes the issue. Now the difference in the differences is \(d_{L} + t_{L} - t_{E} - {\mathrm{\Delta}d}_{E}\) (Column 4, Row 3; \({\mathrm{\Delta}d}_{E}\) refers to the change in the treatment effect between pre- and post-late period for the early treated group). In other words, to represent an unbiased estimate of the treatment effect on the late treated (\(d_{L}\)), it requires the parallel trends assumption as before (\(t_{L} - t_{E} = 0\)), but also a constant treatment effect over time (i.e., \({\mathrm{\Delta}d}_{E} = 0\)).
The TWFE estimator uses already-treated units as controls for later-treated units, generating bias. Estimators have been developed to avoid this – e.g., only using comparisons with never-treated or not-yet-treated groups; see textbooks from Cunningham (2021) and Huntington-Klein (2022) for further details. Goodman-Bacon (2021) shows that a DiD estimator that combines data from groups treated at different times is a weighted average of the separate 2x2 DiD comparisons that can be constructed. Weights depend on the group sizes but also on variation in treatment status, so are larger for groups treated near the middle of the observation window. This also means weights (and resulting estimates) can differ by changing the length of the observation window. The details of this are technical and beyond the scope of this document; see Cunningham (2021), Huntington-Klein (2022), or Goodman-Bacon (2021) for further details.
