title: 5.6 Difference in Differences
text:
5.6.2 Applications
Li & Avendano (2023) use MCS data to assess the employment and mental health impacts of the Lone Parent Obligation (LPO), a welfare-to-work scheme that placed job-search requirements on lone parents on benefits that was introduced during MCS cohort members’ childhoods. The authors use a DiD design, comparing children in lone-mother and two-parent households before and after the rollout of the policy to MCS-aged households in 2012. They find that, relative to the change in outcomes in the two-parent group, the introduction of the LPO was associated with greater maternal employment but also greater maternal and cohort member psychological difficulties in lone-parent households. The authors also find some evidence in support of the parallel trends assumption when looking at pre-treatment trends. However, their analysis assumes that parallel trends would occur post-LPO, which in this case would be during the cohort members’ adolescence – it is possible there are unique difficulties at this age in lone-parent households, which would violate parallel trends. Further, there were policy changes other than the LPO over the period which may have disproportionately affected lone parents (e.g., benefit cap, move to universal credit, and so on).
An additional limitation with the study was that the treatment variable – lone-parent household – is in fact time-varying and could be biased by changing composition of this group, especially if the LPO influences partnership decisions. However, they observed similar results when restricting to households whose partnership status did not change. An additional analysis that was not explored by the authors but could have been informative would be to compare lone-parent households according to whether they were or were not in receipt of income support pre-LPO (and thus may vary in their exposure to the policy).
Avendano & Panico (2018) also use the Millennium Cohort Study for policy evaluation. Specifically, they estimate the wellbeing and health effects of a 2003 legislative change that encouraged, though did not mandate, employers to implement flexible working practices (e.g., part-time and school-term contracts). Using a DiD design, they compare a group likely unaffected by the law (working mothers whose employers in Sweep 1 – prior to the law’s implementation – already offered flexible working) with a group who could be (working mothers whose employers did not offer flexible working in Sweep 1). They find no consistent evidence of an effect of the policy on mothers’ health and wellbeing in Sweeps 2-4 (2003-08). As the pre-treatment period comprised only Sweep 1, the authors were not able to assess differences in pre-treatment trends.5
Note, the estimand targeted in this study is the causal effect of the law upon mothers employed (at baseline) by firms yet to offer flexible working practices. While relevant for policy, such an effect would presumably mainly operate among the subset of women whose employers begin to offer flexible working practices. The estimand is therefore not the effect of the flexible working practices per se. Moreover, mothers expected to benefit most from flexible working practices could feasibly have chosen employers already offering these prior to the law’s enactment. The estimand therefore does not represent the effect of flexible working practices on those who choose such firms either. Both of these factors may explain the null results and have ramifications for the interpretation of the study.

title: 5.6 Difference in Differences
text:
5.6.3 Opportunities
Given the length and breadth of CLS’s cohorts, there are potentially many opportunities to use DiD designs with the data, both for policy evaluation and to assess the effect of events happening within cohort members’ (or their families’) lives (unemployment, divorce, etc.). This is also helped by the large, diverse samples that the cohorts comprise as this can make it possible to identify groups plausibly affected and unaffected by an exposure (e.g., as with lone- vs. two-parent households in Li & Avendano, 2023).
The cross-sectional variation used in the Li & Avendano (2023) and Avendano & Panico (2018) analyses described above was exposure due to being a potential target of the policy. Other opportunities can arise from geographic variation. For instance, Hawkins et al. (2011) use MCS data to compare smoking rates in Scotland and England before and after the introduction of anti-smoking legislation in Scotland.6 DiD designs can also arise from temporal variation in birth dates, though this is limited in CLS cohorts due to the recruitment criteria for members of some cohorts (e.g., NCDS cohort members were born in a single week of March 1958), but does not apply to cohort members’ families (e.g., parents). Temporal variation can also appear due to variation in interview dates (see Section 5.8).

title: 5.6 Difference in Differences
text:
Several authors have used Snow’s Grand Experiment to introduce Difference-in-Differences or placed in a DiD framework. See, for example, Caniglia & Murray (2020), Coleman (2019), Cunningham (2021), and Huntington-Klein (2022)↩︎
Even where the assumption is violated, the DiD estimator would be less biased than the simple fixed effects one (Section 5.5) where the difference is time trends (\(t_{L} - t_{SV}\)) is smaller than the time-trend in the treated unit itself (\(t_{L}\))↩︎
Readers may also explore the Synthetic Control method, which weights untreated observations to create a synthetic control data unit such that pre-treatment trends in the outcome for treated and synthetic control are similar. See Cunningham (2021) for further detail and Vagni & Breen (2021) for an application in cohort data.↩︎

title: 5.7 Study-Initiated Experiments
text:
5.7.1 Method
Several of CLS’s cohorts have embedded randomised experiments to test the effect of different survey methodologies on participation rates or measurement. We discuss these experiments here as we believe they are underutilised presently. That said, the material is somewhat out of keeping with the rest of this document as it is not focused on making causal inferences with observational data. This section can therefore be safely skipped if it is not of interest. Note, experiments have their own methodological considerations which interested readers will need to explore if opting to analyse the data.
Many of the experiments in CLS’s cohorts have only been implemented in small pilot studies and used to inform ongoing data collection, but some have been implemented among a plurality of cohort members. Almost all have appeared in recent sweeps as the studies have become more complex and as survey technologies have developed. Below is a brief overview of experiments in CLS’s cohorts that we are aware of. Further details can be found in academic publications (see next subsection) or sweep-specific technical reports.
An important feature of these experiments is that the interventions implemented could have effects on both response rates and measurement. For instance, offering a web questionnaire in a sequential mixed-mode design can incentivise more cohort members to respond (Goodman et al., 2022), but it may also affect data quality if, for instance, lack of interviewer presence in the web mode leads to more hurried interview completion. Given that measurements are only taken from cohort members who choose to participate, simple comparisons of observations across experimental arms may be biased due to implicitly conditioning on participation, a collider variable (Figure 5.8).
The differential non-response this implies should be accounted for in statistical analysis. Potentially suitable methods include multiple imputation (Section 5.4) and/or quantitative bias analysis (Section 5.20). Bias from differential non-response may be detected by examining the distribution of baseline covariates in each experimental arm or using negative controls (variables unlikely to be impacted by the experimental treatment; Section 5.15) as alternate outcome variables. In practice, absolute differences in response rates may be small, limiting the size of the bias arising from selection.

title: 5.7 Study-Initiated Experiments
text:
Table 5.4: Experiments in CLS’s Cohort Studies.






Experiment
Description




NCDS Age 55y (Sweep 9) Mixed-Mode Survey Experiment
Cohort members with a known UK telephone number (n = 10,558) were randomised to telephone-only (n = 1,499) or a web-then-telephone sequential mixed-mode design (n = 9,059).


BCS70 Age 42y (Sweep 9) Targeted Interviewer Experiment
A set of cohort members who had refused prior surveys (n = 1,009) were randomly allocated to ‘high performer’ interviewers known to achieve high response rates or to other interviewers.


Next Steps Age 25y (Sweep 8) Early-Bird Web Incentive Experiment
Participants in a soft launch sample (n = 2,215) were given £10 to complete the survey which, for half the sample, increased to £20 if the survey was completed within three weeks of invite and via web questionnaire.


Next Steps Age 25y (Sweep 8) Progress Bar Experiment
Participants responding via web were randomised to see a progress bar or not while completing the questionnaire, though an error in coding meant no participants early in fieldwork saw the progress bar. The experiment was originally intended to be run only during the soft launch but continued when there was no clear evidence of effects on completion rates; such results-driven decisions can increase the risk of false positives (Simmons et al., 2011).


Next Steps Age 32y (Sweep 9) Differential Incentive Experiment
Participants in a soft launch sample (n = 3,206) were given a tapered incentive, which for some participants was dependent on their response at the Age 25y sweep. In one trial arm, Age 25y non-respondents were offered £35 to complete the Age 32y survey (£25 after the first three weeks) while respondents were offered £25 (£15 after the first three weeks). In the other arm, a single tapered incentive was used (£30, dropping to £20 after the first three weeks). Offering a greater incentive to non-respondents did not boost participation rates, so the single tapered incentive was used post-soft launch.


Next Steps Age 32y (Sweep 9) Interview Length Experiment
Non-respondents from a soft launch sample (n = 1,337) were randomised to be invited to complete either a short or long version of a mop-up web questionnaire. As the short version was more successful at boosting response, it was used for (post-soft launch) non-responding cohort members.


MCS Age 9m (Sweep 1) Health Records Experiment
In the sweep dress rehearsal, parents of cohort members were randomised to be asked to give consent for either (a) the interviewer to copy information from the cohort member’s Personal Child Health Record (Red Book) or (b) for routinely collected health data to be linked to survey responses.


MCS Age 7y (Sweep 4) Refusal Experiment
Refusals at this sweep were randomised to one of four groups in a 2x2 design where (a) cohort members’ families were sent or not sent a leaflet encouraging a response and (b) all refusing families were reissued or only those judged to be soft or circumstantial refusals were reissued.


MCS Ages 7y-11y (Sweeps 4-5) Between-Sweep Mailout Experiment
In 2010, cohort families (n = 15,653) were sent letters requesting contact information. Families were randomised to receive letters that used formal or informal and simpler language, the latter also being signed by the cohort maintenance officer, rather than the study Principal Investigator.


MCS Age 11y (Sweep 5) Interviewer Pay Experiment
For cohort families in the first wave of fieldwork, interviewers were randomised to receive a bonus fee for successful interview or not.


MCS Age 23y (Sweep 8) Mixed Mode Survey Experiment
Cohort members in the soft launch sample were randomised to face-to-face interview-only or a web-then-face-to-face sequential mixed-mode design.


MCS COVID-19 Wave 3 Survey Incentive Experiment
Cohort members were randomised to receive a £10 incentive for successful completion of the survey or no financial incentive whatsoever.

title: 5.7 Study-Initiated Experiments
text:
5.7.2 Applications
Several studies have used data from experiments in Table 5.4. Goodman et al. (2022) used data from the NCDS Age 55y mixed-mode experiment in which eligible cohort members were randomised to telephone-only or sequential mixed-mode (web-then-telephone) survey designs, in order to estimate effects of survey mode (telephone interview vs. web questionnaire) upon item and sweep non-response rates and measured responses (e.g., on socioeconomic status, health behaviours, and physical and mental health). Sweep response rates were higher for cohort members in the sequential mixed-mode arm, and there were differences across arms in reported values for several socially valent characteristics such as mental health and alcohol consumption (the web survey was entirely anonymous, unlike the telephone survey). Given the (small) difference in response rates by mode, missing values for non-respondents were imputed via multiple imputation under the Missing at Random assumption. As ‘treated’ participants were randomised to the web-then-telephone sequential mixed-mode design, rather than to web specifically, treatment group was used as an instrumental variable (Section 5.9) to obtain a ‘complier average causal effect’ (CACE) – here, the average causal effect of web participation (relative to telephone response) among those who ‘complied’, i.e., responded via web instead of telephone when offered. Among other things, this analysis assumes that assignment to mixed-mode itself did not influence measured responses among those who instead responded via telephone.
Calderwood (2014) examined the effectiveness of a redesigned letter sent to MCS participants between waves to minimise loss to follow-up. She found that cohort families sent the redesigned letter were more likely to return the completed forms early, including among non-English-speaking families and families with parents who had no qualifications, subpopulations for whom effects were expected to be greatest. However, longer-term effects on returning of forms were more muted. Booth et al. (2024) investigated the effect of a monetary incentive given to MCS participants to complete a COVID-19 survey – the incentive was associated with both increased response rates and improved data quality. As data quality could only be ascertained from respondents, statistical adjustment was used to account for selection resulting from differences in response rates by treatment arm.

title: 5.7 Study-Initiated Experiments
text:
5.7.3 Opportunities
Existing studies that have exploited experiments embedded within the cohorts have focused on short-term outcomes – e.g., response rates or measurement at the sweep in which the experiment took place. As further sweeps become available it will be possible to examine long-term outcomes – for instance on attrition from the cohorts or the measurement of change across time (e.g., ageing and other trajectories). It is possible that incentives to participate have only short-term effects on retention if marginal participants drop out at subsequent sweeps. Alternatively, the offering of incentives in just one sweep could reduce long-term response, if the removal of financial incentives reduces intrinsic motivation (cf. Gneezy & Rustichini, 2000). Existing studies assessing effects of survey design on measurement have also focused on univariate descriptive statistics, but this is only one type of analysis performed with cohort data. Bias in sample means and proportions may not translate into material levels of bias in, e.g., associational analyses, which could be tested in the experimental data.
Studies that have investigated the effects of survey design on measurement and data quality have used statistical control (Booth et al., 2024) or multiple imputation (Goodman et al., 2022) to account for differential non-response. Quantitative Bias Analysis (Section 5.20) could instead be used to estimate effects under various plausible models of selection, though differences in response rates across treatment arms are typically small and selection effects may not be large enough to make substantive differences to results.
It is sometimes the case that variables capturing treatment arm within the experiment are not available in the standard datasets on the UK Data Service and require bespoke data access instead. It is also sometimes the case that data on the UK Data Service are only available for participants at a given sweep, though non-respondents may have been part of the experiment, too. As noted, non-response can lead to bias in analyses of experiments, so data from non-respondents may be required. This is the case for the NCDS Age 55y mixed-mode experiment, at least. Data enquiries can be sent to the CLS Data team.

title: 5.8 Natural Experiments
text:
5.8.1 Method
In RCTs, researchers intentionally use a procedure to assign people to treatment groups at random. The outcome of the procedure is – in expectation – not systematically related to factors, besides the treatment it determines (and consequences thereof), that may affect subsequent outcomes of interest, both known and unknown. In so far as the randomisation procedure can be said to affect outcomes, it is via the intervention that membership of a particular treatment group entails. For example, in sufficiently large RCTs that use the results of a fair coin toss to determine assignment, the results of coin tosses should not be correlated with participants’ sex, age or other characteristics, other than through chance, but could still be related to outcomes through the treatment group the coin tosses determine. This bears repeating: the coin toss can have a causal effect on outcomes, but it is only through its effect on treatment group.
Analogous processes sometimes occur without a researcher’s input. Most clearly, this occurs where randomisation is adopted for reasons other than sating academic interest – for instance, to allocate a resource. During the Vietnam War, the US Government used a lottery to draft soldiers. Besides being a politically palatable method of conscription, the draft has also been a valuable tool for understanding the effects of military service on various life outcomes (see, e.g., Conley & Heerwig, 2012). Games of pure chance, such as roulette and national lotteries, provide players with an endorphin rush, but also help researchers study the effects of wealth shocks on, e.g., health (Cesarini et al., 2016). Note, in each of these, randomisation occurs only among people who are entered into the lottery. In the Vietnam draft, this was healthy males of conscription age. In gambling lotteries, it is individuals who have bought a ticket (Figure 5.9). Comparing draftees or prize winners with everybody else, entrant or not, would not recover a causal effect.
The Vietnam draft and national lotteries are examples of natural experiments and have the same properties that justify RCTs – assignment (a) influences exposure, (b) only has an effect on outcomes via its effect on exposure, (c) is not determined by other causes of the outcome, and (d) individuals (or other relevant observational units) subject to the natural experiment had a non-zero chance of both exposure and control. As with RCTs, these properties arise because of the explicit use of a randomisation procedure. But it is these properties that are of value, not randomisation itself.
There are many other cases where random processes are used to allocate resources. Sometimes this is an intentional feature of the process, as with lotteries. Other times it is a byproduct of other concerns. In social housing, individuals at the top of a waitlist may be offered whatever accommodation comes available first (Silva et al., 2025). In health, being born on a weekday rather than the weekend influences staff availability and thus the breastfeeding advice a new mother and her baby receive (Fitzsimons & Vera-Hernández, 2022). Processes like these are not random in the sense that exposure occurred for no predictable reason; housing becomes available when someone leaves a property and hospitals lower costs by reducing staff levels on weekends. Rather, the reasons for exposure are unrelated to potential outcomes: expectant mothers have little control over whether they go into labour on a Friday or a Saturday, and people on a housing waitlist do not control which houses become vacated as they move to the top of the list. Assignment mechanisms like these are said to be “as-if random” and have the properties that justify RCTs – assignment only has an effect on outcomes via the effect on exposure and assignment is not determined by other causes of the outcome.
Many natural experiments appear in survey data due to as-if random assignment to interview dates. The Unexpected Event During Survey Design (UESD; Muñoz et al., 2020) exploits large-scale events, such as major sporting competitions (e.g., the Olympics or the World Cup), political incidents, natural disasters, and terrorist atrocities occurring at some point during survey fieldwork and which bifurcate the sample into those surveyed before the event and those surveyed during or after. On the assumption that interview timing is unrelated to potential outcomes, comparing groups surveyed before and after the event can be used to determine the event’s causal effects, such as its effect on measures of psychological wellbeing, behaviour and political and social attitudes.
Assessing whether the assumption of as-if random interview timing is plausible in a given application requires detailed knowledge of the survey being utilised, its design and how it was conducted. The assumption may be violated if, for example, participants with the lowest chance of response are allocated to be interviewed first, so that further contact attempts could be made before the end of fieldwork, if necessary. In many surveys, participants are allocated to fieldwork ‘waves’ based upon shared characteristics – random assignment to interview date within these groups may be plausible, but between groups, not. The assumption of random timing can also be violated if the event itself affects survey design (e.g., delaying fieldwork) or a participant’s likelihood of responding. Another way the assumption can be violated is if there are pre-existing time trends that would have produced different average outcomes before or after the date of the event had it not actually occurred (e.g., if there is seasonality in recorded wellbeing). Further, the assumption can be violated if there are other events occurring simultaneously or there are collateral events, in which case the effect of the event itself cannot be identified or generalised to similar events that do not produce the same sequelae. Events like these are examples of ‘fat-handed interventions’ (Bailey et al., 2024) that involve a bundle of possible causes of an outcome, making it difficult to determine which aspects are operative.
Another usual assumption of the UESD is that the participants surveyed after the event were in fact exposed to the event (i.e., aware of it). There are several ways of assessing this, including indirectly: in the absence of a specific survey item on the event, analysts can use data sources such as Google Trends, contemporaneous polling, or news headline aggregators to assess the likelihood a person knew about the event. If exposure is less than 100%, any ‘causal’ estimate will be downward biased in inverse proportion to the extent of exposure. (This is equivalent to an Intention to Treat analysis, discussed further in Section 5.9.) In practice, differences in awareness can be beneficial as an elaborate theory would predict weaker or non-existent associations in groups less likely to be exposed – for instance, among those who do not read a newspaper or own a television (see James, 2024, for an example in this vein).
The UESD design does not map onto a single statistical method, though it has clear similarities with the strict Regression Discontinuity Design (discussed further in Section 5.10). UESD analyses can proceed cross-sectionally, with responses compared in groups recorded before and after the event (potentially in subgroups for whom the assumption of random timing is more plausible, as discussed above). The longitudinal nature of CLS cohorts can also be exploited – for instance, by performing fixed effects analysis to account for time-invariant confounders (Section 5.5) or matching upon prior measurements of the outcome (Section 5.2) to strengthen the plausibility that interview timing is independent of potential outcomes. Note, assumptions about random event timing can also be tested in part by (a) assessing covariate balance either side of the event and (b) assessing trends in the outcome variable in the period prior to the event occurring (i.e., to examine whether there were pre-existing time trends).
There are other natural experiments contained in CLS’s cohort data, including those related to the timing of birth (e.g., influencing relative age in school year and the minimum age of school leaving), the rollout of public policies, and the nature of how systems distribute resources. There likely exist others that are as yet unidentified as uncovering these requires detailed knowledge of relevant policy areas (e.g., awareness about how social housing is allocated). Several natural experiments are analysed in Instrumental Variables or Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) frameworks, for reasons that will be discussed in Sections 5.9 and 5.10. It is worth noting, though, that some events may at first glance appear random but in fact are not. For instance, one may expect dying by murder or from accidents to reflect happenstance, but smokers have a higher chance of the former (Davey Smith et al., 1992) and women using HRT have lower odds of the latter (Petitti et al., 1986).

title: 5.8 Natural Experiments
text: Figure 5.9: DAG representing a study using lottery wins to examine the effect of wealth on health. In observational data, the association between wealth and health may be biased by a host of confounders U (e.g., education level). Lottery wins represent a source of random variation in wealth, though only among lottery players – the decision to enter a lottery may be influenced by factors that also influence health (e.g., education level), but which player wins is a random process (unless rigged). More accurately, the total number of lottery tickets bought determines the expected win amount, so an ideal lottery study would condition upon number of tickets bought.

title: 5.8 Natural Experiments
text:
5.8.2 Applications
The UESD is relatively underutilised in CLS’s cohorts. Two studies have used data from Next Steps to examine the effect of the 07 July 2005 London Bombings, which were followed by rises in reported hate crimes committed against Muslims (Astorga-Rojas, 2023; Hole & Ratcliffe, 2020). Hole & Ratcliffe (2020) show a specific decline in happiness (though not an increase in depression) among Muslim girls in the period after 07 July, as well as an increase in their expectation of discrimination in the labour market. Supporting a causal interpretation, the authors also show the effect is specific to Sweep 2 of Next Steps, during which the event happened, rather than also present in Sweep 4, when measures of mental health were again collected. Astorga-Rojas (2023) uses a similar set-up and shows lower reported expectation to remain in full-time education after compulsory schooling among Muslim cohort members post 07 July.
Multiple papers have used data from individuals in social housing, exploiting the quasi-random nature of housing offers for those at the top of waiting lists at various times in the UK in the 20th and 21st centuries (Fumagalli & Fumagalli, 2019; Patacchini & Zenou, 2011; Silva et al., 2025). For instance, Fumagalli & Fumagalli (2019) use data from Next Steps and find lower social participation (operationalised as ‘hanging around’) in areas with greater ethnic diversity (which housing offers produce exogenous variation in). Note, a key issue with this design is that, although allocation to neighbourhood may be random, neighbourhoods vary on many different dimensions simultaneously. Though neighbourhood of residence may not be related to individual (baseline) characteristics among social housing tenants, it is not clear what aspect of neighbourhoods may be driving effects.
Several papers have used month of birth as a potentially exogenous determinant of relative age in one’s school year – in the UK, people born in September are the oldest in their class, whereas those born in August are usually the youngest, but parents have limited control over the time of year they conceive. Month of birth is often analysed in an RDD framework (Section 5.10) with data from multiple year groups pooled (e.g., comparing students born August or September in a given calendar year), but due to the design of CLS’s cohorts, comparing individuals within a school year is the only feasible approach, and only for MCS and Next Steps (which roughly span one school year), rather than NCDS and BCS70 (which only span a single week).1 Crawford et al. (2011) examine month of birth effects on multiple developmental outcomes in MCS and Next Steps cohort members, and show that, among other factors, cohort members born early in the school year have greater educational attainment and higher scores on cognitive tests than those born late in the school year.

title: 5.8 Natural Experiments
text:
5.8.3 Opportunities
As noted, the UESD is relatively underutilised in CLS’s cohorts, especially given the cumulative timespan of data collection represented. Several cohorts also contain data on accidents, though as discussed, the occurrence of accidents can be related to participant characteristics. Data on income and wealth shocks may also be available. We recommend reading the original UESD paper (Muñoz et al., 2020) as it is filled with practical advice and may spark ideas. A research-enabling project would be to produce databases of (a) policies and headlines detailing important events that have occurred during CLS survey fieldwork and (b) interview date ranges and (sub)samples where interview timing is plausibly exogenous (identified, e.g., by assessing sample balance around an index date). Note, however, exogeneity of interview timing only needs to be met with respect to potential outcomes of interest – there may be systematic reasons why individuals were interviewed on given dates, but if unrelated to potential outcomes, the assumption of (conditional) exchangeability would not be violated.

title: 5.9 Instrumental Variables
text:
5.9.1 Method
One issue with RCTs is that not everyone may comply with the intervention to which they have been assigned – in a medical trial, some of the ‘treated’ may stop taking the drug they have been given, and some of the ‘control’ may find the drug through other means, instead of remaining on placebo. Analogously, in natural experiments not everyone may receive or follow their expected intervention. For instance:
Simply comparing outcomes by assignment (known as an Intention to Treat [ITT] analysis), while often useful in policy terms, will not necessarily identify the causal effect of the treatment itself. Individuals are typically only randomised to receive encouragement to follow a certain treatment, rather than to adopt the treatment, per se – for instance, they are provided a box of medication and given instructions to take it, rather than administered it through force. To identify the causal effect of treatment, we instead need to look at those who comply.
This is not as simple as comparing outcomes among those who used the treatment because it is not use of treatment that is randomised. For instance, if we compare, among those entered into the Vietnam lottery, those who served and those who didn’t, we would compare on the one hand those who (1) served because they were drafted (compliers), (2) served because they would serve regardless of being drafted (always takers), or (3) served because they were not drafted (non-compliers) with, on the other hand, those who (a) did not serve because they weren’t drafted (compliers), (b) did not serve despite being drafted (never takers), or (c) did not serve because they were drafted (non-compliers). These are not equivalent groups and they are not necessarily identical according to their potential outcomes. See Table 5.5, which continues this worked example.
Accounting for non-compliance in the estimation of causal effects can instead be achieved using the Instrumental Variable (IV) design (Figure 5.10a). This design utilises variables that create – or are associated with (Goetghebeur et al., 2020) – exogenous variation in treatment, nudging subjects to a particular level of the exposure, rather than another, analogous to the role of a coin in an RCT. For instance, being picked in the Vietnam draft raised the probability a person would serve, but did not make it inevitable, while giving birth on a weekday makes it more likely, but by no means certain, that a mother will breastfeed.
In addition to meeting the assumptions of positivity, consistency and no interference, to be valid, an instrumental variable must have four properties (Goetghebeur et al., 2020). First, it must be associated with exposure (relevance; Z → X in Figure 5.10a). Second, it must be unrelated to any unmeasured confounders of the exposure-outcome relationship (independence; no Z ← U → Y). Third, it must be independent of the outcome conditional on the treatment and unmeasured confounders (exclusion restriction; Z → X → Y, the only directed path from Z to Y), unless these are conditioned upon (Figure 5.10b); the lottery used in the Vietnam War draft is an instrumental variable but only among males eligible to serve.1 Fourth, the size of the treatment effect must be independent of the instrument (homogeneity) or, where there is effect heterogeneity, there cannot be both compliers (people who use treatment only when encouraged) and defiers (people who use treatment only when discouraged) within the same study population (monotonicity).2
Under these assumptions, it is possible to use estimates of the association between the instrument and the exposure and the instrument and the outcome (in Figure 5.10, paths Z → X and Z → X → Y, respectively) to obtain an estimate of the causal effect of the exposure upon the outcome (X → Y); in effect, exploiting exogenous variation in the exposure related to the IV (Z → X). Several IV estimators exist. The most commonly used, two-stage least squares regression (IV-2SLS), uses the instrument to predict the exposure variable, and then uses these predicted values to estimate associations with the outcome variable. Unlike ITT analysis, this procedure provides an estimate of the change in the outcome per unit change in the exposure. Similarly, the widely used Wald estimator scales the association between the instrument and the outcome by the instrument’s association with the exposure.
Where there is treatment effect heterogeneity and the monotonicity assumption is met, IV methods estimate a specific quantity termed the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE). This is the average effect of the exposure within the variation induced by the instrumental variable, i.e., among compliers – people whose level of the exposure is sensitive to (changes according to) the level of the instrument (for instance, those who served in the Vietnam War only because they were drafted). The LATE, which is sometimes referred to as the Complier Average Causal Effect (CACE), can differ from a global average treatment effect because causal effects may be heterogeneous according to why someone was exposed. For instance, the effect of military service on income among those who only served due to the draft could be different to those who served voluntarily (especially if the latter did so in expectation of serving’s beneficial effect on their outcomes).
Discrepancies between observational associations and IV estimates may therefore arise not just because of bias in the observational association, but also because a different quantity is being estimated. It is generally not possible to identify which individuals are compliers because the ‘fundamental problem of causal inference’ (Holland, 1986) reappears: we cannot see both states of the world, where a person receives the instrument and doesn’t. However, characteristics of the population of compliers can be observed (assuming monotonicity) by comparing the attributes of the exposed among those with the instrument and those without. Nevertheless, this population may not be of particular scientific or policy interest; we may wish to know the effect of military service on recruits in general, for example. The price of internal validity is potentially lower external validity.
Where treatment effects are heterogeneous, monotonicity is required because, otherwise, the total effect of the instrument on the exposure becomes a net combination of opposite responses, making the resulting instrumental variable estimate difficult to interpret (for worked examples demonstrating this, see Cunningham, 2021; Huntington-Klein, 2022). IV methods can exploit multiple IVs, which can increase statistical power and precision, but make interpretation more challenging where treatment effects are heterogeneous as the estimated treatment effect is then an average across different groups. Additionally, where the exposure is continuous, rather than binary, the LATE is a weighted average where compliers are weighted in proportion to how affected they are by the IV (i.e., those whose exposure changes the most are weighted more highly), again making interpretation challenging.
Many instruments have been proposed and used in the empirical literature, particularly in economics. Examples include (Baiocchi et al., 2014; Cunningham, 2021; Hernán & Robins, 2023; Huntington-Klein, 2022; Mellon, 2025):
However, the popularity of these IVs can itself be a cause for concern (Gallen & Raymond, 2020; Mellon, 2025). For instance, weather has been linked with over 190 treatment variables, such as income and food prices, through which it may plausibly affect outcomes (Mellon, 2025). Such disparate effects suggest exclusion restrictions do not hold, though Mellon (2025) discusses conditions under which this may not be the case (e.g., the exclusion restriction holds for the specific population under study), as well as outlining a procedure for determining whether this matters for a planned IV study.
Note, IV estimates can be especially sensitive to violations of assumptions (Hernán & Robins, 2023), in particular where the instruments are ‘weak’ (have small associations with the exposure; J. W. Jackson & Swanson, 2015). Baiocchi et al. (2014) and Cinelli & Hazlett (2025) describe quantitative bias analysis methods for IV designs.
Another class of IVs that are routinely used are genetic variants – i.e., as in Mendelian Randomisation (MR) analysis. (Almost) every human trait is heritable (Polderman et al., 2015; Turkheimer, 2000). Mendelian inheritance means parents pass on a random half of their genomes to their children, and thus, conditional on parents’ genomes, a child’s genes potentially represent a source of exogenous variation in a trait. For instance, variants of the ALDH2 gene are related to the comfort with which one metabolises alcohol and have thus been used to instrument alcohol consumption and determine its effect upon health (L. Chen et al., 2008), a canonical example of a difficult question to answer with standard observational data. An advantage of using genetic variants as instruments is that they are inherited at conception and so are not subject to reverse causality. However, this also comes with the disadvantage that genes are carried across life and so it is difficult to determine or isolate specific timing of exposure (though, see Richardson et al., 2020).
Due to data unavailability, MR analyses are generally undertaken without genetic data from multiple family members and therefore cannot condition on family and so do not necessarily have the characteristics motivating MR. (MR with family-level data is discussed further in Section 5.14.) Genetic variants are not randomly distributed around the population (Abdellaoui et al., 2019, 2022), and population-level MR analysis can be biased by (population) genetic phenomena, including population stratification and assortative mating, as well as genetic nurture (effects of parental genes on offspring via parental behaviour) and other indirect genetic effects. Population stratification refers to differences in particular genes across groups, which can lead to (non-causal) association between genes and environments – famously, genes that are more prevalent among individuals of East Asian ancestry will be associated with chopstick use, despite this having a cultural explanation (D. Hamer & Sirota, 2000). Assortative mating refers to the phenomenon of individuals not mating randomly, which can lead to associations between phenotypes (and thus the genetic variants they are influenced by) without one phenotype having a causal effect upon another. For instance, if highly educated people are more likely to mate with taller individuals, then genes that influence either will become correlated and a population MR analysis would suggest education influences height (or vice versa) when this is not the case. Both population stratification and assortative mating represent violations of the independence assumption.
An additional issue with MR analyses (including those using family-level data) is horizontal pleiotropy, where a genetic variant has an effect on multiple phenotypes, not due to the main trait of interest having an effect on the others (vertical pleiotropy): many genes have effects on multiple phenotypes, a necessary consequence of the limited number of protein-coding genes (~20,000) in the human genome. Horizontal pleiotropy represents a potential violation of the exclusion restriction assumption. Horizontal pleiotropy can also arise through linkage disequilibrium (LD), whereby variants located close together on a chromosome are correlated because recombination of DNA during meiosis (formation of sex cells, gametes) rarely separates nearby loci, so DNA is inherited in blocks. Thus, a genetic variant which has a causal effect on one trait may be in LD with a variant that has an effect on another trait, creating a correlation between the two traits.
The risk of horizontal pleiotropy is heightened when polygenic scores (PGS) are used as instruments. PGS aggregate the effect of many genes (e.g., hundreds or more) into a single weighted summary variable, with the individual weights determined from Genome-Wide Association Studies, which use a hypothesis-free approach. Unlike with single genetic variants like ALDH2, the pathways linking PGS to a trait may thus be poorly understood. This is a particular concern when studying complex traits, such as education, that are genetically influenced through multiple other traits (e.g., cognitive ability, conscientiousness, and physical health), which may themselves have independent effects on outcomes. As individual genes often have only weak effects, there is a trade-off between using genetic instruments that most plausibly satisfy the exclusion restriction (and independence) assumptions and using instruments that are well-powered. Researchers often strike a balance by using PGS created from the top ‘hits’ in a GWAS (e.g., variants exceeding the genome-wide significance, p <= 5x10-08, level). Multivariable MR, in which PGS for related traits are also used (Davies et al., 2019), may also reduce bias in this situation. PGS also raise difficulty for meeting the consistency assumption.
Note, however, whether population stratification, assortative mating, or horizontal pleiotropy matter in a particular MR application is an empirical question – some traits are not subject to assortative mating, nor do some genes vary in prevalence in important ways across populations, and horizontal pleiotropy may not be relevant in a specific situation. Further, as discussed in Section 5.16, clever cross-context designs may be used to elaborate the theory that the gene has an exogenous effect on the exposure and provide compelling causal evidence.

title: 5.9 Instrumental Variables
text:
5.9.2 Applications
Fitzsimons & Vera-Hernández (2022) use data from the MCS to assess the effects of breastfeeding on various measures of child development using time of birth and day of birth as instruments for the likelihood that someone received breastfeeding support in hospital. Major strengths of their study are their ability to demonstrate that day of birth was not related to mothers’, babies’ and pregnancy characteristics and that associations were confined to low-SES individuals for whom breastfeeding support was particularly likely to have an effect on breastfeeding rates. Further, the authors augment their analysis using an external dataset containing detailed data on postnatal care to demonstrate that the relevance assumption is plausible (e.g., that day of birth is related to receiving advice and active support with breastfeeding).
Hyppönen et al. (2022) use data from parents in the NCDS to assess the effect of BMI upon mortality using cohort members’ (i.e., offspring) BMI as an instrumental variable; the authors’ argument is that offspring BMI is unlikely to be confounded by underlying disease, a major confounder of the BMI-mortality association in observational studies (i.e., reverse causality; Davey Smith et al., 2009). The authors find that associations between BMI and mortality are stronger when using the IV. However, they find evidence that offspring BMI is confounded by socioeconomic position (confounding bias can be amplified when using IVs; J. W. Jackson & Swanson, 2015). It is also possible the exclusion restriction is violated if, e.g., offspring socioeconomic position (which could have a causal effect on offspring BMI) affects parental mortality. Further, because the instrument captures the stable familial component of BMI, the analysis disregards temporary variation in parental BMI, and so estimates target the effect of long-run – rather than contemporaneous – adiposity.

title: 5.9 Instrumental Variables
text:
5.9.3 Opportunities
The temporal and geographical range of the CLS cohorts, as well as linkage with admin data, potentially opens up many opportunities for novel instrumental variable analyses. However, the discovery of plausible IVs depends on deep domain-specific knowledge. Given the wide range of data that are available in the cohorts, there may be a case for extending previous successful IV applications – e.g., to extend the Fitzsimons & Vera-Hernández (2022) work to outcomes captured later in life (e.g., educational attainment) or other domains (e.g., to personality traits); though whether IV assumptions are met for these additional outcomes would need to be examined. Data on offspring and/or parents are available in each cohort and can enable IV analyses using family members’ traits. However, again, whether the IV assumptions are met will need to be assessed for the exposure and outcome under study. Finally, PGS for a wide range of traits are now available in each cohort (Shireby et al., 2025) and could be used in MR analyses. For researchers wishing to exploit single genetic variants, raw genetic data can be accessed via application to CLS.

title: 5.9 Instrumental Variables
text:
Typically, and as displayed in Figure 5.10, the three IV assumptions are stated referring to causal effects rather than (conditional) associations. For instance, relevance is defined as the IV having a causal effect on the exposure and exclusion restriction as the IV not having causal effects on outcomes except via the exposure, X. In the causal framing, not conditioning on U1 in Figure 5.10b may be classified as a violation of independence (i.e., presence of open back-door paths) rather than exclusion restriction as above. In the causal framing, selection paths (e.g., adding Z → S ← Y to Figure 5.10b) do not fall easily under any assumption’s definition, whereas they sit straightforwardly under exclusion restriction as the assumptions are defined above.↩︎
There are various (relatively technical) versions of the homogeneity assumption. See Goetghebeur et al. (2020) and Hernán & Robins (2023) for more detail.↩︎

title: 5.10 Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
5.10.1 Method
Instrumental variable designs use variation in a third variable (the instrument) as a source or marker of exogenous variation in an exposure. Sometimes there are variables that have an effect on an exposure and vary over a wide range. While overall these variables may be associated with confounding factors, narrow parts of their variation can lead to large differences in the likelihood of exposure. Within this narrow range, variation is therefore strongly related to the exposure, but may be only weakly related – if at all – to the confounding factors.
Take democratic elections – does becoming a Member of Parliament (MP) increase one’s salary after the end of one’s parliamentary career (Eggers & Hainmueller, 2009)? We can’t simply compare people who win elections with those that lose them because rational political parties field their most promising candidates in safer seats and voters give their support to candidates they perceive as more able. People who win large majorities differ from those who lose handily in ways that could allow them to obtain higher wages absent becoming an MP. But winners take all in a first-past-the-post system, whether the majority is one or twenty thousand. People who lose by a small amount are likely similar, on average, to those who win by a small amount. Within a small margin, random factors can be decisive (Figure 5.11).1
As its name suggests, the Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) takes advantage of small perturbations around discontinuities such as this. RDD comes in two flavours: sharp and fuzzy (Figure 5.12). In sharp RDD, exposure is zero on one side of the discontinuity and complete on the other. The first-past-the-post election system represents a sharp discontinuity; one is voted in, or one isn’t. In fuzzy RDD, probabilities of exposure are intermediate, but around the discontinuity, the likelihood of exposure changes substantially. Age-based eligibility criteria for vaccination represent a fuzzy discontinuity; some people below the threshold may be eligible for vaccination for other reasons, while those above the threshold may opt against vaccination. But ageing a matter of days can still generate large jumps in vaccination rates and by itself would not notably affect outcomes of interest (Basta & Halloran, 2019).
Discontinuities are common wherever there is some form of rationing or where definitive criteria are used to make eligibility transparent or implementation more straightforward. This is a feature of most bureaucracies and administrative systems, including clinical settings where treatment protocols are used. Discontinuities graft sharp changes onto otherwise continuous characteristics. While a person may be identified as requiring medical attention based on strict criteria, underlying risks change more gradually; hospitals may use a cut-off for low birth weight of 2.5 kg but weighing 2.51 kg is little better than 2.49 kg. Discontinuities also arise through cleavages in time – a policy is enacted whereas before it was not. People born on August 31st are the youngest in their school year, while people born on September 1st are the oldest. People born August 31st 1957 were able to leave school at age fifteen, if they so wished, but people born a day later had to wait until age sixteen thanks to the passing of an Act of Parliament, which raised the minimum school leaving age.
In RDD parlance, the variable determining exposure is referred to as the ‘running variable’ (Cunningham, 2021).2 The basic identification strategy of RDD is to estimate the difference in the outcome around the discontinuity (for instance, vote share and wealth; Figure 5.13), because the units of analysis are, in theory, exchangeable at the time the exposure is assigned. This can be achieved using parametric or non-parametric methods.
In a simple parametric set-up, the relationship between the running variable and the outcome is modelled with continuous terms, and a binary variable for whether the running variable is above the discontinuity is also included in the regression (see Equation 5.1). The continuous terms capture the association between the running variable and the outcome that would appear absent the variable influencing exposure. The binary term captures the effect of the exposure on the outcome at the cut-off.
where i indexes individuals, \(x_{i}\) represents the level of the running variable for person i, and \(D\left( x_{i} \geq X \right)\) is a binary variable equal to 1 where \(x_{i}\) is at or above the discontinuity cut-off point (\(X\)).
The parametric design uses data from a wide range of the running variable. It relies on modelling the association between the running variable and the outcome appropriately – incorrectly modelled non-linearities may yield a spurious non-zero coefficient for the binary discontinuity term. In the non-parametric set-up, only data from around the discontinuity are used, with weighting possibly used to place greater emphasis on observations particularly close to the cut-off. The non-parametric approach is more data-intensive as it requires sufficiently large samples close to the discontinuity but has the advantage that it does not rely on appropriately modelling the correct functional form. The sample size requirement can be relaxed by increasing the width around the discontinuity from which observations are used, but this comes at the cost of reducing the plausibility that confounding factors – including the running variable itself – are the cause of associations with the outcome variable.
In fuzzy RDD, the running variable is associated with exposure above and below the discontinuity, and being above the cut-off is effectively an ‘encouragement’. Instrumental variable methods (Section 5.9) are therefore used to rescale the effect by the cut-off’s influence on probability of exposure. The causal effects estimated in sharp and fuzzy RDD are local to the cut-off, with the added proviso that in fuzzy RDD this is the causal effect among those who ‘comply’ with the encouragement – i.e., were exposed due to just sitting above the cut-off (as such, fuzzy RDD requires homogeneity or monotonicity assumptions discussed in Section 5.9). These estimands can reflect relevant research and policy quantities if the causal effect arising from the imposition of the cut-off is of research interest.
A major strength of the RDD approach is that some of its assumptions can be falsified (though not verified). Several tests present themselves to the budding RDD analyst. First, similar to RCTs, balance in baseline (observed) covariates around the cut-off can be examined. Second, models can be repeated using placebo cut-offs. These cut-offs should not be related to jumps in the probability of treatment and so any association would be evidence that the model is misidentified or its assumptions are violated. For instance, using an imaginary decision rule for elections where the ‘winning’ candidate wins if they receive 20% more votes than their closest rival, or imagining the school leaving age was raised in 1971 or 1973 instead of 1972.
RDD is not without its limitations, however. First, as intimated, the general form between exposure and outcome needs to be appropriately modelled; mismodelling can lead to discontinuities appearing which aren’t there in practice, or vice versa (Gelman & Imbens, 2019; Huntington-Klein, 2022). A key issue with sharp RDD is that there is no ‘common support’ – i.e., treated and untreated individuals do not overlap in their value of the running variable. Counterfactual values therefore have to be extrapolated, rather than directly drawn from observed data from those in the comparator group.
A second limitation is that the same threshold may be used in multiple systems, analogous to violations of the exclusion restriction in the IV design (Section 5.9). For instance, in the UK, turning eighteen allows one to buy alcohol legally but also to gamble and buy cigarettes, too, each of which could affect health outcomes. Similarly, being the oldest in one’s school year may increase academic confidence, but also physical maturity and social confidence. Each might impact educational attainment.
A third limitation of RDD is that, as regression discontinuities are most frequently found in administrative systems, the ‘treatments’ one can examine are limited by those implemented by these systems. These treatments may be relatively narrow (Bann et al., 2024). For instance, just meeting eligibility criteria for more generous welfare payments may be plausibly exogenous, but the total effect of these payments on income or wealth may be smaller, shorter-lived, and easier to compensate for than changes in income observed more generally and which are of greater interest (e.g., in social epidemiology top and bottom quintiles of income are often compared).
Finally, and most subtly, individuals, or the people acting on their behalf, may be aware of cut-offs and their implications and may act to ensure they are eligible for the treatment – or ineligible, if the treatment is undesirable. For example, some individuals who are close to being classified as long-term unemployed might accept a job offer more readily in light of looming cuts to welfare cheques(Card et al., 2007). Businesses that would be subject to increased regulation if they grow might opt against hiring an extra employee (Garicano et al., 2016). In these cases, there may be confounding even close to the cut-off; checking the distribution of covariates and density of observations either side can help assess this. Another subtle issue is misreporting or other fraudulent behaviour to meet eligibility criteria.3 In this case, there is potentially non-differential or non-independent measurement error in the running variable.

Limiting to a narrow range in which the running variable (Panel B) has a substantial effect on determining exposure X (e.g., at a cut-off where R determines eligibility for X), variation within the running variable is not sufficient to itself cause differences in the outcome or be associated with other causes (U) of the outcome. title: 5.10 Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
5.10.2 Applications
Several studies have applied RDD to CLS’s cohorts. One popular object of study in the RDD literature is the 1972 Raising of the School Leaving Age (ROSLA, discussed above). In fact, the UK (or rather its constituent countries) has undergone several ROSLAs, including in 1947 and more recently in 2013 and 2015, with the raising of the minimum ‘participation age’ in education or training. As discussed in Section 5.8.2, though there is little variation in birth dates among CLS cohort members, there is plenty among their family members, including their parents. Sabates & Duckworth (2010) exploit the 1947 ROSLA and use data from the NCDS to assess the effect of increased maternal education upon cohort members’ developmental outcomes, finding positive effects on maths ability but no effects on reading or behaviour. One drawback of this approach is that studying parental effects within a birth cohort necessarily conditions upon fertility and the parent’s age at birth. It is possible that both are influenced by parental education.
Another RDD often used in the educational literature is test scores as these are widely used to determine entry into specific institutions (e.g., minimum A-Level grades for acceptance into top universities or degree requirements for entry into competitive graduate schemes).4 In the UK, entry into selective grammar schools is largely based on results on the ‘eleven-plus’, a test similar to an IQ test. Pastore & Jones (2023) use data from cognitive tests at age 11 years in the NCDS to proxy for eleven-plus scores to assess the effect of attending grammar school on several educational, labour market, and health outcomes. However, an issue is that, as they only use a proxy measure and (unobserved) qualifying eleven-plus scores for grammar school varied across England and Wales, they have to estimate the threshold determining grammar school entry from the NCDS data themselves. They do however successfully perform several ‘negative control’ tests (Section 5.15), which support a causal interpretation (e.g., no association between grammar school attendance at the discontinuity and cognitive ability scores at age 7 years).

title: 5.10 Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
5.10.3 Opportunities
We have noted that discontinuities most frequently arise when an individual interacts with a (government) service. Specific criteria are frequently used to determine eligibility for services or duties (e.g., for income support) and hard geographical boundaries determine the bodies under whose purview one sits – for instance, residents of Bassetlaw in Nottinghamshire are eligible for three rounds of IVF, whereas their neighbours in surrounding districts (including across the same street, in some cases) are only eligible for one (Patel & Sissons, 2024). Befitting this, geographic and admin data linkages have the potential to be particularly useful for performing RDD in CLS’s cohorts. For instance, educational admin data linkages may enable examination of the effects of educational access or attainment on various outcomes – universities offer places based on letter grades, though the underlying exam scores are continuous. An additional advantage of geographic (or other) variation is that some policies may be only rolled out in specific areas or groups over time. In this case, temporal variation could be used to identify causal effects with unaffected groups used for comparison – for instance, eligibility for the latest increase in the education participation age depends on birth date but has only been implemented in England and not Scotland or Wales. An issue with performing RDD in the cohorts is that sample sizes may be relatively limited around a cut-off, and so parametric methods – or pooling data across cohorts and with other data sources – may be necessary.

title: 5.11 Target Trial Emulation
text:
5.11.1 Method
So far, we have mainly discussed the benefit of the randomised controlled trial (RCT) design as its use of randomisation to achieve exchangeability. But RCTs have additional features that are beneficial for causal inference (Hernán et al., 2025). Specifically, they encourage the individuals involved in designing the RCT to ask well-defined causal questions by specifying study design and analysis plans that realise these questions as estimands (quantities one wishes to estimate); as discussed in Section 2.1, clearly stating the estimand one wishes to estimate is a key component of any good causal research.
RCT study designs detail the eligibility criteria for the study participants, the treatment strategies that will be compared, the method of treatment assignment, the outcomes of interest, the start and end of follow-up, the causal contrast of interest, and the analysis plan. These components, when combined (and written well), enumerate the population, exposures and outcomes of interest for which a causal comparison is to be made. For instance, an RCT of COVID-19 vaccination on mortality may include individuals if they have not had a vaccine or COVID-19 infection so far, compare two dosages of active vaccine vs. placebo, assigned randomly, with mortality rates determined five years post-randomisation. Comparing survival rates in vaccination vs. placebo groups would provide an intention-to-treat estimate of the effect of the vaccine on mortality assuming no differential loss to follow-up.
Not every failure of observational studies arises due to problems with the underlying process that generated the data (e.g., confounding, measurement, and response biases). Some are “self-inflicted” due to decisions that are made by the data analyst in the design of their study (Hernán et al., 2016). Notable among these are decisions relating to eligibility, treatment assignment, and the definition used to begin follow-up time (‘time zero’). Where these do not coincide, there is the potential for one of two related but distinct forms of selection bias: immortal time bias and prevalent (or ‘healthy’) user bias (Hernán et al., 2016).
Immortal time bias occurs when treatment assignment is determined after the start of follow-up (time zero). Most commonly, this occurs whenever the treatment is defined in relation to a minimum amount of time, e.g., if participants taking anticoagulants only count as ‘treated’ when they have been taking the medication for at least 5 days. Anyone who dies between the start of treatment and the designated time required to achieve ‘treated’ status will not be eligible for classification as ‘treated’, making this time ‘immortal’ as no deaths (or other outcomes of interest) can occur in this group during this time. In contrast, the ‘untreated’ group does not require a minimum amount of time to count as ‘untreated’ and all events occurring during this period are counted as normal. Since the ‘treated’ group has already survived a minimum required period that does not apply to the ‘untreated’ group, any apparent benefit of treatment may be overestimated as an artefact of this immortal time.
Prevalent user bias (also known as ‘depletion of susceptibles’) arises when treatment assignment occurs before the start of follow-up. Most commonly, this occurs in observational settings where comparisons are made between ‘exposed’ (‘treated’) and ‘unexposed’ (‘untreated’) individuals (e.g., those with and without heart disease). In this setting, the ‘treated’ must remain ‘treated’ long enough to make it into the sample at the start of follow-up. Any events occurring due to treatment before the start of follow-up would be missed and undercounted in the ‘treated’ group. For instance, when studying the effect of unemployment on depression, those whose mental health deteriorates soon after job loss may make greater effort to find a job quickly or may leave the labour force entirely. The individuals observed as unemployed at the start of follow-up (rather than the start of unemployment), then, would be disproportionately made up of those who are unaffected by unemployment’s deleterious effects (Figure 5.14).
The more harmful the exposure is and the longer the time between exposure initiation and start of follow-up, the more likely it is for those susceptible to the outcome to be depleted from the treated group sample. Prevalent user bias is a particular challenge with cohort data because of the length of time between data collections – participants may be more likely to experience a harmful exposure and then experience the outcome, or drop out of the study, before their exposure status is collected at the next wave. Note, prevalent user bias can affect both internal and external validity as (regarding internal validity) remaining exposed is a potential collider variable (Figure 5.14) and (regarding external validity) treatment effects may vary depending on ‘susceptibility’.
These self-imposed analytical mistakes have generated several notable failures in observational research. For instance, Hernán et al. (2008) show that the supposedly protective effect of hormone replacement therapy on coronary heart disease, identified in observational studies but not RCTs (which found the opposite), disappears when prevalent user bias is avoided. It is thought that those most susceptible to death after HRT initiation will have been depleted from the sample before the start of follow-up, meaning the protective effect seen in many observational studies is due to prevalent user bias. Dickerman et al. (2019) show the protective effect of statins on lower cancer rates arises due to a combination of immortal time bias and prevalent user bias. First, existing studies compared long-term statin users with non-users, where long-term users were defined as those with at least 4 years of statin use. Those who go on to be classified as long-term users must have therefore survived during this period without developing cancer (introducing immortal time bias). In addition, existing studies also included those already on statins before the start of follow-up, which may have led to depletion of susceptibles (introducing prevalent user bias).
The target trial emulation (TTE) framework (Hernán & Robins, 2016) specifically attempts to avoid such design biases by emulating the features of an RCT.1 In particular, TTE involves specifying the protocol for a hypothetical (‘target’) trial, including eligibility criteria, treatment assignment procedures, follow-up, outcome, estimand, and analysis plan.2 This protocol is then used to design a second protocol, detailing the design of the observational study which will be used to emulate the hypothetical target trial (Hernán et al., 2025). This mapping is iterative and based on what is possible with the data – it does not recreate an ideal RCT that one may wish had been run, and some features of an RCT, such as treatment allocation blinding and explicit randomisation, will not be possible to emulate (i.e., the target trial may often be a ‘pragmatic trial’). Preparing data for a target trial emulation can involve significant data wrangling (e.g., restricting to an eligible sample). For instance, to assess the effect of job loss on mental health, data may be restricted to those in continuous employment before exposure ‘assignment’.
The TTE does not map to a single statistical method – instead it is a framework for designing studies and defining estimands. As such it can be used alongside – or rather, specify the use of – any of the methods (e.g., regression adjustment), study designs (e.g., Regression Discontinuity Designs), and falsification tests (e.g., negative controls) discussed elsewhere in this document. Just like an RCT, TTE can be used to estimate a range of estimands. In an RCT, the intention-to-treat effect estimates the effect of being assigned to a treatment, regardless of adherence. Typically, the observational analogue of the ITT is the effect of initiating a treatment, regardless of adherence during follow-up. In an RCT, there may also be a range of estimands of interest which involve being assigned to treatment and adhering to it for the duration of follow-up (traditionally referred to as ‘per protocol’ effects). However, just like an RCT, there is no single ‘per protocol’ effect and the exact adherence strategy and therefore estimand must be pre-specified in advance. This requires appropriately accounting for post-treatment confounding and selection, including any time-varying confounding. This is discussed further in Section 5.12.
TTE is popular in pharmacoepidemiology and with large-scale health record data, but it is increasingly used in other fields, including social epidemiology and criminology (see, e.g., Cornish & Brennan, 2025; Matilla-Santander et al., 2023). It has also been applied in cohort data, including the CLS cohorts (see below). Cohort data have the advantage that variables are measured repeatedly which can make it possible to restrict eligibility to individuals without exposure prior to time zero, though as mentioned previously, the time gap between data collections can cause issues. Repeated measurement also allows for a nested trial design, where individuals are entered into multiple successive ‘trials’ until they become exposed.
A final benefit of the RCT design that is naturally encouraged by the TTE framework is specifying a well-defined intervention that can, hypothetically, be assigned experimentally. In observational studies, it is often unclear what the equivalent intervention may be, and hence the interpretation of the causal effect one is actually estimating (Hernán & Robins, 2023). For instance, a researcher may wish to estimate the effect of body mass index (BMI) on stroke. However, it is not straightforward to ‘assign’ a certain BMI, even in a trial. Instead, different levels of BMI can be achieved via numerous interventions (e.g., diet, exercise, Ozempic, amputating a limb). The same change in the exposure (e.g., transitioning from BMI of 30 to BMI of 25) can therefore be achieved through different means, each of which may have distinct effects on the outcome (stroke), making the estimand (the causal effect being estimated) unclear. Since the effect will be a mixture of different possible interventions, it has limited practical utility and limited transportability. This problem is much more easily avoided when we attempt to conceptualise the exposure as a hypothetical intervention as it explicitly encourages us to think about well-defined causal contrasts with clearer interpretations.

title: 5.11 Target Trial Emulation
text:
5.11.2 Applications
Vagni (2026) uses data from BCS70 to estimate the causal effect of becoming a mother upon social class (the ‘Motherhood Class Penalty’). The author uses an explicit TTE framework to define the exposure, outcome, eligibility criteria, time zero, and the estimand of interest. Comparator women (women who remain childless at age 46) are identified by matching upon Mahalanobis distance with a novel use of sequence analysis (Gabadinho & Studer, 2010) to identify pairs of treated and untreated individuals with similar pre-motherhood class trajectories. The author finds that motherhood has a large effect on class mobility, with mothers facing long-term lower likelihood of attaining or remaining in professional occupations following childbirth. Strengths of the study include: the clear and transparent statement of the study design, estimands, and assumptions; the use of external data (Annual Population Survey and British Household Panel Survey) to assess potential bias from attrition; and the use of data visualisations to display the results and provide compelling evidence estimates are causal (e.g., showing estimated differences in occupational class are confined to the post- and peri-childbirth period).

title: 5.11 Target Trial Emulation
text:
5.11.3 Opportunities
The TTE approach is relatively underutilised in CLS cohort data, despite the cohorts having several features making the approach tractable (as noted above), including longitudinal assessment to determine eligibility and to implement nested trial designs to increase statistical power.
