Note, as the allocation procedure in observational data is not randomisation, the target trial protocol sets out the steps designed to estimate the target estimand (e.g., regression adjustment or use of an IV).↩︎

title: 5.12 G-methods for Time-Varying Exposures
text:
5.12.1 Method
Most of the methods outlined so far focus on the effect of exposures occurring at a single timepoint. In many applications, however, researchers are interested in how the effect of the same exposure depends on when it occurs or in how exposure sustained or accumulated over time influences later outcomes. CLS’s cohorts are particularly well suited to answering such questions. However, time-varying exposures introduce additional challenges for causal inference, some of which cannot be addressed by conventional statistical methods (e.g., ordinary least squares regression). In this section, we outline these challenges and briefly discuss potential solutions.
Before turning to time-varying confounding – which was briefly introduced in Section 2.2.3 – it is important to note that the problems and methods discussed here apply specifically to causal questions about the effects of exposure patterns over time. This is more specific than simply studying an exposure that may vary over time, since such exposures may still be analysed as time-fixed depending on the causal question. For example, for some target population, one might ask about the effect of high versus low depressive symptoms at age 16 on blood HbA1c concentration at age 30, a biomarker of diabetes. (For simplicity, we treat the exposure as binary and set aside concerns about consistency – that is, we assume “high” and “low” depressive symptoms are ‘sufficiently well-defined’.) The causal question is valid, but it concerns exposure at a single age and its total effect on later HbA1c through all subsequent pathways. Although depressive symptoms and other influences may change between ages 16 and 30, the causal contrast is defined only in terms of symptoms at age 16. From an interventionist perspective, this corresponds to asking what the average HbA1c concentration at age 30 would be under hypothetical interventions that set everyone’s depressive symptoms to high vs. low levels at age 16, while allowing later symptoms to evolve naturally thereafter. This matches the definition of the average treatment effect as provided in Section 2.2.1, and its estimation does not require methods for time-varying exposures that we discuss in this section.
Alternatively, a researcher may be interested in the effects of different exposure patterns over time. We will refer to these as ‘regimes’. Extending the previous example, one might ask about the effect on HbA1c at age 30 of experiencing the treatment regime of high levels of depressive symptoms at age 16 and again at age 24, compared with the regime of experiencing low levels of depressive symptoms at both timepoints. This defines a different type of causal question. Here (again using an interventionist perspective), we are interested in the joint effect of intervening twice: first in adolescence and again in early adulthood. More formally, for this contrast, the average treatment effect could be expressed as \(E\left\left[ Y^{X_{1} = 1,{\ X}_{2} = 1} \right\right] - E\left\left[ Y^{X_{1} = 0,{\ X}_{2} = 0} \right\right]\), where X1 and X2 denote exposure levels at the two timepoints. Other causal contrasts are also possible, depending on which exposure regimes are compared. For example, one could consider HbA1c levels under high depressive symptoms at age 16 but low symptoms at age 24, and vice versa. Naturally, the very same principle could be extended to more exposure timepoints, giving rise to an even higher number of possible contrasts.1 For this reason, defining the causal contrast of interest becomes more challenging in time-varying settings. Despite this additional complexity, comparisons of different exposure regimes allow researchers to formalise pressing causal questions. They are especially relevant when the aim is to learn whether exposures have different effects at different stages of the life course, whether accumulated exposure has distinct effects, or which exposure regimes may have the greatest effect and as such be targeted in policy making.
When estimating the effects of exposure regimes, a new complication arises with respect to confounding. We illustrate this using the simplified example introduced earlier. Consider the DAG in Figure 5.15, which represents the setting introduced above. In this DAG, X1 and X2 represent the two exposure instances and L1 and L2 represent sets of time-varying confounders (e.g., one’s overall health).2 Suppose we wish to estimate the effect of high depressive symptoms at both timepoints, compared with low symptoms at both timepoints, on later HbA1c. The graph is best read sequentially, from left to right over time. At the first exposure timepoint, the situation looks familiar: to estimate the effect of depressive symptoms at age 16 (X1) on HbA1c at age 30 (Y), we would wish to condition on common causes of X1 and Y – in this case, L1. The situation is also familiar at the second timepoint: to estimate the effect of depressive symptoms at age 24 (X2) on HbA1c at age 30 (Y), we would wish to condition on common causes of X2 and Y, including prior exposure (X1), and the time-varying confounders taking place before the second exposure (L1 and L2).
So, we have identified two different, though partly overlapping, sets of confounders, one for X1–Y and the other for X2–Y. If we were to estimate these effects separately, we could simply fit two separate models, each focusing on one exposure instance and conditioning on the respective set of confounders. However, we wish to estimate an effect that compares different exposure regimes, so X1 and X2 must be considered jointly. Consequently, confounding relevant to both the earlier and later exposure–outcome relationships must be addressed when estimating that joint effect. The difficulty arises when confounders of the later exposure–outcome relationship (here L2) are themselves affected by the earlier exposure. This scenario is known as treatment-confounder feedback and confounders affected by past exposure levels are referred to as intermediate confounders. In our example, health status in early adulthood could be an intermediate confounder: it may affect both later depressive symptoms and later HbA1c but may also itself be affected by earlier depressive symptoms. Intermediate confounders have a dual role: they confound the later exposure–outcome relationship (X2 ← L2 → Y) but also lie on the causal pathway from the earlier exposure to the outcome (X1 → L2 → Y).
In the presence of treatment-confounder feedback, conventional methods will generally fail to estimate the effects of exposure regimes correctly, even when all relevant confounders are measured. To see why, consider what the dual role of intermediate confounders implies for the adjustment set. To address confounding of the X2–Y relationship, L2 must be conditioned upon. But for the X1–Y relationship, conditioning on L2 would block part of the earlier exposure effect. Standard methods therefore face a problem with no satisfactory solution: conditioning on L2 removes part of the causal effect X1 has on Y, whereas not conditioning on L2 leaves the X2–Y relationship confounded.3
To address this problem, a family of methods has been developed, which are collectively referred to as g-methods (the letter g stands for ‘generalised’). The three main approaches are: g-computation, also known as the parametric g-formula (Robins, 1986); inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW; Robins et al., 2000), already encountered for single time points in Section 5.3; and g-estimation of structural nested models (Robins, 1989; Vansteelandt & Sjolander, 2016). The naming convention can cause some confusion. IPTW belongs in the g-methods family despite containing no signposting letter g, while g-estimation is, despite its name, a method that is fully distinct from g-computation. Nevertheless, all three methods share the ability to estimate effects of exposure regimes even in the presence of treatment-confounder feedback.4 While discussing the details of the three g-methods is beyond the scope of this work, we briefly outline the intuition behind g-computation and IPTW. We do not discuss g-estimation further, as it would require additional technical context not well suited to the brief treatment possible here. Readers interested in more detail on all three g-methods are referred to Hernán & Robins (2023).
In the most common implementation, g-computation uses a series of regression models to simulate, step by step and forward in time, what each person’s intermediate confounders and outcome would be under a particular exposure regime, given the covariate history up to the respective timepoint. Using these simulations, one could first estimate, for example, the expected outcome under a regime in which everyone was exposed at each timepoint. Next, the process is repeated under a different regime (e.g., no one exposed at any timepoint). The simulated outcomes are averaged under each regime, and the resulting means can be compared, for example by taking the mean difference.
This approach naturally accommodates the dual role of intermediate confounders. As the simulations are carried out forward in time under each exposure regime, they preserve the influence of earlier exposures on later intermediate confounders and their resulting effect on the outcome. The final comparison is made directly between the estimated mean potential outcomes under different regimes, so intermediate confounders contribute to the differences in the estimated mean potential outcomes only insofar as they are changed by the exposure regime. The resulting comparison can be interpreted as the estimate of the respective causal effect, provided that the identifying assumptions hold (discussed below) and that all models for the intermediate confounders and outcome are correctly specified.
Unlike the usual implementation of g-computation, IPTW does not attempt to simulate counterfactual trajectories. Recall from Section 5.3 that, in the single-exposure setting, the weights are defined as the inverse of the probability of receiving the observed exposure level, conditional on confounders. Reweighting observations by these weights aims to create a pseudo-population in which the exposure is independent of the measured confounders. For time-varying exposures, IPTW extends this same principle: if successfully implemented, it reweights observations so that, at each exposure timepoint, the exposure is independent of the covariate history (conditional on past exposure levels). In its simplest form, weights can be derived separately for each exposure instance, for example using regression models for the exposure conditional on the covariate and exposure history up to that point. These timepoint-specific weights are then multiplied across timepoints to give a single weight for each individual. The resulting weights can then be used to estimate the effects of exposure regimes, which can be obtained through methods such as weighted regression. For a simple worked example, see Thoemmes & Ong (2016).
IPTW generally relies on the same identifying assumptions as g-computation, but the two methods have different requirements for statistical modelling. The standard version of g-computation requires a correctly specified model for each intermediate confounder as well as the outcome, whereas the implementation of IPTW described here requires a correctly specified model for each exposure instance. In most analyses, there are many more potential confounders than there are exposure instances, so IPTW typically has the benefit of making fewer parametric assumptions than g-computation. That said, this may come at a cost of lower efficiency of IPTW, producing wider confidence intervals. In practice, IPTW can also be more prone than g-computation to numerical instability, especially in settings with many timepoints and complex covariate histories, where extreme weights are more likely to arise. Importantly, this comparison applies to the standard versions of the two methods, but other implementations can be used to relax some of the modelling assumptions (see, for example, Huffman & van Gameren, 2018; Karim et al., 2017; Zivich et al., 2024). The strengths of the two methods can also be combined in doubly robust estimators (Bang & Robins, 2005; van der Laan & Gruber, 2012). The flexible and doubly robust approaches typically come at the cost of greater complexity.
While progress has been made in statistical methods, identification of exposure regime effects relies on strong assumptions. The methods outlined above generally require a sequential version of the conditional exchangeability assumption. In practical terms, this typically implies that, at each exposure timepoint, one must account for common causes of the exposure and the outcome.5 Even when only a single exposure instance is considered, it is rare that all confounding has been fully accounted for, and some bias due to unmeasured confounding may remain. As additional timepoints are introduced, the number of confounders can only increase, so this assumption becomes more difficult to justify. Other identifying assumptions, including positivity, consistency, and no interference, also generalise to sequential versions and may likewise become harder to satisfy (see Hernán & Robins, 2023, for details).
The strong identifying assumptions, together with the added analytical complexity, have an important practical implication. When many exposure timepoints are available, researchers may be tempted to define exposure regimes that involve all of these instances, hoping to make full use of the available information. Yet it may be preferable to focus on fewer exposure timepoints than are available in the data, so that the required assumptions remain more plausible. For example, one should consider the availability of confounders at or before each exposure timepoint. Another reason for limiting the number of timepoints is so that the causal question becomes clearer. As additional exposure occasions are introduced, the number of possible exposure regimes increases rapidly, and it may become unclear which contrasts are substantively meaningful. Therefore, it may be more informative as well as practical to focus on a few timepoints that correspond to meaningful developmental periods or plausible intervention points, than to model every observed measurement occasion.

title: 5.12 G-methods for Time-Varying Exposures
text: Figure 5.15: A DAG representing a simple setting with a time-varying exposure at two timepoints (X1 and X2). L1 and L2 are time-varying confounders. To estimate the effect of X2 → Y, one must condition on the full history of the covariates and the exposure, including L1, L2, and X1. To estimate the effect of X1 → Y, one needs to condition on L1, but must not condition on L2. If one wishes to estimate the joint effect X1 and X2 have on Y, a problem arises, because the two instances require mutually exclusive adjustment sets (that is, one needs L2 to be conditioned upon, whereas the other needs that it is not conditioned upon). Standard estimation methods cannot accommodate this structure, and g-methods are required.

title: 5.12 G-methods for Time-Varying Exposures
text:
5.12.2 Applications
Hope et al. (2019) use MCS to examine the effect of time-varying maternal distress upon childhood mental health problems across ages 3, 5, 7, and 11 years. Using marginal structural models and allowing for treatment-confounder feedback (prior child mental health influencing maternal distress) and time-varying confounding via family circumstances, they show that maternal distress increases the risk of future mental health problems in children, even net of future maternal distress. A strength of the study is the use of QBA (Section 5.20) to examine sensitivity of the results to unobserved confounding, showing that – according to their reading of the literature – implausibly strong unobserved confounding would be necessary to explain associations.
Pinto Pereira et al. (2020) use data from the NCDS and the National Survey of Health and Development (NSHD, the 1946 British Birth Cohort Study; for a cohort profile, see Wadsworth et al., 2006) to assess the causal effect of early- and mid-adulthood obesity upon physical functioning in mid-life. Using the parametric g-formula and an explicit counterfactual framework, the authors compare the causal effect of multiple treatment regimes: never obese, persistent obesity, and obesity beginning at particular ages. Their results suggest that obesity increases the risk of low physical functioning in mid-life, with greater effects attendant with obesity that began earlier in the life course. The authors also perform a causal mediation analysis; we delay discussion of this until Section 5.13. Strengths of the study include: sharing of analytical code, the reduction of a complex exposure history to a small number of substantively interpretable regimes, and explicit discussion of study estimands, the assumptions upon which these are based, and the causal interpretation that can be made, subject to the assumptions being met.

title: 5.12 G-methods for Time-Varying Exposures
text:
5.12.3 Opportunities
Given repeated measurement of many factors across the life course, there is ample opportunity to assess the effects of time-varying exposures in CLS’s cohorts, as well as to include time-varying confounders in such analyses. Further, unlike many other cohort studies, data collection in CLS cohorts began at birth or early in life. This allows for testing of a wider range of life course theories, but also averts an issue with cohorts that have data collection starting later. Specifically, that exposure is implicitly assumed to begin at the point at which variables are measured (e.g., at recruitment in adulthood), though in practice exposure would likely begin before then (Gilsanz et al., 2022, term this late-study start confounding).
As discussed, a key limitation is the age gap that can appear between consecutive sweeps – for instance, ten years elapse between the age 23 and 33 year sweeps in the NCDS. This could warrant focusing upon life course stages where measurement was more frequent (i.e., from age 42 years onward in the NCDS), or upon MCS and Next Steps, whose earlier sweeps are more closely spaced. Data linkages offer a further route around the problem, as administrative records may capture relevant information more frequently than survey sweeps.
To our knowledge, most existing applications of g-methods in CLS’s cohorts have been causal mediation analyses (Section 5.13) rather than comparisons of exposure regimes. Exposures that are measured repeatedly but to date have been studied largely with descriptive trajectory methods – e.g., on poverty spells, parental mental health, employment histories, housing tenure, area deprivation – could be fruitfully reassessed within a counterfactual framework.

title: 5.13 Causal Mediation
text:
5.13.1 Method
In the previous sections, we have considered settings united by a common motivation: to understand what would happen to some (population-average) outcome if the exposure were changed, whether at a single time point or across multiple time points. Such questions concern a particular end result of interest under specified (hypothetical) interventions on the exposure and are typically agnostic about the processes set in motion by those interventions. For example, one may learn that, in some target population, prescribing one type of medication reduces the five-year risk of developing heart disease by 20%, compared to an alternative prescription. This may be sufficient to conclude that prescribing the medication is beneficial over the alternative in preventing heart disease, but it does not explain how that benefit is produced. For instance, the medication could be more effective because patients are more likely to take it than the alternative, or because it acts on different physiological pathways involved in heart disease, or because of some combination of these and other pathways. Questions about intermediate pathways linking the exposure to the outcome have motivated the development of mediation analysis.
Besides being of inherent scientific interest, understanding the mechanisms by which a causal effect is produced can provide several real-world benefits. First, there may be no known way to intervene on the exposure itself in the real world, or such interventions may be costly, impractical, or otherwise undesirable. Downstream processes may be more feasible to intervene on and provide alternate levers for producing the desired causal effects. For instance, policymakers may not have latitude to fully prevent adverse childhood experiences (primary prevention), but do have more scope to implement interventions to avert some of their negative psychological sequelae (secondary prevention; e.g., talking therapies; Ning et al., 2024). Second, understanding intermediate processes may help refine interventions. Rather than treating an intervention as a black box, researchers may wish to know which components, behaviours, or biological changes are most important for producing the outcome of interest. For example, if obtaining a degree increases wages simply by signalling human capital, rather than increasing it, a policy goal of maximising university attendance might be withdrawn. Third, identifying intermediate pathways can help inform tailoring: different pathways may be more relevant in different populations, settings, or stages of life. For instance, if the effect of job loss on mental health operates via financial strain, resources could be focused on those without savings or other sources of income.
In general, mediation analysis has often been understood as an attempt to answer such questions by decomposing the total effect of an exposure on an outcome into direct and indirect components. In the simplest setting, an exposure X is thought to affect an outcome Y, at least partly through an intermediate variable M, referred to as the mediator. The indirect effect is then understood as the part of the effect of X on Y that operates through M, while the direct effect is understood as the part that operates through paths that do not involve M.
To make this discussion more concrete, we return to the example introduced in Section 5.12, with some changes. Suppose we are interested in the effect of high versus low depressive symptoms at age 16 (X), on HbA1c at age 30 (Y), a biomarker of glycaemic control. We suspect that depressive symptoms may also influence health behaviours, including smoking, and smoking may in turn affect HbA1c. We may therefore be interested in whether the effect of depressive symptoms on HbA1c operates, at least in part, through smoking frequency (M), measured at age 24. As in the previous section, we set aside consistency issues for simplicity, assuming that both “high” and “low” depressive symptoms and smoking frequency are sufficiently well-defined.
Although the motivation for mediation analysis may seem clear at first glance, translating a general interest in “understanding mechanisms” or the notion of “direct” and “indirect” paths into well-defined causal effects is challenging. Traditional approaches to mediation developed from path analysis (S. Wright, 1934), an early framework in which hypothesised relationships between variables are represented through a system of equations (this was later generalised within structural equation modelling, SEM). These approaches to mediation define effects through statistical models and make no reference to formal causal frameworks. While a full description of traditional mediation frameworks is beyond the scope of this work, we provide a brief illustration of the simplest approach, where the three effects are defined through linear regression coefficients (Baron & Kenny, 1986; MacKinnon et al., 2007):
We have outlined the simplest regression-based approach to mediation, but many extensions have been developed, including mediation in traditional SEM, longitudinal mediation models, multilevel mediation, and others (see MacKinnon, 2008, for an overview). However, greater modelling complexity does not solve the central problem: these frameworks do not specify what these quantities represent outside the statistical models in which they are defined. It is therefore unclear what precise causal questions they answer and under what conditions a causal interpretation is justified.
Work using counterfactual frameworks shows the quantities only correspond to certain mediational causal effects under restrictive conditions. For example, regression-based definitions rely on a simple linear structure, and the usual decomposition breaks down in the presence of exposure-mediator interaction. Intermediate confounding (partly due to problems discussed in Section 5.12) and collider bias (Section 2.2.4) can also create issues. Formal causal frameworks are therefore needed both to define the causal estimands and to clarify the conditions under which they coincide with these regression-based definitions (De Stavola et al., 2015; Vanderweele & Vansteelandt, 2009).
Despite what the term might suggest, causal mediation analysis is not a single analytical method. Instead, it can be understood as an umbrella term for analyses that explicitly target direct and/or indirect effects defined through counterfactual frameworks. Because many formulations of these effects exist, we briefly outline some of the most widely used options and discuss their assumptions, focusing primarily on issues of confounding.
We begin with an illustrative causal diagram in Figure 5.16. In this diagram, X influences Y both through M and through other, unspecified pathways that do not involve M. For pedagogical clarity, we depict three distinct sets of confounders that may be relevant depending on the causal effect of interest: C1 for the exposure–outcome relationship, C2 for the exposure–mediator relationship, and C3 for the mediator–outcome relationship. Notice that C3 is influenced by X, making it a set of intermediate confounders. This separation is a simplification, as the same variable may confound more than one of these relationships; that is, many pre-exposure confounders may influence X, M, and Y, and causal relationships also exist among the confounders themselves.
As in traditional approaches, we begin by defining the total effect. The total effect captures the net effect of the exposure on the outcome, without separating the pathways through which this effect occurs. In the previous sections of this guide, we have already encountered such a quantity: the average treatment effect. In the context of mediation analysis, the average treatment effect is usually referred to as the total average causal effect, or just total effect (TE). For a binary exposure, this is the difference in mean potential outcome had everyone been exposed compared to no one having been exposed:
\[TE = ATE = E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1} \right\right] - E\left\left[ Y^{X = 0} \right\right]\]
In our example, this would be the difference in mean HbA1c had everyone experienced high depressive symptom levels, compared to everyone experiencing low depressive symptoms. We have already encountered the assumptions required for identifying this effect from data. Specifically: (conditional) exchangeability (i.e., by accounting for all common causes of the X–Y relationship), (conditional) positivity, consistency, and no interference.
Several attempts have been made at defining the direct effect. Intuitively, to conceptualise the effect “not through M”, one might imagine changing the exposure while preventing any corresponding change in the mediator. The controlled direct effect (CDE) formalises this idea through joint hypothetical interventions on the exposure and mediator, where the exposure is changed while the mediator is held fixed at a specified value (Pearl, 2001; Robins & Greenland, 1992).
For example, one might compare mean HbA1c if everyone experienced high rather than low depressive symptoms at age 16, while preventing everyone from smoking at age 24 in both scenarios (thus setting everyone’s smoking frequency to 0). Because smoking frequency is fixed at the same value under both exposure scenarios, any difference in mean HbA1c cannot operate through depression-induced changes in smoking frequency. More generally, the mediator need not be set to 0. A CDE can be defined at any fixed mediator value M = m:
\[CDE(m) = E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = m} \right\right] - E\left\left[ Y^{X = 0,\ M = m} \right\right]\]
In this equation, \(E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = m} \right\right]\) denotes the mean potential outcome had everyone been exposed and had their mediator set to value m. This is compared with \(E\left\left[ Y^{X = 0,\ M = m} \right\right]\), the mean potential outcome had no one been exposed while also having their mediator set to the same value m. The CDE can also be viewed as a special case of the joint exposure regime effects described in the previous section, with the mediator treated as a second exposure occurring after X.
To identify the CDE, we require the assumptions needed to identify the effect of the joint intervention on X and M. This includes all the assumptions invoked for the TE, but also additional assumptions concerning the mediator intervention. In particular, one must account for confounders of the mediator-outcome relationship (C3) as well as confounders of the exposure-outcome relationship (C1). Much like the effects of exposure regimes, the estimation of CDEs is more complex in the presence of exposure-confounder feedback (i.e., when some members of C3 are influenced by X and are therefore intermediate confounders). In that case, the CDE can still be identified if these confounders are measured and accounted for, but g-methods are typically required for its estimation. In addition to assumptions about confounding, identification requires sequential versions of positivity, consistency, and no interference, which are detailed elsewhere (Daniel & De Stavola, 2019).
While CDEs are appealing, a conceptual challenge is that researchers must select the value at which the mediator will be fixed. This matters in the presence of exposure-mediator interaction on the chosen effect measure scale. For example, suppose depression has a more detrimental effect on HbA1c among smokers, perhaps because depressive symptoms activate inflammatory pathways that amplify the metabolic consequences of smoking. The CDE would then differ according to the smoking frequency at which M is fixed. It may also not be obvious which value is most scientifically or practically relevant. A further consideration is that the CDE has no corresponding indirect effect, and therefore does not attempt to decompose the TE (Vanderweele & Vansteelandt, 2009). Nevertheless, CDEs can answer policy-relevant questions when fixing the mediator at the chosen value corresponds to a feasible intervention, such as whether intervening on X would provide any additional benefit once M had already been fixed through a separate intervention (see the example in T. Q. Nguyen et al., 2021).
Another related approach to conceptualising the direct effect is the natural direct effect (NDE, Pearl, 2001; Robins & Greenland, 1992). Earlier, we described the general idea behind a direct effect as a thought experiment in which the exposure is changed while any resulting change in the mediator is prevented. The NDE follows this intuition more literally: rather than setting everyone’s M to the same arbitrary value, it sets each person’s M to the value it would have naturally taken under non-exposure (or under another comparison exposure level for non-binary exposures).
In our example, this means comparing mean HbA1c under two hypothetical scenarios. In the first, everyone experiences high depressive symptoms at age 16, but each person’s smoking frequency at age 24 is set to the value it would have taken had they instead experienced low depressive symptoms. In the second, everyone experiences low depressive symptoms at age 16, and each person’s smoking frequency is set to that same person-specific value, namely the value it would naturally have taken under low depressive symptoms. More generally, we write:
\(NDE = E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = M^{0}} \right\right] - E\left\left[ Y^{X = 0,\ M = M^{0}} \right\right]\)
where M0 denotes the mediator value under non-exposure. The first term \(E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = M^{0}} \right\right]\) is the mean potential outcome had each person been exposed while having their mediator set to its person-specific value under non-exposure. The second term \(E\left\left[ Y^{X = 0,\ M = M^{0}} \right\right]\) is the mean potential outcome under non-exposure, with the mediator set to that same person-specific value. Since M0 is precisely the value the mediator would naturally take under X = 0, this second term reduces to the mean potential outcome under non-exposure, \(E\left[ Y^{X = 0}\right]\).
Importantly, the NDE has an indirect counterpart, the natural indirect effect (NIE). To understand the intuition behind the NIE, it is helpful to revisit the fundamental logic of mediation: the exposure shifts the mediator, and this exposure-induced shift in the mediator then affects the outcome. The NIE attempts to quantify the effect of this shift on the outcome. It starts from a scenario in which everyone is exposed, and then asks how the mean outcome would change if each person’s mediator were shifted from the value it would have taken under non-exposure to the value it would have taken under exposure:
\[NIE = E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = M^{1}} \right\right] - E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,\ M = M^{0}} \right\right]\]
Here, \(E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = M^{1}} \right\right]\) is the mean potential outcome under exposure and mediator set to its corresponding value under exposure, and \(E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,\ M = M^{0}} \right\right]\) is the mean potential outcome under exposure while the mediator is set to its value under non-exposure. In our example, this would be the effect of changing each person’s smoking frequency from the value it would have taken under low depressive symptoms to the value it would have taken under high depressive symptoms, while keeping depressive symptoms themselves high in both scenarios.
The NDE and NIE align with some of the intuition underpinning traditional mediation analysis. This is reflected in their mathematical properties; for example, they decompose the TE, so that \(TE = NDE + NIE\) for effects on the difference scale. Importantly, the NDE and NIE are best considered thought experiments, as some of the hypothetical interventions they represent could not realistically be enacted in the real world.
\[NDE + NIE = E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = M^{0}} \right\right] - E\left\left[ Y^{X = 0,\ M = M^{0}} \right\right] + E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = M^{1}} \right\right] - E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,\ M = M^{0}} \right\right] = E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = M^{1}} \right\right] - E\left\left[ Y^{X = 0,\ M = M^{0}} \right\right] = E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1} \right\right] - E\left\left[ Y^{X = 0} \right\right] = TE\]
While some properties of the NDE and NIE may seem conceptually appealing, identification of these effects rests on strong assumptions that are implausible in many applied settings. Both the NDE and NIE involve what are referred to as cross-world counterfactuals – quantities that combine exposure and mediator values from different hypothetical scenarios that cannot be observed together for all individuals. For example, the NDE contains \(E\left\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = M^{0}} \right\right]\), where each person’s exposure is set to 1, but their mediator is set to the value it would have taken had their exposure been 0. This quantity cannot be observed for any individual whose level of the mediator differs according to the exposure, because we cannot simultaneously observe that person under both exposure and non-exposure. Identifying natural effects therefore requires extrapolating from observed data to these cross-world quantities. This relies on the assumption of cross-world independence. The general formulation of this assumption is beyond the scope of this guide, but in practice, the main implication of this assumption is a requirement of no intermediate confounding: natural effects cannot generally be identified when any mediator-outcome confounder is affected by the exposure.1 The violation of this assumption is represented by an arrow from X to C3 in Figure 5.16. Even if all intermediate confounders are known and measured, natural effects are generally not identified, and thus they also cannot be estimated, even if g-methods are used.
Apart from the absence of intermediate confounding, identifying natural effects requires accounting for confounders of the exposure–outcome relationship (C1), and the mediator–outcome relationship (C3), much like identifying the CDE. In addition, one must also account for confounders of the exposure–mediator relationship, C2. This is because the NDE and NIE require the conditional distribution of mediator values under exposure and non-exposure (i.e., reflecting the causal effect of the exposure on the mediator) to be recoverable from the observed data. Finally, identifying natural effects also requires extended versions of positivity, consistency, and no interference, which are detailed elsewhere (Daniel & De Stavola, 2019).
In applied research, the assumption of no intermediate confounding required for the standard identification of natural effects is often difficult to justify.2 Therefore, in many settings, other formulations of the direct and indirect effect that do not make this assumption are more relevant. A popular approach is provided by (randomised) interventional analogues of natural effects, including the interventional direct and indirect effect (IDE, IIE; Didelez et al., 2006; VanderWeele et al., 2014). We provide only a brief introduction to these effects, but readers interested in further intuition and examples are referred to Nguyen et al. (2021).
The interventional analogues follow a similar logic to their natural counterparts but differ in an important way. Intuitively, the NDE and NIE involve personalised hypothetical interventions on the mediator: each person’s mediator is set to the value it would naturally have taken for them under a particular exposure scenario. Interventional effects instead involve changing the distribution of the mediator, without requiring each person to receive their own person-specific value under that exposure level.
To define these effects, let \(G_{x|C}\) be a random draw from the mediator distribution that would arise under exposure level \(X = x\) in strata \(C = c\). Then, for the binary exposure, we define:
\[IDE = \ E\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = G_{0|C}}\right] - E\left[ Y^{X = 0,M = G_{0|C}}\right]\]
\[IIE = E\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = G_{1|C}}\right] - E\left[ Y^{X = 1,M = G_{0|C}}\right]\]
To illustrate, much like the NIE, the IIE starts from a scenario in which everyone is exposed. It then asks how the mean potential outcome would change if the mediator distribution shifted from that under non-exposure to the distribution that would arise under exposure, within strata of relevant covariates. The IDE instead keeps the mediator distribution at that which would arise under non-exposure (within strata of C) and compares the mean potential outcome when everyone’s exposure is changed from 0 to 1.
Under the assumption of cross-world independence, natural effects equal their interventional analogues. When intermediate confounding is present, IDE and IIE can still be identified, as they do not require cross-world independence, but they will no longer coincide with natural effects and no longer decompose the TE.3 Additionally, all other assumptions listed for natural effects are still required, and intermediate confounders must be measured and properly accounted for. It is also worth noting that interventional effects answer their own causal questions (Miles, 2023; Moreno-Betancur & Carlin, 2018), and this should be reflected when selecting the target effect and interpreting the findings. Although they may sometimes serve as approximations to natural effects, this correspondence does not hold in general, so using them as proxies should be explicitly justified (see Gervais et al., 2025) or at least noted as a limitation.
Apart from interventional analogues of natural effects, other estimands have also been developed. While discussing all alternatives is beyond the scope of this guide, we note separable effects as an option gaining popularity especially in medical research (Stensrud et al., 2022). These effects may be relevant when one can plausibly separate the exposure, or treatment, into two distinct components that act along different causal pathways: one component that may affect Y only through M, and another component that may only affect Y through pathways not involving M. This assumption may be more plausible for some exposures or treatments that act through relatively well-understood and distinct biological mechanisms (for example, see Andrews et al., 2023).
Another response is to reformulate the question more fundamentally. Natural effects have been criticised not only because of the assumptions they require, but also because they rely on nested counterfactual quantities that do not correspond directly to interventions that could be enacted in a single real-world setting (Robins et al., 2022). Related concerns can arise for interventional analogues of natural effects, as the implied intervention on the mediator distribution is challenging to connect to a concrete action. From this perspective, such effects may serve as conceptual tools, but they may not always be the most appropriate targets for actionable input. Researchers may instead focus on causal effects corresponding to more explicitly defined interventions on the exposure, the mediator, or both. CDEs provide one example of such effects, but other joint interventions can also be studied, as outlined in Section 5.12 (for example, see Stacey et al., 2019). Alternatively, other interventional direct and indirect effects may be formulated to correspond explicitly to a hypothetical target trial of specified mediator interventions.
We have covered several options for effects one may focus on when conducting causal mediation analysis and discussed some of their challenges. Importantly, researchers need not choose a single causal effect. If several effects answer substantively meaningful questions, they may be reported alongside one another, provided that their interpretation and identifying assumptions are clearly distinguished. For example, researchers may be interested in the thought experiments represented by natural effects or their interventional analogues, but may also estimate the effects of specified interventions on the exposure, mediator, or both that could plausibly be implemented in practice, thereby providing more directly actionable evidence.
Depending on the target causal effect, different statistical methods may be used for estimation. Although several algorithms and software implementations are available, the choice is more limited in practice when intermediate confounding is present. In these settings, g-methods are typically required. For example, CDEs, IDE, and IIE may be estimated using g-computation, for example with gformula in Stata (Daniel et al., 2011) or CMAverse in R (B. Shi et al., 2021). A causally informed SEM approach has also been proposed for some settings with intermediate confounding, under additional parametric assumptions (De Stavola et al., 2015), although g-methods typically offer greater flexibility and are more commonly used in this context.
Research questions may also involve multiple mediators of interest, and extensions are available for such settings (for example Daniel et al., 2015; Vansteelandt & Daniel, 2017). However, broadening the question to distinguish effects involving additional mediators adds further requirements to an already demanding set of assumptions.
Much like analyses of time-varying exposure effects, causal mediation analyses can place substantial demands on the time resolution available in the data and related assumptions. Researchers must carefully consider the temporal ordering of the exposure, mediator, outcome, and any relevant confounders, as well as whether the assumptions required for the chosen causal effect are plausible. Even if only a single mediator is studied, we encourage users to start by asking whether (some form of) causal mediation analysis provides answers that match their substantive questions better than alternatives. If it does, they should then consider whether the available data can support the required assumptions, and whether the research team has sufficient expertise to implement the analysis accurately and interpret the findings appropriately. In some cases, it may be preferable to reformulate the research question around less demanding causal effects, especially when the assumptions required to identify those effects are more defensible.

title: 5.13 Causal Mediation
text:
Total effect: The first step is to regress the outcome on the exposure and a baseline set of covariates C1, C2, …, Cn. In our example, this is done by simply running a linear regression model with HbA1c as the outcome, depressive symptoms as the exposure, and including some baseline covariates, giving \(Y = \alpha_{0} + \alpha_{1}X + \alpha_{2}C_{1} + \ ...\  + \ \alpha_{n + 1}C_{n} + \varepsilon_{1}\). The coefficient for the exposure \(\alpha_{1}\) represents the total effect, which, in our example, gives the total effect of depressive symptoms on HbA1c.
Direct effect: The outcome model is refitted with the mediator (smoking frequency) also included: \(Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}X\  + \ \beta_{2}M\  + \beta_{3}C_{1} + \ ...\  + \ \beta_{n + 2}C_{n} + \varepsilon_{2}\). The exposure coefficient \(\beta_{1}\) estimates the direct effect of the exposure on the outcome. The idea underpinning this step is that by ‘controlling’ for M, we hold it constant, so the regression coefficient for the exposure gives the X–Y association that is independent of M.
Indirect effect: The mediator is regressed on the exposure and covariates: \(M = \gamma_{0} + \gamma_{1}X\  + \gamma_{2}C_{1}\  + \ ... + \ \gamma_{n + 1}\ C_{n} + \varepsilon_{3}\). Following the path-tracing rule, the effect along a path is obtained by multiplying the coefficients that make up that path. Therefore, the indirect effect can be defined as \(\gamma_{1}{\cdot \beta}_{2}\) (because \(\gamma_{1}\) represents the X–M path and \(\beta_{2}\) represents the M–Y path).









Figure 5.16: Illustrative DAG for causal mediation analysis, comprising exposure X, mediator M, and outcome Y. Depending on the causal effect of interest, three sources of confounding may need to be considered: confounding of the exposure–outcome relationship by C1, the exposure–mediator relationship by C2, and the mediator–outcome relationship by C3. The DAG is simplified for educational purposes. In applied settings, the same baseline variable may confound more than one of these relationships, as some confounders may influence X, M, and Y, and causal relationships may also exist among the confounders.

title: 5.13 Causal Mediation
text:
5.13.2 Applications
Ning et al. (2024) perform a particularly impressive study of the effect of early-life adversity upon adolescent mental health using data from MCS. Testing the predictions of a theoretical model, the Dimensional Model of Adversity and Psychopathology (DMAP), the authors estimate indirect effects of two aspects of adversity (deprivation and threat) via cognitive ability and emotional dysregulation, which, according to the DMAP, they are differentially expected to affect. Though they find limited evidence that either dimension of adversity has a net non-zero effect on adolescent mental health, the authors find evidence in support of the DMAP, with deprivation having a stronger indirect effect upon mental health via cognitive ability than via emotional dysregulation, and threat having a stronger indirect effect via emotional dysregulation than via cognitive ability.
The study has several strengths. The authors follow a pre-registered analysis plan, with deviations noted and justified. They also clearly state their estimands and the assumptions under which a causal interpretation can be made. They develop a DAG paying particular attention to the relationships between variables – for instance, they separate exposure-mediator-outcome and mediator-outcome confounders, and they treat threat as an intermediate confounder of the deprivation pathway. Because natural effects are not identified in the presence of intermediate confounding (see above), they accordingly target the interventional indirect effect for deprivation, estimated using the g-formula, while targeting the natural indirect effect for threat, where no such confounder arises. Finally, they use a child-reported, rather than parent-reported, measure of adolescent mental health, given concerns with the accuracy of the latter; they note this decision may have meant they observe no net (total) effect of adversity upon the outcome.
Hope et al. (2021) use MCS data to assess the effect of hypothetical interventions to reduce social inequalities in childhood mental health problems (MHP). Though it may not immediately appear so, this can be treated as a mediation question. Using marginal structural models, the authors first estimate the controlled direct effect of income upon childhood MHP with parenting practices treated as a mediating factor and fixed at observed levels. They then simulate the effect of interventions that improve parenting practices by re-estimating the CDE at predicted values for the mediator; the intervention may thus narrow inequalities by reducing differences in this mediator between groups. A key strength of their study is that the hypothetical interventions they evaluate vary in their effectiveness, uptake, and targeting (e.g., offered to families on means-tested benefits only), with these parameters selected based upon reviews of the literature (e.g., meta-analyses of the effectiveness of parenting interventions) and expert discussions (e.g., on plausible targeting strategies). A limitation is that they do not account for potential reverse causality between (early) child mental health problems and parenting behaviour.
Pinto Pereira et al. (2020) – discussed in Section 5.12.2 – assess mediation of the effect of early- and mid-adulthood obesity upon mid-life physical function using data from the NCDS and the NSHD. Using the parametric g-formula to estimate IDE and IIE for different treatment regimes (never obese, persistent obesity, and obesity beginning at particular ages), they find little of the total effect is mediated via physical activity. However, as the authors note, an issue is their dichotomous measure of physical activity, which may have little discriminant validity, thus biasing estimates of the indirect effect towards the null.

title: 5.13 Causal Mediation
text:
5.13.3 Opportunities
The attributes of CLS’s cohorts discussed in Section 5.12.3 also make the data well suited for causal mediation analyses. Specifically, the availability of multiple data collections and the breadth of data collected overall mean that temporal ordering can be established and there are variables for many important mediators and time-varying confounders. Data collection from birth and the repeated measurement of the same characteristic mean measures for many baseline confounders are also available (e.g., pre-exposure measures of mediators).

title: 5.13 Causal Mediation
text:
The requirement of no intermediate confounding is the main practical implication of cross-world independence. However, cross-world independence is a broader assumption and is not identical to the requirement of no intermediate confounding. For technical details, see Andrews & Didelez (2021).↩︎
In some cases, cross-world independence may be replaced with additional parametric assumptions instead (Petersen et al., 2006), although these alternative assumptions may be equally implausible in many applied settings. Alternatively, one may forego point identification and instead estimate bounds or run a sensitivity analysis to obtain a model-based range of plausible effects (Breum et al., 2025; Daniel et al., 2015). These approaches can be more demanding to implement and interpret compared to approaches relying on point identification, and they remain uncommon in applied research.↩︎
Specifically, as \(E\left\left[ Y^{X = x,M = G_{x|C}} \right\right] \neq E\left\left[ Y^{X = x} \right\right]\)↩︎

title: 5.14 Family Designs
text:
5.14.1 Method
In Section 5.5, we discussed the longitudinal fixed effect design which exploits repeated measurement of the same individuals to control for time-invariant confounders by design rather than through explicit statistical control. Family designs similarly exploit features of the data-generating process to control for broad classes of confounders. There are several family designs that can be used with CLS’s cohort data, including designs that precede the molecular genetics revolution and those that use genetic data directly.
Multiple CLS studies have data on siblings, either from a small number of multiparous births or from data collections on a larger number of cohort members’ siblings; for instance, Sweeps 2 and 3 of the MCS included a questionnaire for older siblings. Like longitudinal fixed effects, the sibling comparison design exploits variation in exposure within siblings, this time to account for factors that are common between them (Sjölander et al., 2022). This includes aspects of family background (e.g., parenting styles, family socioeconomic position) and shared genetics (50% on average for dizygotic twins or full siblings; 100% for monozygotic twins).
The usefulness of the sibling design depends on the extent to which confounding factors are in fact shared. The behaviour genetics literature suggests the contribution of shared environments to traits and other outcomes is relatively weak and declines in predictive power as individuals age (Davey Smith, 2011; Plomin, 2018; Plomin & Daniels, 1987). Importantly, this literature also shows that children elicit responses from their environment, including the parenting they receive (see, e.g., Selzam et al., 2018; Wertz et al., 2019) – in other words, less of the family environment may be ‘shared’ than initially expected. The range of influences accounted for by the sibling design plausibly decreases as the age gap between siblings becomes greater, given differences in childhood environment will be larger and as common events will be experienced at different developmental stages. Again, as with longitudinal designs that exploit within-person variation, the sibling design in fact only captures common environments that make siblings more similar to each other than to other people – to the extent that a common exposure has a heterogeneous effect (e.g., because its effects interact with other exposures, such as prior unique developmental experiences) it will not be fully controlled for by design in this set-up.
Moreover, in some circumstances, the sibling design can in fact increase bias, relative to a standard observational design. This is partly due to problems which affect fixed effects designs more broadly (see Section 5.5): where there is measurement error, a greater component of within-sibling variation in the measured factor will be noise, and where a relatively strong confounder causes the variation within siblings, exploiting just within-sibling variation can increase bias, analogous to the issue of Z-bias discussed in Section 5.1. Further, some issues are (arguably) unique to the sibling design, including ‘carryover’ effects (Sjölander et al., 2016), where one sibling influences another, and the existence of shared mediators (Sjölander et al., 2022), which are absorbed into the fixed effect along with shared confounders – financial resources could be shared within families, for example. As sibling designs only exploit siblings who are discordant on exposure, they can also suffer from power issues and low generalisability to the general population, which includes singletons and families with siblings who are not discordant on exposure.
Another family-based method that can be used with CLS data is the adoption design. The NCDS and BCS70 were born during periods when adoption was relatively common (Rushton et al., 2020) and contain data from ~ 300 adoptees in total, who can be combined, including with adoptees identified in other studies, to increase total sample sizes. As discussed in Appendix Section 8.2, a major and consistent finding in the behaviour genetics literature is that almost all human traits are heritable: parents and their (biological) offspring resemble each other at least in part because they share the same genes. The adoption design exploits the fact that children and their adoptive parents are not expected to be genetically related. Therefore, associations between adoptive parental traits and family environments and children’s outcomes should not be explained by direct genetic transmission. However, it is still possible for children to elicit specific parenting behaviours and other environmental responses (evocative gene-environment correlation), a form of reverse causality. Moreover, adoption placements can be selective, including where children are adopted by relatives. It is necessary to confirm non-familial adoption as otherwise genetic relatedness would still be present, albeit to a lesser extent than with one’s natural parents.
The adoption and sibling designs use facts of genetic inheritance indirectly, but the advent of molecular genetics has led to the development of designs that use measured genetic variation. Biological parents and offspring in the MCS were genotyped in Sweep 6 (age 14 years) of the survey, yielding data from more than 2,700 sets of genetic ‘trios’ (mother-father-offspring) and ~ 8,500 (overlapping) sets of ‘duos’ (mother-offspring or father-offspring pairs). An increasingly popular design is the genetic nurture design (Bates et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2018). This exploits the fortuitous feature of Mendelian inheritance that offspring inherit a random half of their parents’ DNA. With genetic data from parents and offspring, parental genetic data can be decomposed into variants that were inherited by the offspring and variants that were not. Any causal effect of the ‘non-transmitted’ genetic variants upon offspring can only be via the environment – e.g., through the impact on parental behaviour (so-called genetic nurture). Any association cannot reflect direct genetic transmission, meaning – quite remarkably – that genes can be used to study the environment, even if one isn’t interested in genetics per se. Conversely, the effect of transmitted genes on offspring’s outcomes is a combination of genetic nurture and direct genetic effects, and so, analysed alongside non-transmitted variants, transmitted variants can be used to determine the impact of direct genetic effects.
Genetic nurture analyses proceed in one of two ways. With access to raw genetic data, polygenic scores (summary measures of genetic liability to a trait capturing the effect of many genes; Choi et al., 2020) can be constructed for non-transmitted alleles and transmitted alleles, separately, and used in analyses (Kong et al., 2018). Alternatively, with existing polygenic scores (PGS) constructed from all alleles, transmitted and non-transmitted (as available on the UK Data Service), researchers can condition on child PGS and use parental PGS to identify indirect genetic effects (Bates et al., 2018). In both cases, the parental PGS can be used as instrumental variables for a trait of interest in Mendelian Randomisation (MR) analyses. See Figure 5.17 for DAGs reflecting these designs. Note, it is not necessary that the parent’s (exposure) and child’s (outcome) trait are the same – see, for example, Hughes et al. (2024), who use genetic trio data to assess the effect of parental education on child’s mental health.
As Mendelian Randomisation is a form of IV, under treatment effect heterogeneity (and meeting the monotonicity assumption), the estimand in this analysis would be a Complier Average Causal Effect (CACE; Section 5.9). The exact interpretation of who compliers are may be difficult or impossible to ascertain and have consequences for generalisability.
Another issue with the genetic nurture design is that genetic nurture effects can be biased by population-level phenomena such as assortative mating and population stratification. But the design does allow one to determine direct genetic effects accounting for these phenomena. As with other Mendelian Randomisation analyses (Section 5.9), this design can be biased in the presence of horizontal pleiotropy, a particular problem when looking at complex traits or when using PGS rather than single well-understood genetic variants, for both indirect and direct genetic effects. Nevertheless, accounting for direct genetic transmission may be an improvement on what has gone before. Genetic nurture studies are also power hungry – current PGS typically only explain a small amount of variation in their relevant traits – so combining MCS with other data sources containing genotyped families (e.g., Born in Bradford, the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children [ALSPAC], and the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study [MoBa]) may be necessary.

title: 5.14 Family Designs
text: Figure 5.17: Genetic nurture designs that utilise genetic trio data. In observational data, parental traits and offspring traits are correlated but this may be due to direct genetic transmission, rather than an environmental effect of parental traits/behaviours upon their children. Molecular genetic data can be exploited to account for this. (a) Polygenic scores (PGS) are derived from parents’ and children’s genetic data to determine which alleles from each parent have been transmitted to their child and which haven’t to construct PGS of transmitted and non-transmitted alleles (Kong et al., 2018). Non-transmitted PGS can only have a causal effect via the ‘environment’ (e.g., due to parental traits) and so (under specific conditions – e.g., exclusion restriction) can be used as instruments for parental traits. (b) Conditioning upon child’s PGS closes the direct genetic transmission path, leaving the indirect ‘genetic nurture’ path between parental PGS and children’s traits (Bates et al., 2018). Again, parental PGS can be used as instruments for their own traits (under appropriate conditions).

title: 5.14 Family Designs
text:
5.14.2 Applications
Adoption and genetic nurture designs have each been used in CLS’s cohorts. Dearden et al. (1997) use data from the NCDS to calculate father-son correlations in educational attainment, comparing these correlations in natural and adoptive families to assess whether intergenerational stability is genetic, though due to small sample sizes, estimates are imprecise. Sacerdote (2002) performs a similar analysis with the same data, showing associations between adoptive families’ SES and adopted children’s reading test scores, likelihood of university attendance, and marriage.
Wright et al. (2025) use trio data from MCS to examine genetic nurture of BMI, finding that, although there is widespread observational evidence that parental BMI is related to offspring BMI, when accounting for direct genetic transmission, there is only evidence that mother’s BMI is related to offspring BMI. However, BMI is a complex phenotype, influenced by multiple traits and behaviours, and there is a substantial possibility for horizontal pleiotropy to explain maternal results. Nevertheless, the study shows that associations between fathers’ and children’s adiposity may be explained by direct genetic transmission, rather than father’s behaviour or related environments. Tanksley et al. (2025) use a similar set-up but focus on unbiased estimation of the direct genetic effect of an externalising PGS upon phenotypic externalising behaviour (as measured by the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire) – associations between the child’s PGS and the SDQ scores are similar whether parental PGS are included in regression models or not, suggesting the variants captured in the PGS have a causal effect on the child’s behaviour.

title: 5.14 Family Designs
text:
5.14.3 Opportunities
The MCS sibling questionnaires are presently underutilised and contain several items also asked of cohort members, enabling sibling analysis. The MCS genetic trio and duo data are also underutilised. Rectifying this is straightforward: ready-made PGS for a wide array of traits are available via Special Licence Access on the UK Data Service; see the CLS Genetics website for more details.

title: 5.15 Negative Control Outcomes and Exposures
text:
5.15.1 Method
In Section 3.3, we discussed making theories “elaborate” as a way to support causal inference. A broad concern in observational research is that an exposure, X, may be associated with an outcome, Y, due to an unobserved – or poorly measured – confounding factor, U. That the exposure and outcome are materially confounded by U is a competing theory to the possibility that the exposure has a causal effect on the outcome.
Competing theories should be treated seriously; one way of treating a competing theory seriously is to ask what predictions it makes about the world. A given confounding process may imply a larger set of associations than simply a spurious one between X and Y. For instance, the confounding factor may generate an association between X and a larger set of outcomes, or between Y and a larger set of exposures. But these associations may not be predicted by the central theory that X causes Y, and there may be no plausible reason the alternate exposure would cause Y or X would cause the alternate outcome.
The negative control exposure and outcome designs encapsulate this logic (Lipsitch et al., 2010).1 In the negative control outcome design (Figure 5.18b), a ‘placebo’ outcome, YNC, is identified which should only have an association with X through a confounding factor U that is thought to bias the association between X and Y. If an association is observed between X and YNC, this may indicate the main study analysis is biased by U.2 To take an example, let’s say we are interested in the effect of breastfeeding on child cognitive development (Lawlor et al., 2016). Breastfeeding is strongly socially patterned in the UK, with more socioeconomically advantaged parents more likely to breastfeed; an association between breastfeeding and child cognitive development could therefore be expected due to higher socioeconomic position (SEP) of parents or even direct heritability of cognitive ability. But SEP is difficult to measure accurately, so residual confounding may persist even if measured SEP is controlled for. Home invasion by mice during childhood is also socioeconomically patterned, but we would not expect it to be influenced by breastfeeding. Home invasion by mice is therefore a plausible negative control outcome because any association with breastfeeding should be spurious rather than causal. What’s more, it would be spurious for similar reasons that a link between breastfeeding and child cognitive development could be spurious.
The negative control exposure design is similar (Figure 5.18c), but in this case a ‘placebo’ exposure, XNC, is identified that should not have a causal effect on the outcome but would be likely confounded by the same factors as X, the exposure of interest. An example of a negative control exposure design is using paternal smoking to assess whether maternal smoking during pregnancy has a causal effect upon child health, in cases where the smoking is hypothesised to have an effect by influencing the intrauterine environment. As mothers’ but not fathers’ behaviour has a direct effect on the intrauterine environment, one would expect to see specific associations between mother’s smoking and child health. On the other hand, as both mother’s and father’s smoking are patterned socioeconomically, a countervailing theory that associations are driven by confounding through SEP would also predict an association between father’s smoking and child health. Thus, if paternal smoking is related to offspring outcomes (conditional on maternal smoking), it would suggest an association between maternal smoking and child outcomes is also biased (Brion et al., 2007).3
Negative control designs are sometimes referred to as placebo, specification or falsification tests (Eggers et al., 2024). The success of the negative control outcome and exposure design depends on the negative control sharing the same confounders as the true exposure or outcome of interest – referred to as ‘U-comparability’ (Lipsitch et al., 2010). Since it refers to unobserved confounders, the assumption of U-comparability is untestable. In practice, the proposed negative control(s) may only share part of the confounding structure. In the absence of full U-comparability, an observed association with the negative control will not necessarily indicate residual confounding in the X–Y association, and a null association with the negative control will not necessarily indicate absence of residual confounding. Nevertheless, the negative control design may still provide useful information on the presence or absence of bias on major confounders – e.g., on SEP, as in the examples above.
It is not just the presence of the confounders, but similarity in the strength of their relationship with the true and negative control exposures or outcomes that is important. For instance, given the additional possible health risks of smoking during pregnancy, one may expect greater selection into smoking among mothers, compared with fathers. For this reason, a negative control test may represent only a weak test of the competing theory. Showing an association between the negative control and true exposures or outcome would suggest the true exposure-outcome association is biased, but the reverse may not be true: not finding an association with the negative control is not necessarily dispositive evidence that the true exposure-outcome association is unbiased.
In practice, it may be difficult to identify negative controls that have no causal association with the true outcome or exposure, whatsoever. For example, it is possible that father’s smoking influences the intrauterine environment, albeit indirectly via the mother inhaling smoke second-hand. In this case, the pattern and overall size of associations would be informative, rather than only observing a null association for the negative control: given father’s effects on the intrauterine environment should be weaker than mother’s, we would expect child health to (a) have a weaker association with father’s smoking than mother’s smoking and (b) for the absolute size of the association with father’s smoking to be small. Otherwise, strong confounding bias is likely to be present.4
The negative control method can therefore involve a degree of uncertainty for the analyst and require some persuading of the reader. Operating under this uncertainty requires discipline and transparency as it can be tempting to spend “researcher degrees of freedom” (Simmons et al., 2011) in light of inconvenient results – one should not jettison a negative control analysis after seeing the results, if the results motivate one to think ‘maybe the confounding structures are not quite the same’ or ‘perhaps there is a causal relation the association represents’.
Nevertheless, there are general strategies for identifying plausible negative controls. These focus on finding situations where a hypothesised active ingredient linking exposure and outcome is missing or an essential mediating pathway is not present (Lipsitch et al., 2010; X. Shi et al., 2020) or, less restrictively, is weaker. The parental comparison design (Davey Smith, 2008; Richmond et al., 2014) used in the smoking example above follows this logic, and is frequently used in settings where maternal exposures are expected to operate via the intrauterine environment given fathers do not influence this directly. In pharmacoepidemiology, negative control outcomes can be relatively straightforward to identify as treatments may be expected to have causal effects on only a limited set of health outcomes. For instance, flu vaccination, which would plausibly reduce hospitalisation rates due to respiratory problems, should not lower rates of hospitalisation due to injury or trauma (L. A. Jackson et al., 2006).
Another strategy is to take measurements from periods where the exposure should not have an effect on outcomes – for instance, flu vaccination should not have an effect on hospitalisation prior to, or after, flu season, when vaccination might actually cause illness to be avoided (L. A. Jackson et al., 2006). Using outcome measurements prior to exposure or exposure measurements post outcome can also represent expressions of this idea – for instance, a future measurement of environmental pollution when looking at hospital admissions for asthma (Flanders et al., 2011). Height, which has been repeatedly used as a negative control outcome in the health and social sciences (Cohen-Cole & Fletcher, 2008; L. Wright, 2020; L. Wright et al., 2021), can have this property as it is largely set from late adolescence. It is also very highly heritable, so large associations with environmental factors (within a population) are likely spurious. Cohen-Cole & Fletcher (2008) show that in addition to obesity ‘spreading’ between friends in social networks (Christakis & Fowler, 2007), so do height, acne and headaches.
Negative control tests are routinely used in some particular study designs. For instance, as discussed in Section 5.10, sharp RDD studies typically exploit a placebo test, where arbitrary cut-offs in the running variables are chosen that are known to have no bearing on treatment, but could still be related to unmodelled confounders. Sanderson et al. (2021) discuss using phenotypes determined prior to outcome and exposure as negative controls in MR studies, e.g., tanning ability and hair colour.
So far, we have described negative control designs for detecting bias from unobserved confounding. But negative controls can also be used to detect selection and measurement biases (Arnold et al., 2016); regardless of the source of bias, the purpose of the negative control exposure and outcomes is to identify variables that have similar (hypothesised) biasing structures to the main association of interest. For instance, recall biases can generate spurious associations between exposure and outcome if the accuracy of recall of exposure is related to the outcome (e.g., disease cases more likely to remember a childhood ailment). Yet, recall bias may also apply to negative control exposures that have no plausible causal effect on outcomes. Zaadstra et al. (2008) examine recall bias in a study of multiple sclerosis (MS) using negative control exposures for broken limbs, concussion, and tonsillectomy, each of which is not expected to have a causal effect upon MS. Returning to genetics studies, sex is a particularly useful negative control when using polygenic scores as these are typically calculated from autosomal (i.e., non-sex-specific) chromosomes; any association with observed sex must therefore be due to selection bias.
Negative controls can be used not just for bias detection, but also bias correction or reduction (X. Shi et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2024). Again, strength of association between negative controls and true outcomes and exposures can be revealing. For instance, VanderWeele (2011) notes that although height, acne and headaches are correlated within friendship groups (Cohen-Cole & Fletcher, 2008), the size of this correlation is lower than that for obesity, and so greater confounding would be required to explain the obesity spreading hypothesis.

title: 5.15 Negative Control Outcomes and Exposures
text: Figure 5.18: Negative control outcome and negative control exposure design. (a) We are interested in the causal effect of X upon Y, but anticipate there may be confounding via a common (unmeasured) cause U. Any association between X and Y could reflect this confounding pathway. (b) U may also be a common cause of another ‘negative control outcome’ (YNC) which we have good reason to expect X would not have a causal effect on. Any association between X and YNC would therefore reflect the confounding by U. (c) U may additionally be a common cause of another ‘negative control exposure’ (XNC) which we have good reason to expect does not have a causal effect on the outcome of interest, Y. Conditional on the exposure of interest (X), any association between XNC and Y would therefore reflect the confounding by U. Note, in practice, some confounders may be measured, and these would be conditioned upon in the negative control analysis.
crumbs: 19  5.15 Negative Control Outcomes and Exposures

title: 5.15 Negative Control Outcomes and Exposures
text:
5.15.2 Applications
Libuy et al. (2024) use MCS data to assess the effect of changing proximity to fast food restaurants on weight gain. Given fast food restaurants are spatially patterned, they use proximity to several other types of commercial establishment (e.g., employment and career agencies) as negative control exposures, arguing that time-varying changes in these might reflect unobserved confounding processes, such as gentrification. However, the plausibility of the assumption behind the negative control analysis is not explored and other types of commercial establishment not examined could feasibly more closely share confounding structures with fast food restaurants (e.g., betting shops). Hamer & Batty (2020) used data from BCS70 to investigate the association between infection requiring hospital admission and later diabetes risk, using non-infectious reasons for admission as a negative control exposure. This has a more plausible common confounding structure (e.g., health consciousness).
Tabor et al. (2025) use data from MCS and BCS70 alongside data from other cohorts to examine the effect of sexual minority status on asthma. Their theory suggests effects should only occur in adulthood so they use childhood asthma as a negative control outcome, an application of the idea that measures prior to plausible causal effects occurring can be used as negative controls. Wright et al. (2021) use data from Next Steps to assess the effect of youth unemployment on later mental health, using height and patience as negative control outcomes. A question in both papers is whether confounding structures are sufficiently similar to the focal associations of interest.
