title: 5.15 Negative Control Outcomes and Exposures
text:
5.15.3 Opportunities
Given data collection from parents and children, including on characteristics prior to the cohort members’ births, there are ample opportunities to employ the parent comparison design in CLS cohorts. The cohorts have each collected data on a wide variety of factors and traits, which may be useful more generally (e.g., height, suncream use, etc.). Data linkages also increase the possibility for negative control designs, including links with health record data, enabling assessment of multiple health outcomes, which can serve as negative control outcomes. A variety of data on health outcomes is also collected in standard survey data collections. Longitudinal measurements add further possibilities as there is ample pre-exposure measurement of many variables. Finally, there is also an opportunity for research-enabling activity reviewing plausible negative controls and determining their possible use in CLS data.

The flip-side of specificity is coherence among outcomes (Rosenbaum, 2019) – some variables can be used as “positive controls” to determine that statistical models perform as expected (Gutierrez et al., 2025).↩︎

title: 5.16 Cross-Context Analysis
text:
5.16.1 Method
In Section 5.15, we saw that one way to make a theory elaborate is to enumerate which variables an exposure should have a causal effect upon (and which it should not) or which variables an outcome should be causally affected by (and which it should not), given the set of predictions a theory can make. Another way to make a theory elaborate is to draw out the settings or individuals a hypothesised causal effect should exist in or in which the effect would otherwise be stronger or weaker than usual. A competing theory may be able to explain the presence of an association between X and Y in general, but not specific patterns of association between these different cases. Alternatively, a causal effect may be similar in different settings, but (hypothesised) confounding structures may change, so consistency of association across these settings is evidence compatible with the causal theory being true. Cross-context analysis encapsulates this logic by performing analyses in different (subsets of) data or populations (Eggers et al., 2024; Gage et al., 2016; Piccininni & Stensrud, 2024).
There are three types of comparison that are particularly relevant for CLS’s cohort studies. First, time – a causal effect may be anticipated in some periods, cohorts, or stages in the life course, but not others. Second, space – a causal effect may be anticipated in some geographies, but not others, or the confounding structure may be anticipated in some, but fundamentally different in others. Third, population subgroups – there may be certain sections of the population for whom a causal effect would not be anticipated. These are best explained by way of examples.
Time
Space
Population Subgroups
The examples where the causal effect is expected to differ share a common feature that an essential mechanism transmitting the effect is missing, or is otherwise weaker, in one setting than another. For instance, for the bedroom tax, in Scotland, the essential ingredient – lower income – was not present. Readers may notice the similarity between the cross-context design and the negative control outcome design – rather than choose different variables for analysis, different sections of the data are used for which, e.g., causal effects should not exist. Cross-context designs where there is an absence of a causal effect in the comparator population but biasing processes are otherwise the same have been termed negative control population designs (Piccininni & Stensrud, 2024).
Like the negative control design, convincing cross-context analyses require knowledge of the subject area. However, here the barrier for entry may be lower, and the arguments easier to make. For instance, the ALDH2 example largely requires identifying a group with very low alcohol consumption regardless of the ALDH2 variant they carry. Also, like the negative control design, the cross-context design can still be useful when the strength of a causal mechanism varies across settings, rather than the mechanism being absent or blocked entirely. The elaboration of the theory is predicting an overall pattern of results. In their discussion of cross-context designs, Gage et al. (2016) describe a test of the hypothesis that cannabis has a causal effect on psychosis due to its tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) content: a corollary is that as levels of THC in cannabis have increased, associations between cannabis use and psychosis should have similarly increased, if this is the causal mechanism.
Where the cross-context design is motivated by an argument that the causal effect of the exposure of interest will vary across populations, plausibility relies on the extent to which bias processes are similar, akin to the assumption of U-comparability in the negative control outcome and exposure designs (Section 5.15). Additionally, where it is the biasing processes that are hypothesised to vary across populations, an assumption is that the causal effect should be similar in each population, but effects may be heterogeneous and could themselves lead to cross-context differences in associations.
Cross-context designs are extensively used in the genetics literature in the study of gene-environment interaction (GxE; Pereira et al., 2022). For instance, studies have examined the association between polygenic scores (PGS) and attained education as access to education has expanded (Herd et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2026), or between PGS and body mass index before and amidst the obesity epidemic (Conley et al., 2016; L. Wright, Davies, et al., 2024) or in other groups for whom genetic effects should be stronger (e.g., among those genetically predisposed to obesity and living near fast food outlets; de Roo et al., 2024). Again, adding a cross-contextual element supports causal interpretations by testing for a predicted pattern of associations. However, a drawback of GxE studies is that the environment may be ‘endogenous’ (determined in the system; e.g., people may choose where to live based on their genetic predispositions). Further, for complex traits, the associations between PGS and phenotypes may reflect pleiotropic effects (also see Westerman & Sofer, 2024 for discussion of issues in GxE studies). Note, birth year – and the cohort effects it implies – more plausibly represents exogenous environments, as genetic changes occur at a relatively slow rate. A drawback however is the lack of specificity in which aspects of the environment have changed (e.g., aspects of the obesogenic environment in general).

title: 5.16 Cross-Context Analysis
text:
Cognitive ability is hypothesised to have a beneficial effect on health due to greater knowledge and better decision making among those with higher cognitive ability (Gottfredson, 2004). Knowledge about diseases – and how to prevent them – varies across time as scientific discoveries are made and technologies are introduced (Clouston et al., 2016). Given this, if cognitive ability causes health, we should expect inequalities in health according to cognitive ability to grow after facts about a disease are first discovered and to decline as technologies are introduced that reduce the difficulty of avoiding or managing a disease.
In the UK, maternal smoking during pregnancy has become less prevalent but more strongly associated with socioeconomic adversity over time. If associations between maternal smoking and offspring outcomes are merely driven by confounding through socioeconomic position, we would therefore expect stronger associations in more recent cohorts (Sellers et al., 2020).



Between 1999 and 2010, the UK Government implemented a well-funded strategy to halve teenage pregnancies in England (Hadley, 2017). Teenage pregnancies did fall over this period (Wellings et al., 2016) but may have done so absent the strategy. Was the Teenage Pregnancy Strategy successful? At the very least, we would expect pregnancy rates to fall faster than in other countries which did not implement such strategies, such as Scotland and Wales (Baxter et al., 2021; Craig et al., 2016).
The 2013 Removal of the Spare Room Subsidy (the so-called ‘Bedroom Tax’) reduced benefits for working-age individuals in social housing with an unoccupied bedroom. This reduction in entitlements for individuals already more likely to be on low incomes may be expected to reduce mental and physical health (cf. Reeves et al., 2016). However, a curious feature of the policy’s implementation is that, in Scotland, the government compensated any reduced benefits with Discretionary Housing Payments, meaning the bedroom tax did not affect incomes for residents in that country. We should therefore not expect any association between being subject to the bedroom tax and mental health in Scotland but should expect to see one in England and Wales.
The social patterning of breastfeeding varies across the world. For instance, in the UK, socially advantaged mothers are more likely to breastfeed, but this is not the case in Brazil. If the association between breastfeeding and child development is simply a product of socioeconomic confounding, we would expect positive association in the former, and little association in the latter (Brion et al., 2011).



As discussed in Section 5.9, certain variants of the ALDH2 gene are related to better cardiovascular health. This is hypothesised to be due to the effect of ALDH2 on reducing alcohol consumption by determining the comfort with which one metabolises alcohol. In East Asian cultures, women typically drink little, regardless of which ALDH2 variant they carry, while men are more likely to drink and for this to be related to ALDH2. If ALDH2 has a causal effect only via alcohol consumption, we should therefore expect associations with cardiovascular disease in East Asian men but not women (L. Chen et al., 2008).
Unexpected events (Section 5.8) should only have effects among those who are aware of them. For instance, the release of the Royal College of Physicians’ (1962) report on smoking and health was a watershed moment in public appreciation of the harms of smoking, but if access to information is sufficient to alter the decision to smoke, then smoking among TV owners or newspaper readers – likely more aware of the RCP report – should have declined the most (James, 2024).
Cholera being transmitted via infected water, rather than miasmic air, predicts that people who live near the Broad Street pump, but do not take its water, will be less likely to succumb to the disease, and that those who live far away, but still have its water delivered, will become infected (Section 3.3).

title: 5.16 Cross-Context Analysis
text:
5.16.2 Applications
Sellers et al. (2020) compare associations between maternal smoking in pregnancy and offspring development (birthweight, conduct problems and cognitive ability) in the NCDS and MCS – as discussed, social patterning of maternal smoking was stronger in the more recent cohort. Associations between maternal smoking and birthweight were similar in each cohort, whereas associations were stronger in the MCS for other outcomes assessed, consistent with material bias from confounding. However, causal effects becoming larger in more recent cohorts is also compatible with the results.
Wright et al. (2024) examine the association between a PGS for BMI and phenotypic BMI across life in the NSHD, NCDS, BCS70, and MCS, which collectively span a period before and during the obesity epidemic – the NSHD grew up during post-war rationing, while childhood obesity rates reached 20% in the MCS. They find stronger associations in more recent cohorts, particularly comparing the MCS with earlier generations, consistent with theory that the PGS reflect genes that have effects on adiposity via modifiable behaviours. However, this is evidenced only indirectly using birth year as a proxy for exposure to the ‘obesogenic environment’ – it is unclear which aspects of the environment are operative (if any).

title: 5.16 Cross-Context Analysis
text:
5.16.3 Opportunities
Opportunities for cross-context analysis arise from the temporal and geographic expanse represented in CLS’s cohorts. For instance, education systems have historically differed in England, Scotland and Wales, e.g., on rules on minimum school leaving ages, which (over some time frames) entail that individuals born earlier in a school year in England are able to leave school at a younger age than if they went to school in Scotland (Del Bono & Galindo-Rueda, 2007). Geographic range can also be extended by harmonising with studies from other countries where, e.g., different confounding structures for exposures and outcomes of interest may be present.
There are numerous opportunities for GxE in the cohorts, including comparing genetic effects across cohorts, given the generational differences they represent (Morris et al., 2026; L. Wright, Davies, et al., 2024). Opportunities also exist linking genetic data with geographic data (e.g., to identify differences according to pertinent features of the local environment) and with other survey data, given the extensive phenotypic data available (e.g., association between genetic risk and depression among victims of crime), notwithstanding potential endogeneity of these latter environments. Again, harmonisation with other international data could also expand possibilities for GxE cross-context analysis.

title: 5.17 Biases of Known Direction
text:
5.17.1 Method
Though it would be optimal and most useful to identify a precise and unbiased causal estimate, sometimes only determining the overall direction of a causal effect or that it exceeds a minimum effect size is sufficient or still insightful. A valid test of a theory may be that X increases Y, however large or small (though it is of course usually better to know that X is an important causal factor of Y), and one may only need to know that a causal effect exceeds some defined quantity to make a good decision – for instance, knowing that an intervention will yield higher benefits than the alternative. Health economists have a useful concept, ‘value of information’, which denotes the higher expected utility one would obtain if able to make decisions on more accurate data (Tuffaha et al., 2014); if decisions are unlikely to change following further data collection, then the information collection does not have much value instrumentally. Analogously, in some circumstances, one may be satisfied with a biased estimate of a causal effect if removing the bias would not yield further valuable information.
While the precise extent of a bias may not be known, its direction may be guessed at with high certainty, and this can be used to draw causal inferences even where biases are present and acknowledged (Rosenbaum, 1989, 2020). For instance, an observed positive association will only get larger if a confounding factor positively related to X but negatively to Y (or vice versa) were controlled for. Readers will be aware of this type of reasoning – it appears frequently in discussion sections of papers where authors note the possibility of a source of bias but discard its importance as it implies the observed association is a conservative (under)estimate of a true causal effect. One oft-repeated case of this is independent, non-differential (i.e., classical) measurement error in the exposure variable which, in expectation, should bias an association towards the null, proportionate to the size of the measurement error (i.e., regression dilution).
Biases of known direction need not only enter at the interpretation stage of a study – they can also motivate study design. One example of this is to choose a setting in which confounding structures run opposite to a hypothesised causal effect – for instance, in many developing countries, obesity is related to higher socioeconomic status (Dinsa et al., 2012), so observational estimates of the causal effect of obesity upon health conditions are likely biased towards the null. Another possibility is the judicious choice of a comparator group that provides a greater hurdle for a causal effect to surmount. For instance, in a study examining the effect of banning individuals with prior convictions from purchasing guns (and discussed in Rosenbaum, 2020), Wright et al. (1999) compare rates of violent crime among those affected by the law against individuals who had previously been arrested for a crime but found not guilty; one may expect that, if both were able to purchase guns, those who have been convicted of crimes would have a greater likelihood of committing further crimes than those only previously suspected of criminality.
Exploiting biases of known direction can be especially compelling when it is possible to obtain two or more estimates biased in opposite ways, in which case these estimates can provide an upper and lower bound to “bracket” the true causal effect. The main way this can be achieved is through the use of multiple comparator groups (Rosenbaum, 1987). For instance, in the difference-in-difference design (Section 5.6), such a bracketing analysis would work by identifying comparator groups who violate the parallel trends assumption, one anticipated to have stronger time trends than the treatment group and one to have weaker time trends than the treatment group (Ye et al., 2024).1 Hasegawa et al. (2019) bracket the effect on homicide of the repeal of a Missouri state law requiring a background check for gun purchases using two groups of comparator states that had either higher or lower homicide rates than Missouri prior to the repeal of the law.
Exploiting biases of known direction is not without its problems, however. Most obviously, in many cases it may not yield any useful information because it would suggest an estimate is anti-conservative (i.e., if anything an association is biased away from the null). Examples of this abound – for instance, in studies of the effect of socioeconomic position on health, both causal and confounding (health-related selection) anticipate poorer health in more socioeconomically deprived groups. Additionally, it may not be straightforward to identify comparator groups biased in opposite directions (and thus obtain a bracket for the causal effect), or the resulting bracket may be too wide to be useful.
In other cases, only one bias may be known but others not, and it may not make sense to emphasise the one known factor. This is particularly the case where biases interact, yielding unclear direction of bias on aggregate. For instance, bias from classical measurement error is not necessarily towards the null where there is unobserved confounding (Smith & Phillips, 1996).2 Given incentives within academia to overclaim evidence for a proposition, it is possible for motivated reasoning to lead authors to focus attention on those known biases that lend support, rather than those that don’t (Fox et al., 2021).

title: 5.17 Biases of Known Direction
text:
5.17.2 Applications
Ermisch & Pevalin (2005) use data from the BCS70 to assess the effect of teenage parenthood upon partnership status and partner quality at age 30y. They use multiple comparison groups, including women who did not have a teenage birth and – using miscarriage as an IV – women whose teenage pregnancy ended in miscarriage. Though not reported so explicitly, using miscarriage as an IV could bias towards a “benign view” of teen motherhood (Ashcraft et al., 2013) as miscarriage can occur due to factors related to poorer outcomes in general (e.g., smoking and alcohol consumption), whereas teen mothers tend to have worse outcomes than other women more generally, even if they hadn’t had a child. Provided no other biases are present, the OLS and IV estimates therefore arguably bracket the true causal effect.

title: 5.17 Biases of Known Direction
text:
5.17.3 Opportunities
Whether the method can be applied in CLS’s cohorts depends on the specific research question as the direction of known biases depends on information that is not captured in the data collection. Assessing this requires domain-specific knowledge. A key benefit of CLS’s cohorts is the depth of data collection and the sample size which means multiple comparator groups can be defined.

title: 5.18 Differential Effects
text:
5.18.1 Method
The negative control exposure design exploits situations where the same set of confounders has effects on multiple ‘exposures’ only some of which plausibly have a causal effect upon the outcome of interest. Confounders like these are said to be “generic” (Rosenbaum, 2019), having multiple impacts on the world. For instance, a generalised disposition to risk may influence consumption of several drugs, meaning that people who are more likely to smoke crack cocaine may be more likely to inject heroin. A generalised interest in health could lead one to exercise more and follow a good diet.
The effects of a generic bias may be competing or the overlap between them incomplete – for instance, one may become addicted to one drug, but not another. Those who perform just one of these behaviours may be more similar in terms of the confounding factor to those who perform only the other than to those who perform neither, but in standard observational research both would appear in the comparison group. Instead of comparing exposed vs. non-exposed groups, the differential effect design (Rosenbaum, 2006, 2013) compares individuals exposed to only one of two factors in lieu of the other to reduce imbalances on generic confounders – e.g., those who exercise a lot but don’t follow a good diet may be more similar to those who follow a good diet but don’t exercise a lot, than those who exercise a lot are similar to those who don’t exercise a lot (regardless of either group’s diet).
The differential effects design is another expression of the principle Zubizarreta et al. (2018) term ‘isolation’ – a smaller comparison is made that is less biased than the overall association in the wider system. Two examples discussed by Paul Rosenbaum in Design of Observational Studies (Rosenbaum, 2020) clarify the differential effects design as well as highlight its limitations:
By comparing two exposures, the ‘effect’ identified is not directly informative of the effect of an exposure vs. its absence. However, this may still be useful if the comparison factor does not plausibly have an effect on the outcome (i.e., it is a type of placebo test; Example #1) or where the effect of one is known and so the effect of the other can be back-transformed, or where the direction of effect of the comparator is known and exceeding this is informative (similar to reasoning in Biases of Known Direction, Section 5.17). The differential effect design can be particularly beneficial in drug safety research where side-effects for a specific health complaint may only be expected to exist for one treatment under study (again, as with Example #1). Regardless, the information gleaned from the differential effects design may be useful in any case as part of a strategy of triangulation. An additional limitation of the design is that, where behaviours are rare, by focusing on subgroups of the population, statistical power may be much lower.

title: 5.18 Differential Effects
text:
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as ibuprofen, may reduce the risk of Alzheimer’s, but pre-clinical Alzheimer’s may reduce pain sensitivity leading to lower ibuprofen use. However, pain sensitivity should affect the use of other analgesics, too, including ones that are not anti-inflammatory, such as paracetamol. Comparing exclusive ibuprofen users with exclusive paracetamol users is useful for gauging the effect of anti-inflammatory drugs on Alzheimer’s as this would likely reduce imbalance on pain sensitivity, though other confounders may remain.1
Understanding the effect of cannabis use during pregnancy on child development is challenging as mothers who smoke cannabis during pregnancy differ sharply from those who do not (Columns 2, 3 & 5, Table 5.6). Cannabis users are more similar to those who use crack cocaine than those who use no drug, however; comparing exclusive cannabis users with exclusive crack cocaine users leads to an analytical sample less imbalanced on potential confounders (Columns 3-4, Table 5.6). Nevertheless, maternal crack cocaine use likely has an independent effect on childhood development.

5.18.2 Applications
Applications of this method using any data appear to be few and we identified none using CLS data – according to Google Scholar, the Rosenbaum (2006) paper only has 45 citations (as of January 2026), many of which are other methodological papers.

title: 5.18 Differential Effects
text:
5.18.3 Opportunities
Several behaviours plausibly reflect common traits and impulses – e.g., health-seeking behaviour or risk aversion, in general. Given the variety of behaviours (e.g., on drug use) measured in the cohorts, there may be many possible applications. However, as the differential effects design uses only subsets of the data, the opportunities to obtain sufficient sample sizes with the method in CLS data may be fewer, though will increase if the cohorts are combined together or with similar studies.

title: 5.19 Reasons for Effects
text:
5.19.1 Method
Theories that predict a causal effect of an exposure on an outcome typically invoke a set of mechanisms linking the two. One way of making a theory elaborate is to consider intermediate effects. For instance, the theory that cognitive ability improves health by influencing health-related decision making assumes that (a) cognitive ability influences health-related decision making and that (b) decision making influences health. While it may be difficult to directly empirically assess the causal effects of cognitive ability upon health, in general, these ‘reasons for effects’ provide extra targets for empirical study (Rosenbaum, 2005, 2020). A causal theory may fail at the first step, if no link between intermediate factors can be shown. For instance, one may discard a hypothesis that blood alcohol limits reduce car fatalities by disincentivising drink-driving, if these limits have no observed effects on drivers’ drinking behaviour.
One advantage of subjecting reasons to empirical scrutiny is that certain links in a causal chain may be more amenable to causal effect estimation or to more persuasive testing than others. For instance, in their sociological study of diabetes patients, Lutfey & Freese (2005) provide compelling evidence of the difficulties individuals with lower cognitive resources have in managing the illness. From there, if one is interested in the effect of cognitive ability upon diabetes survival, one needs to establish that poor disease management negatively affects prognoses, which some might consider self-evident. Consider also papers that repeatedly show that youth unemployment is related to poorer mental health later in life (see L. Wright, 2021, for a review). This association is hypothesised to partly reflect youth unemployment having a deleterious long-term effect on labour market outcomes – i.e., individuals who were previously unemployed may have poorer mental health later because they are more likely to earn low wages at the point of measurement of mental health. One would therefore expect youth unemployment to negatively affect labour market prospects. This can be tested experimentally, albeit in a somewhat artificial way, with correspondence studies – a type of field experiment in which curricula vitae (CVs) are sent to real-world employers and interview offers recorded. These CVs are manipulated and sent randomly to determine the effect of applicant attributes on job prospects. For instance, CVs may vary in whether an individual has experienced an episode of unemployment (Eriksson & Rooth, 2014). Thus, while the main estimate of interest may be biased, one can still have good, empirically well-supported reasons for thinking a causal effect exists. Indeed, because of their expense, RCTs frequently use surrogate outcomes – outcomes preceding the true outcome of interest (e.g., blood pressure in an RCT of a drug designed to reduce cardiovascular disease mortality) – on the logic that established ‘reasons for effects’ will translate into clinical outcomes.
Reasons for effects are conceptually similar to Bradford Hill’s (1965) ‘criterion’ of “biologic plausibility” and form further pieces of evidence to assess whether an association of interest is causal. To be clear, here the object of inquiry is independent assessment of the effect of the exposure upon intermediate outcomes, or intermediate outcomes upon final outcomes or even other intermediate outcomes, in the causal chain, rather than performing a mediation analysis.
There are four issues with solely relying on ‘reasons for effects’. First, there may be several mechanisms of action – cognitive ability is proposed to influence health not just through decision making, but also by affecting socioeconomic position (Deary et al., 2021). Discounting one mechanism does not mean causal effects may not be transmitted through other pathways (Gerring, 2010), including pathways that have not yet been thought of. Second, mechanisms may counteract, producing an unknown aggregate effect – this indeterminacy may in fact be motivation for assessing total causal effects empirically in the first place. Third (and related), assessing reasons for effects does not straightforwardly translate into determining effect sizes. Rather, it most straightforwardly informs qualitative judgements about a causal effect being present or not, limiting its usefulness, especially given effects may need to be of a certain minimum size to be practically important.
Fourth, the populations used to estimate effects at each step along a causal chain may vary and results may not generalise across these. It is possible that the overall chain may be broken for the target population of interest. For instance, one may observe a causal effect of youth unemployment on short-term employment prospects and a later effect of contemporaneous income on obesity at age 50 years, but by age 50 years, any labour market disadvantage arising from an episode of youth unemployment may be compensated for (e.g., through faster within-firm job promotions once a job is found).

title: 5.19 Reasons for Effects
text:
5.19.2 Applications
Decades of research has shown that socioeconomic and psychosocial adversities are related to poorer health outcomes (Marmot, 2016). Major theories conceptualise adversities as stressors that, experienced chronically, alter and cause “wear and tear” of multiple systems within the body’s regulatory systems (cardiovascular, metabolic, immune, etc.; Delpierre et al., 2016) and lead to a state of chronic inflammation. Wear and tear is operationalised as measures of “allostatic load”, which combine measures of biomarkers across multiple systems, while chronic inflammation is most commonly indexed by elevated levels of C-reactive protein (CRP). Several studies have used data from the biomedical sweep of the NCDS to examine associations between socioeconomic (Barboza Solís et al., 2016) and psychosocial (e.g., adverse childhood experiences; Barboza Solís et al., 2015; M. Chen & Lacey, 2018) adversity and allostatic load or CRP, in an effort to provide mechanistic understanding of the association between these adversities and clinical health outcomes. While these studies show such associations, issues are that (1) chronic stress is only one pathway and (2) the same factors that may confound the association between adversity and health plausibly also confound the association between adversity and allostatic load and CRP. Counterclaims would make the same set of predictions; biases are replicated (Rosenbaum, 2001).

title: 5.19 Reasons for Effects
text:
5.19.3 Opportunities
Given the rich data collection reflected in CLS’s cohorts, data related to causal mechanisms may be available (e.g., on biomarkers, health behaviours, and so on).

title: 5.20 Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
5.20.1 Method
In Section 5.17, we discussed approaches to exploiting biases of known direction to support causal inference. These approaches incorporate information on bias qualitatively – e.g., to identify appropriate groups for study, contexts to draw data from, or to ascertain in which direction an estimate is likely to be biased. A drawback with this approach is that it does not allow the analyst to determine by how much an estimate is likely to be biased or what an unbiased estimate would plausibly look like. It is also not useful in situations where bias runs in the same direction as the anticipated causal effect or where the causal effect is hard to predict a priori – in these cases, a given estimate would be compatible with a null or opposite signed effect.
As the name suggests, quantitative bias analysis (QBA) instead incorporates or produces quantitative information on bias. QBA methods allow analysts to produce bias-corrected estimates or to ascertain the size of bias necessary to overturn a substantive result. This makes better use of the information the analyst may have – for instance, analysts may be able to make reasonable assumptions about the size of bias, as well as its direction. By providing data on the likely material effect of bias, QBA can support better decision making, enable more plausible comparisons of alternatives, and inform the direction of research resources to areas where the expected consequences of reducing uncertainty in a biasing factor would be greatest. QBA can also focus disagreement (Fox et al., 2021): instead of unproductive debates over whether an estimate is or is not biased, discussion can centre on whether bias is plausibly sufficiently strong in practice or whether it has been appropriately operationalised by the analyst performing the QBA.
The term QBA denotes a broad aim rather than a single method. An arsenal of QBA methods exists, though not all are advertised under this name – sensitivity analysis is a popular alternate term (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020; Rosenbaum, 2020; VanderWeele & Ding, 2017), though this is also sometimes unhelpfully used synonymously with ‘robustness checks’ – additional analyses performed to check incidental analytical decisions (e.g., the coding of variables) do not influence results. There are QBA methods for measurement error, selection bias, and confounding; some can be combined to deal with each within a single analysis (Fox et al., 2021). QBA methods vary in their complexity, spanning post hoc deterministic methods applied to summary data (e.g., regression coefficients) to simulation-based stochastic methods that adjust record-level data repeatedly using random draws from hypothesised distributions for biasing factors.
Methods also vary in what they produce. Some methods – like the E-Value (VanderWeele & Ding, 2017) – produce bounds on the size of bias required to entirely explain an observed association; larger bounds mean stronger – potentially implausibly strong – bias is required to explain an association absent a causal effect. Other methods – like Pattern Mixture Modelling (Leurent et al., 2018; C. D. Nguyen et al., 2025; Tompsett et al., 2018) – can produce a bias-corrected estimate reflecting the researcher’s best guess at what the causal effect is, given assumptions put into the QBA model. These methods can also be used for tipping-point type analyses to assess whether only a large degree of bias could explain an association (Y. Liu et al., 2025). Given the large number of QBA methods, what follows is a selective review.

title: 5.20 Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
There is a quantitative question. Cigarette smokers have a ninefold greater risk of developing lung cancer than nonsmokers, while over-two-pack-a-day smokers have at least a 60-fold greater risk. Any characteristic proposed as a measure of the postulated cause common to both smoking status and lung-cancer risk must therefore be at least ninefold more prevalent among cigarette smokers than among nonsmokers and at least 60-fold more prevalent among two-pack-a-day smokers. No such characteristic has yet been produced despite diligent search.
Cornfield et al. (1959)






5.20.1.1 Methods using Summary-Level Data
As discussed in Section 1, observational studies formed a major source of the evidence in the discovery of the harmful effect of smoking on lung cancer. One reason observational evidence was compelling was the size of the association between smoking and lung cancer observed. In one of the earliest quantitative bias analyses, Cornfield et al. (1959) derived lower bounds on the associations a single binary confounder must have with a binary exposure and binary outcome to fully explain an observed association between the two. Specifically, they show that the exposure-outcome association must be equal to or exceeded by both the confounder-outcome and confounder-exposure associations, rules now referred to as the ‘Cornfield conditions’.
One corollary of their formulation is that the closer the confounder-outcome association is in size to the exposure-outcome association, the stronger the confounder-exposure association must be (and vice versa). This trade-off between confounder-exposure and confounder-outcome associations necessary to explain an exposure-outcome relationship follows a simple equation and can be plotted as contours as in Figure 5.19 – see the figure caption for further details.




Figure 5.19: Graphical representation of the ‘Cornfield Conditions’ (Cornfield et al., 1959) for a binary exposure (X), outcome (Y) and confounder (Z). For a given risk ratio (RR = 2) between exposure and outcome (i.e., P(Y = 1 | X = 1)/P(Y = 1 | X = 0)) and probability Z = 1 given X = 1 (green, orange, and pink lines), the graph shows the combination of association between confounder and exposure (RR[XZ], x-axis) and confounder and outcome (RR[ZY], y-axis) required to fully explain the association. If the confounder-exposure association is weaker (e.g., RR(XZ) ↓ or P(Z = 1 | X = 1) ↓), then the confounder-outcome association must be stronger to explain the same result.



The Cornfield conditions formalise several intuitions, including:

Stronger exposure-outcome associations require a greater degree of confounding to explain results
Confounders must have at least as large a causal effect on the outcome as the observed exposure-outcome association
The strength of effect of the confounder on the outcome must be greater if the effect of the confounder on the exposure becomes weaker (and vice versa).

Using their bounds, Cornfield et al. (1959) offered an unanswerable test to sceptics of the link between smoking and cancer (among whom counted Ronald Fisher): no plausible confounding factors existed that could explain the very large association between the two.
The Cornfield conditions further formalise the intuition that there must be strong imbalance in absolute terms in the prevalence of the confounder between levels of the exposure; otherwise the confounder must have a particularly strong impact on the outcome to compensate (compare the pink, orange and green lines for a given RR(XZ) in Figure 5.19). To give an applied example, parental problematic drug use may be a confounder in the association between parental SES and childhood development, but it is (thankfully) a rare occurrence, so is unlikely to explain much of the association between the two.
The E-Value (VanderWeele & Ding, 2017), a widely used QBA method, builds upon the Cornfield conditions by making two assumptions: first, that the exposure-confounder and confounder-outcome effects are equal, and second, that the prevalence of the confounder among exposed is 100%. The E-Value is represented as a point at the intersection of the pink (P(Z = 1 | X = 1) = 1) and blue (RR(XZ) = RR(ZY)) lines in Figure 5.19. As Fox et al. (2021) and others (e.g., Poole, 2020) note, however, the assumption of complete prevalence of the confounder among the exposed is generally implausible and conservative. Fox et al. (2021) thus introduce the ‘G-Value’, which generalises the E-Value to situations where prevalence of the confounder is lower – Figure 5.19 also displays the G-Value(0.25) (intersection of green and blue lines) where the prevalence of the confounder among treated is 25%. As can be seen, the G-Value is larger than a given E-Value; the confounder has to have a stronger effect on the outcome because it is now less prevalent among the exposed group.
Though both the E-Value and G-Value allow bounds to be represented in a single scalar value, the price of this is the assumption that confounder-exposure and confounder-outcome associations are equal. This is not likely to be plausible in practice. It is instead preferable to posit values of each separately and to determine the consequences of this for bias, as enabled by drawing contours as in Figure 5.19. The utility of the Cornfield conditions and the E-Value and G-Value is that they can be used as a basis for rigorous argument about confounders, including providing a frame for reviews of existing evidence on plausible confounding variables. It is not sufficient to say a confounder exists – it needs to have particular properties. However, this does not appear to be how E-Values and the like are used in practice. In their review of the use of E-Values, Blum et al. (2020) report that few authors assessed whether confounding was likely to overturn results or even noted candidate confounders likely to be missing from analyses.
A further limitation of the E-Value concerns multiple confounders – the E-Value relates to the combined effect of these, so several confounders that are individually too weak to explain away an association may jointly do so (Ioannidis et al., 2019). This joint strength can be particularly difficult to ascertain where individual unmeasured confounders are correlated. On the other hand, the degree of residual confounding depends on the confounders that have been controlled for – some of these (e.g., age and sex) can be strongly related to unobserved confounders, and so partly operate as proxies for these variables (Greenland, 2020). Together, these issues mean the E-Value can give a too optimistic or too pessimistic view of sensitivity to confounding bias (Sjölander & Greenland, 2022).
Though developed for settings with binary variables, the E-Value can be produced for continuous variables too, using heuristics for converting standardised beta coefficients to odds ratios (Mathur et al., 2025). However, similar methods have been developed for settings with continuous outcomes, specifically. Omitted variable bias (OVB) follows a simple formula in linear regression settings: it is the product of the regression coefficient for the confounder had it been included in the regression model and the coefficient from a regression of the confounder on the exposure had it been performed.

True Model: \(Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} \cdot X + \beta_{2} \cdot Z + \varepsilon\)
Estimated Model: \(Y = \widehat{\beta_{0}} + \widehat{\beta_{1}} \cdot X + \widehat{\varepsilon}\ \)
Decomposition: \({\widehat{\beta_{1}} = \beta}_{1} + \beta_{2} \cdot \delta_{1}\ \) (True Effect + Omitted Variable Bias)
Where \(\delta_{1}\) is the solution to regression: \(Z = \delta_{0} + \delta_{1} \cdot X + \mu\)

Note, \(\delta_{1}\) is the solution to the regression of Z upon X, despite this running counter to the direction of hypothesised causality (i.e., X is dependent on Z, rather than the other way round). However, this formulation makes intuitive sense: the observed association between X and Y is equal to the causal effect of X upon Y (\(\beta_{1}\)) plus the effect of Z upon Y multiplied by the association a one-unit difference in X has with Z. This formulation has another advantage: while Z may have a large effect on X, X may have only a weak association with Z if Z explains little of the variance in X overall. Again, absolute effect size is key for driving OVB.
The OVB formula, \(\beta_{2} \cdot \delta_{1}\ \), can be visualised in a contour plot similar to the Cornfield conditions in Figure 5.19. An issue, however, is that the standard OVB formulation depends on the scales used for the exposure and outcome and so identifying appropriate literature on confounder-exposure associations may be difficult. Additionally, the formula does not easily generalise to situations with multiple confounders. To address this, Cinelli & Hazlett (2020) reparameterise OVB in terms of partial R2 (i.e., the residual variance in exposure and outcome a confounder explains after conditioning on covariates).1 With this formula, analysts can determine the required confounding associations to materially change an observed association between exposure and outcome (e.g., attenuate to the null), again assisted using contour plots.
Cinelli & Hazlett’s (2020) method is implemented in the sensemakr R package (Cinelli, Ferwerda, et al., 2024); see Figure 5.20 for an example. The sensemakr package outputs additional information to contextualise analysts’ consideration of whether unobserved confounders can plausibly explain results. This includes a ‘robustness value’ (for both the point estimate and lower confidence interval), which – analogous to the E-Value – specifies the minimum partial R2 that would be required to attenuate the observed association to the null, setting this equal for the partial R2 for both the confounder-exposure and confounder-outcome associations. It also includes information on the associations between observed confounders and exposure and outcome. For instance, in their working example on the effect of experiencing violence during the Darfur war on attitudes to peace (displayed in Figure 5.20), the authors benchmark the effect of the supposed confounder (whether the respondent lived in the centre of a village) against sex, showing that centre would need to have multiple times stronger association with outcome and treatment than sex to explain results (‘[1-3]x female’ sit below the red-dashed line of null association in Figure 5.20). This is helpful because, while not all confounders may be observed, major ones may be. Using the latter to calibrate expectations can therefore help interpretation of the QBA analysis.




Figure 5.20: Contour plot of a Cinelli & Hazlett (2020) type sensitivity analysis. Drawn from the Cinelli & Hazlett (2020) running example examining the potential for confounding in the association between experiencing violence during the Darfur war and attitudes to peace. The authors hypothesise that this association is confounded by whether the survey respondent lived in the centre of the village (more likely to be victimised) or at the periphery, and use the variable ‘female’ to contextualise discussion of whether confounding would be sufficient to reduce the observed association (0.097) to the null. If the confounder were to have 3 times the strength of association with violence victimisation and peace attitudes as female does, this would still not be sufficient to reduce the point estimate to the null (3x female [0.03]). Cinelli & Hazlett (2020) type sensitivity analyses can be performed with the sensemakr R package (Cinelli, Ferwerda, et al., 2024), which also outputs ‘robustness value’ statistics.



Oster (2019) provides another formulation of bias from omitted variables that, like Cinelli & Hazlett (2020), uses observable information from regressions including observed confounders, but also utilising information on the “stability” of coefficients when adding observed confounders to models. Oster’s solution parameterises OVB as a function of four observable and two unobserved quantities: the model R2 from (a) a “short” regression of Y on X (denoted \(\dot{R}\)), (b) a regression of Y on X plus observed confounders (\(\widetilde{R}\)), and (c) a regression of Y on X plus observed and unobserved confounders, would it be possible to run this (\(R_{MAX}\)); coefficients for X in regressions (a) (\(\dot{\beta}\)) and (b) (\(\widetilde{\beta}\)); and a parameter, δ, capturing “proportional selection” – the relative association unobserved confounders have with treatment relative to observed confounders (by necessity, this is also unobserved).
\[\beta^{*} \approx \widetilde{\beta} - \delta \cdot (\dot{\beta} - \widetilde{\beta}) \cdot \frac{R_{MAX} - \widetilde{R}}{\widetilde{R} - \dot{R}}\]
… where \(\beta^{*}\) is the coefficient on X from a regression of Y upon X plus observed and unobserved confounders. δ captures imbalance in the unobserved confounders across exposure levels (though as a function of imbalance in the observed confounders) and \(R_{MAX} - \widetilde{R}\) captures the impact of confounders on the outcome. All else being equal, greater proportional selection and larger effects of the confounders on the outcome will bias coefficients more.
Using this formula, one can reason about the combinations of \(R_{MAX}\) and \(\delta\) that would reduce \(\beta^{*}\) to an important value (e.g., the null, \(\beta^{*} = 0\)) or to determine what plausible values of \(R_{MAX}\) and \(\delta\) would imply for \(\beta^{*}\). A key development in Oster’s (2019) paper is that she identifies heuristics for \(R_{MAX}\) and δ by applying her formula to the results of RCTs, among other analyses. Oster suggests values of \(R_{MAX} = \min(1,\ 1.3 \cdot \widetilde{R})\) and δ = 1 as sensible bounds.
The Cinelli & Hazlett (2020), Oster (2019), E-Value, G-Value, and Cornfield Condition methods each exploit summary-level data and are referred to as ‘simple sensitivity analysis’ techniques. Each is generally used to evaluate bias from unobserved confounding, though can be extended to assess other types of bias, including selection bias or bias from violations of the assumptions of instrumental variables analysis (Mathur et al., 2025; Mellon, 2025). Other QBA methods to obtain bounds that use summary-level data exist, including for (e.g.) bias from differential measurement error (VanderWeele & Li, 2019). We will not cover these methods further here (for more, see Fox et al., 2021).
Another summary-level approach that has been used extensively to account for bias is regression calibration (Keogh & White, 2014), though in this case the purpose is to provide a bias-corrected estimate. Regression calibration applies where there is regression dilution – classical measurement error in the exposure, which would bias the estimate, most commonly towards the null. This attenuation is predictable: in linear regression, the observed association will be attenuated in proportion to the measurement’s reliability (i.e., the correlation between two independent measurements of the same variable). The correction is therefore straightforward – one can divide the estimated coefficient by assumed reliability – though more complex ways of incorporating this information can be performed (e.g., by treating reliability as an uncertain estimated quantity with its own distribution). However, this approach will generate biased results when there are unobserved or mis-measured confounders (Phillips & Smith, 1991; Smith & Phillips, 1996) as the uncorrected estimate will be subject to other biases, rather than just the regression dilution.


5.20.1.2 Methods using Record-Level Data
Another popular method that corrects for measurement error but instead uses record-level data is Simulation and Extrapolation (SIMEX; Cook & Stefanski, 1994). In SIMEX, analyses are re-run adding random measurement error to (continuous) variables.2 Progressively increasing error and then drawing a line of best fit through estimates, before extrapolating back, allows one to predict a situation where no measurement error exists (see Figure 5.21). SIMEX can handle situations where it is confounders, rather than the exposure itself, that are subject to measurement error, but accurate extrapolation requires (a) correct assumptions about the reliability of the initial measurement (which determines how far a line of best fit should be drawn backwards to reflect a situation of no measurement error) and (b) use of an appropriate extrapolation function, which is an inherently uncertain choice.




Figure 5.21: Results of an example SIMEX analysis. SIMEX consists of two steps. First, one reruns analyses, progressively adding random measurement error to the variable hypothesised to be subject to measurement error, in proportion to the amount of error anticipated in the raw variable already. Next, one estimates a line of best fit through the estimates obtained from Step 1 (blue line) and then extrapolates this line back to the point where no measurement error would exist to obtain the measurement-error corrected estimate (orange line for x-axis = 0).



Systematic or differential measurement error can be corrected for via simulation using record-level data (Gallop & Weschle, 2019; Pina-Sánchez et al., 2023; L. Wright, Ploubidis, et al., 2024). For instance, to account for ‘mode effects’ (a type of measurement error where responses vary systematically by mode; Section 2.2.5) in a mixed-mode study in which participants are not randomised to mode, external information on mode effects can be used to simulate values had participants responded in a single mode. For example, experimental evidence may indicate that individuals report 0.2 SD better mental health when responding via telephone rather than web (Goodman et al., 2022; Tomova, Silverwood, & Wright, 2026a). Subtracting 0.2 SD from observed mental health for those in the telephone mode would therefore provide (estimated) counterfactual values which can be used when fitting the substantive model of interest. This approach is very flexible – it can handle multiplicative, or other non-additive, errors and differential measurement errors (Pina-Sánchez et al., 2023), e.g., by incorporating different sized errors according to participant characteristics. The process can be repeated to explore sensitivity of the findings to different magnitudes of measurement error.
Another record-level simulation-based method is Pattern Mixture Modelling (PMM; Leurent et al., 2018; C. D. Nguyen et al., 2025; Tompsett et al., 2018). PMM is used to correct for violations in the Missing at Random Assumption used in multiple imputation (Section 5.4) – i.e., for selection bias. Post hoc adjustment is used to amend imputed values – for instance, if one anticipates missing values to in fact be 0.3 SD lower than as imputed, imputed values can simply be corrected to reflect this and analyses otherwise run as usual (i.e., with estimates pooled with Rubin’s Rules). As with simulation for non-random measurement error, the complexity of the PMM procedure can be increased – for instance, by choosing more complex patterns of MNAR (e.g., larger violations in some groups than in others). Corrections to MNAR should be performed within the ‘Gibbs sampler’ – i.e., within the imputation procedure, rather than once the imputed datasets have been created – so that chained equations models reflect beliefs about MNAR. However, this can be hard to code (some limited functionality exists in the mice R package; C. D. Nguyen et al., 2025) and is more computationally demanding to run as it requires separate imputations for each MNAR assumption posited.
Simulation-based methods can incorporate assumptions on biases stochastically, rather than use single deterministic values – for instance, by reflecting uncertainty as distributions and repeating the simulation using draws. Fox et al. (2021) provide advice on turning beliefs about the size of biases into statistical distributions from which to draw. Often, it may be easier to rule out particular-sized biases, than rule biases in (for instance, mode effects are unlikely to exceed 0.5 SD, but may be within the range 0-0.2 SD; Tomova, Silverwood, & Wright, 2026a). In this case, simulations can be run in a tipping-point-like fashion, or large and implausible biases used to assess whether implausible levels of bias would be insufficient to change substantive conclusions.
Readers interested in QBA can see the textbook by Fox et al. (2021), which includes recommendations for performing and reporting QBA (see also Lash et al., 2014). However, note, as epidemiologists, the authors focus their exposition and examples on cases with binary exposures and outcomes. For comprehensive discussion of QBA for measurement error, specifically, see Keogh et al. (2020) and Shaw et al. (2020).

title: 5.20 Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
5.20.2 Applications
Several papers have calculated E-Values as part of analyses of CLS data (see, e.g., Gondek, Bann, Brown, et al., 2021; Metherell et al., 2023; Moulton et al., 2023; Ning et al., 2021). For example, Gondek et al. (2021) use the E-Values to understand the potential consequences of bias in an analysis of early mental health and later problematic alcohol use using data from the NCDS and BCS70. Though the E-Values were small, they note a paucity of existing evidence on the strength of the confounders they hypothesise, making it difficult to evaluate plausibility. Nevertheless, this evidence may appear in future, so performing the QBA provides information that may still be of use to future readers.
Dräger et al. (2025) perform an Oster (2019) type QBA of the association between school absences and attainment at GCSE using data from the MCS. They show that many of their results are robust to an assumption about relative selection on observables and explanatory power of observables for their outcome. However, this assumption is not well justified and is only compared against a much more conservative assumption, which produces prima facie implausible results for some model specifications.
Bann et al. (2023) use PMM when assessing cross-cohort differences in the association between height and cognitive ability using data from NCDS, BCS70 and MCS, given different levels of non-response and missingness in each of these studies. They perform a tipping-point-style analysis to assess whether differences in missingness mechanisms would be required to explain results.

title: 5.20 Quantitative Bias Analysis
text:
5.20.3 Opportunities
As QBA methods are designed to be used to handle situations where data are missing (e.g., on confounders), they do not make demands upon existing data. Therefore, there is ample opportunity to use these in CLS’s cohorts. That said, as data on many major confounders are available, Cinelli & Hazlett (2020) type QBA may be especially compelling as these confounders can be used to calibrate assessments of unobserved confounding.

title: 6 Discussion
text:
Causal inference is one of the central goals of quantitative health and social science, but also one of its most difficult to attain. The foregoing has shown that there may be ample opportunities for making causal inferences using CLS cohort data and multiple different methods and broad approaches to utilise when doing so.
Viewed individually, each of these methods stands or falls on the validity of their assumptions. Validity depends on the specific situation to which the methods are being applied and usually cannot be ascertained directly. Determining whether assumptions are valid – or close enough to be valid as to still be useful – requires knowledge of a specific research domain and an ability to synthesise evidence and construct arguments, especially when realising that one’s readers need convincing, too (‘The first principle is that you must not fool yourself—and you are the easiest person to fool’; Feynman, 1974).1 Argumentation about whether assumptions are met is necessary regardless of whether model-based approaches (is residual variation as-if random?), design-based approaches (does this IV meet the exclusion restriction?), or Elaborate Theory approaches (is the mechanism of action weaker in this setting, as hypothesised?) are used.
Nevertheless, no single study is likely to be perfect. An RCT may accurately balance treated and controls, but available measures may be inadequate, diluting estimates, or the intervention may be too narrow to generalise directly to situations of interest, necessitating the application of theory to justify any generalisation, perhaps informed by other empirical results (Deaton & Cartwright, 2018). Viewed as one component of a wider literature, however, imperfect studies can still make a contribution. For instance, a study may reduce uncertainty about a hypothesis by testing the effect of a confounder not yet considered in other studies. More formally, one study may have biases unrelated to those in another study, possibly because it used a different study design (e.g., a quasi-experiment rather than statistical control). If these studies nevertheless converge upon the same result, this is stronger evidence of the reliability of the causal effect estimate (Gutierrez et al., 2025; Lawlor et al., 2016). Such “triangulation” can involve evidence of different characters that may even, at first glance, appear only tangentially related. Part of the evidence for the effect of smoking on cancer involved the results of prospective cohort studies (Doll & Hill, 1954), but it also included ecological studies of societal trends in lung cancer mortality, lung autopsies of smokers who died from other causes, and experimental evidence from animal models (Cornfield et al., 1959). Added more recently is evidence from individuals with particular genetic disorders, who provide indirect evidence for later steps in a hypothesised biological pathway, which smoking is thought to precipitate (Rosenbaum, 2015).
Rosenbaum (2015) following Haack (2009) likens such reasoning to completing a “causal crossword”. Considered in isolation, each piece of evidence supporting a causal inference may be weak, but together lend mutual support, as two guesses intersecting with the same letter do for crossword players. Meditating on this and advice to “Make your theories elaborate”, Rosenbaum (2015, p. 209) concludes “If you took [the advice to make your theories elaborate] seriously, then you would ask of each new study what it contributes to the currently incomplete, partly penciled-in puzzle. You would welcome the completion of a new entry, even a small entry, compatible with the current tentative completion. You would also welcome a compelling new entry that challenged some current entries. You would welcome the suggestion that a particular entry is mistaken and constitutes a barrier to correct completion of the puzzle. A pencil and an eraser would be two tools of equal importance.” As with a crossword, two entries may not intersect – may be only tangentially related – but still contribute to the completed whole.
Completing causal crosswords would require quantitative researchers to clearly state their goals and the quantity they are trying to learn with their statistical analysis (the estimand; Lundberg et al., 2021). Several authors have offered powerful critiques of prevailing norms in non-experimental sciences against stating one’s causal ambitions and to instead rely on imprecise euphemisms such as “association” and “relationship” (Dahabreh & Bibbins-Domingo, 2024; Grosz et al., 2020; Hernán, 2018b; Labrecque & Kezios, 2026) – euphemisms, we should say, we have been guilty of using in our own work – and to also claim one is only interested in description or prediction, when in fact that would motivate different analytical choices to those chosen (Grosz et al., 2020; Labrecque & Kezios, 2026). Hiding one’s aims makes productive disagreement more challenging and holds back cumulative scientific progress (Dahabreh & Bibbins-Domingo, 2024; Grosz et al., 2020). It also enables suboptimal practices, such as controlling for mediators in statistical models (Labrecque, 2023) and formulating poorly conceptualised research questions where the intervention is not well-defined (Hernán, 2018b). This taboo has led to the curious practice of researchers cautioning against causal interpretations in their studies while, at the same time, assuming causality when drawing policy and action recommendations from their work (Bann et al., 2025; Haber et al., 2022) – a practice that has been referred to as “Schrödinger’s inference” (Tennant & Murray, 2021).
Authors critiquing current practices have offered several recommendations for the conduct and reporting of studies that aim to generate evidence for causal inference (Dahabreh & Bibbins-Domingo, 2024; Grosz et al., 2020; Haber et al., 2022; Hernán, 2018b; Labrecque & Kezios, 2026). For instance, Hernán (2018b) argues causal language should be used throughout papers except in the results section, where the language of association should instead be used, reflecting the nature of statistical estimates, which only with discussion in methods and other sections can be provided with a causal interpretation. Others have produced “roadmaps” for designing causal inference studies – checklists and processes going from defining a coherent research question and theoretical estimands to choice of appropriate statistical estimator, quantitative bias analyses and falsification tests, and judicious interpretation of results (Dang et al., 2023; Dang & Balzer, 2023; Petersen & van der Laan, 2014).
All of which is to say: beyond simply being a set of methods, causal inference requires an ability to ask good questions, to synthesise disparate lines of evidence to come to reasoned judgements, to be transparent about the plausibility of underlying assumptions, and to be honest about uncertainty. CLS data have many attributes that can support causal inference, but the data alone are not enough.
